problems.title: Dimerization of Acetic Acid
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Dimerization of Acetic Acid

Ethanoic acid or acetic acid ($\ce{CH3COOH}$) is partially dimerized into dimers in the vapor phase. At a total pressure of $0.200\,\mathrm{atm}$, ethanoic acid is 92.0% dimerized at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. By increasing the temperature to $318\,\mathrm{K}$, the degree of dimerization is lowered, with $K_p = 37.3$.

1.1) Calculate the enthalpy and the entropy changes for the reaction, assuming that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ do not vary with temperature.

1.2) Applying the Le Chatelier's principle, an increase of pressure should (select one correct answer)

• ◯ favor the dimerization.
• ◯ not favor the dimerization.

1.3) Continued from question 1.2, the extent of dimerization (select one correct answer)

• ◯ decreases with increasing the temperature.
• ◯ increases with increasing the temperature.

problems.title: Solubility of Calcite
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Solubility of Calcite

Calcite is a stable form of calcium carbonate ($\ce{CaCO3}$). The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) is decreased with increasing temperature; $K_{sp}$ are $9.50\times10^{-9}$ and $2.30\times10^{-9}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, respectively. Estimate the enthalpy change for the solubility process of calcite.

problems.title: Expansion of Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics of Liquid Mixing
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Expansion of Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics of Liquid Mixing

3.1) A quantity of $0.10\,\mathrm{mol}$ of an ideal gas $\mathbf{A}$ initially at $22.2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is expanded from $0.200\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ to $2.42\,\mathrm{dm^3}$. Calculate the values of work ($w$), heat ($q$), internal energy change ($\Delta U$), entropy change of the system ($\Delta S_{sys}$), entropy change of the surroundings ($\Delta S_{surr}$), and total entropy change ($\Delta S_{univ}$) if the process is carried out isothermally and irreversibly against an external pressure of $1.00\,\mathrm{atm}$.

3.2) If $3.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathbf{A}$ is condensed into liquid state and is mixed with $5.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ of liquid $\mathbf{B}$, calculate the changes in entropy and Gibbs free energy upon such mixing at $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. This mixture can be assumed to be ideal.

problems.title: Vibrational Frequency of a Diatomic Molecule
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Vibrational Frequency of a Diatomic Molecule

For the vibrational motion of a diatomic molecule using a harmonic oscillator model, the allowed vibrational energy levels can be described as

$$E_\upsilon = \left(\upsilon + \frac{1}{2}\right)h\nu \qquad ;\ \upsilon = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

where $\upsilon$ is the vibrational quantum number and $\nu$ is the vibrational frequency. The vibrational frequency represented by the harmonic oscillator model is

$$\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}\,,\ \text{where } k \text{ is the force constant and } \mu \text{ is the reduced mass.}$$

For molecule CX, where X is an unknown atom, the vibrational absorption energy from vibrational ground state to the first vibrational excited state is $2170.0\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and the force constant is $1.903\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}$.

4.1) Find the reduced mass of CX in amu.

4.2) What is atom X?

problems.title: Water-gas-shift Reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Water-gas-shift Reaction

In a drive toward cleaner energy production, fuel cell holds great promise because of its capability of generating electricity directly from chemical reactions with environmentally-benign byproducts. In particular, for hydrogen fuel cell, the only waste produced by the device is just water.

In order to use fuel cell at an industrial scale, continuous production of hydrogen that directly feeds into a fuel cell module is required. One option to mass produce hydrogen for this purpose is the conversion of hydrocarbon fuel using hot steam. However, this kind of reaction often leads to mixed products that consist of $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{CO2}$, and $\ce{CO}$. Moreover, $\ce{CO}$ is not only hazardous to human health, but it also degrades fuel cell's active material. The reversible water-gas-shift (WGS) reaction, $\ce{CO + H2O <=> CO2 + H2}$, provides one method of converting toxic $\ce{CO}$ into $\ce{CO2}$ and useful $\ce{H2}$. The efficiency of this reaction strongly depends on the solid catalyst used.

5.1) In one process, an equimolar mixture of $\ce{CO}$ and steam is continuously passed to a WGS reactor containing catalyst at atmospheric pressure and $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assuming that the catalyst is 95.0% efficient in converting the reactants into the products and that the reaction in the reactor is approximately at equilibrium in this condition, estimate the free energy change for this reaction?

5.2) Now assume that a large surface of catalyst is initially available to reacting molecules, and the rate of reaction is measured immediately at the onset of the reaction. Below are the initial rates measured at different initial pressures of $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2O}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Trial} & P_{CO},\ \mathrm{atm} & P_{H_2O},\ \mathrm{atm} & dP_{H_2}/dt,\ \mathrm{atm\,s^{-1}} \\ \hline 1 & 0.10 & 0.90 & 4.0\times10^{-4} \\ 2 & 0.15 & 0.85 & 5.6\times10^{-4} \\ 3 & 0.25 & 0.75 & 8.2\times10^{-4} \\ 4 & 0.28 & 0.72 & \text{X} \end{array}$$

What is X?

5.3) In another condition where the pressure of hydrogen is found to be $0.50\,\mathrm{atm}$, $-dP_{H_2}/dt = 3.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{atm\,s^{-1}}$. According to the information given in questions 5.1, 5.2, and this question, estimate the rate of hydrogen production when the pressures in the reactor of $\ce{CO}$, $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{CO2}$, and $\ce{H2}$ are 0.14, 0.14, 0.36, and $0.36\,\mathrm{atm}$, respectively. (Give your answer to three significant figures.)

5.4) Calculate the Gibbs free energy change for the conditions described in question 5.3.

5.5) Surface coverage, $\theta$, is an important kinetics parameter, especially for reactions on solid surfaces. It can be defined as the number of adsorbed molecules on a surface divided by the total number of adsorbing sites on that surface. For WGS, after the adsorption of $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ on the catalyst's surface, a carbonyl intermediate can be formed, which then dissociates to give surface-bound $\ce{CO2}$ and H atom. If the carbon dioxide is produced at a rate of $1.0\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{molecules\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ with associated rate constant of $2.0\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{molecules\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$, what is the value of $\theta$ for this intermediate?

problems.title: Camphor in Benzene

Problem 6. Camphor in Benzene

The vapor pressure of pure benzene ($\ce{C6H6}$) is $100\,\mathrm{torr}$ at $26.1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the vapor pressure and the freezing point of a solution containing $24.6\,\mathrm{g}$ of camphor ($\ce{C10H16O}$) dissolved in $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of benzene. The density of benzene is $0.877\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. The freezing point and the cryoscopic constant ($K_f$) of pure benzene are $5.50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $5.12\,^\circ\mathrm{C\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively.

problems.title: Decomposition of Nitrous Oxide
problems.problem:
Problem 8. Decomposition of Nitrous Oxide

Nitrous oxide decomposes exothermically into nitrogen and oxygen, at a temperature of approximately $565\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

$$\ce{2N2O -> 2N2(g) + O2(g)}$$

This reaction follows the second-order kinetics when carried out entirely in the gas phase.

8.1) If the reaction is initiated with $[\ce{N2O}]$ equal to $0.108\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, what will its concentration be after $1250\,\mathrm{s}$ have elapsed at $565\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? The rate constant for the second order decomposition of $\ce{N2O}$ is $1.10\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ at this temperature.

8.2) The activation energy for the second order reaction at $565\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $234\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. What is the rate constant for the reaction at $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

problems.title: Avogadro's Number
problems.problem:
Problem 9. Avogadro's Number

An internationally accepted procedure is as follows.

We start with a "perfect" sphere of pure $\ce{^{28}Si}$ isotope. The weight of this sphere is W g. The volume V of the sphere is found from the accurate measurement of the diameter of the sphere. The unit cell of a crystal of silicon is a "diamond cubic lattice", i.e. a face-centered unit cell but with 4 Si atoms inside the cube. The length of the unit cell can be determined precisely from X-ray crystallographic measurements of a single crystal of $\ce{^{28}Si}$ isotope.

The experimental data are as follow:

Weight of sphere, W: $1000.064\,543(15)\,\mathrm{g}$

Volume of sphere: $431.049\,110(10)\,\mathrm{cm^3}$

Length of unit cell, $\alpha$: $543.099\,619(20)\,\mathrm{pm}$

Atomic weight of $\ce{^{28}Si}$, A: $27.976\,970\,029(23)\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$

Number of Si atoms in unit cell, n:

9.1) Write down the equation for calculating Avogadro's number $N_\mathrm{A}$ in terms of the parameters.

9.2) How many silicon atoms are in the unit cell?

9.3) Calculate Avogadro's number using the above data. Give answer to 7 significant figures.

problems.title: Amperometric Titration: Titration of Pb²⁺ with Cr₂O₇²⁻
problems.problem:
Problem 11. Amperometric Titration: Titration of $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ with $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$

Amperometry is one of the sensitive electroanalytical methods used for quantitative determination of electroactive species. A working electrode is held at a certain voltage (vs reference electrode) that is suitable for oxidation or reduction of an analyte. The analyte will be oxidized or reduced at the surface of the working electrode and the current passing through this electrode is measured. This current is directly proportional to the concentration of analyte and is used for quantitative purpose. It can be used for detection of titration end-point. In this example amperometric detection was used for monitoring a titration progress. $20\text{-}\mathrm{cm^3}$ of lead (II) ion solution was titrated with $0.0020\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ potassium dichromate solution. A dropping mercury electrode (DME) was used as a working electrode and the potential of $-0.8\,\mathrm{V}$ (vs SCE, saturated calomel electrode) was applied to this electrode for enabling the reduction of lead (II) ion and dichromate ion with potassium nitrate as supporting electrolyte. The current-volume of titrant data are shown in Table 1.

Reference: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis, 5th edition, John Wiley & Sons, New York, pp630.

Table 1. Titration data

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Volume of } 0.0020\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} \text{ dichromate } (\mathrm{cm^3}) & \text{Current (microampere)} \\ \hline 0.00 & 9.8 \\ 2.00 & 8.0 \\ 4.00 & 6.0 \\ 6.00 & 4.0 \\ 8.00 & 2.2 \\ 10.00 & 3.5 \\ 12.00 & 5.5 \\ 14.00 & 7.6 \\ 16.00 & 9.5 \end{array}$$

11.1) Plot the titration curve and find the titration end point. (The point where the change in the slope of titration curve occurs)

11.2) Write the titration reaction.

11.3) Calculate the concentration of lead (II).

problems.title: Conductometric Titration
problems.problem:
Problem 12. Conductometric Titration

Conductivity detector is an electrochemical technique which applies alternating current (AC) signal to two identical electrodes. The applied AC signal induces ions to move in solution and switching of polarity of the AC voltage avoids electrolytic reaction at the electrode. As a result, the mobility of ions in solution relates to the conductivity of ions in solution. Conductivity probe was used in acid-base titration of $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $\ce{HCl}$ vs $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{NaOH}$. The conductivity signal was recorded during $\ce{NaOH}$ addition. The conductometric titration setup is shown in Fig 1. When standard $\ce{NaOH}$ solution was dropped under gravity force to the titration cell at 3 drops per second and the conductivity value from conductometer recorded, the plot of conductivity of solution vs titration time is shown in Fig 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-12-fig1.png

Fig 1. Conductometric titration setup.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-12-fig2.png

Fig 2. Plot of conductivity of an initial $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $\ce{HCl}$ vs titration time.

12.1) Explain why the slope of titration curve before and after the turning point is different.

12.2) Calculate the concentration of $\ce{HCl}$, if the volume of $\ce{NaOH}$ of each drop is $0.029\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and the turning point is at 108 second.

problems.title: Titration of Cu and Zn in Metal Alloy
problems.problem:
Problem 13. Titration of Cu and Zn in Metal Alloy

A metal alloy which contains mainly Cu and Zn was analyzed for its metal content. An alloy sample of $2.300\,\mathrm{g}$ was placed in a $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ erlenmeyer flask. To this flask, $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of mixed acid (concentrated nitric acid and concentrated hydrochloric acid) was added in a fume hood for dissolution of the alloy. The resulting solution was transferred quantitatively into $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask and adjusted to volume with deionized water.

A $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of sample solution was adjusted to pH 5.5 and titrated with $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ EDTA solution using 1-(2-pyridinezao)-2-naphthol or PAN as indicator. The indicator changed color when $33.40\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ EDTA was added to the sample solution.

Another $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of sample solution was adjusted to neutral pH and mixed with excess $\ce{KI}$. The mixture was then filtered and the resulting solution was titrated against $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ sodium thiosulfate using starch solution as indicator. The titration required $29.35\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ sodium thiosulfate to reach the endpoint. Note: $K_{SP(\ce{CuI})} = 1.1\times10^{-12}$

13.1) Write the oxidative dissolution reaction(s) of an alloy with nitric acid and hydrochloric acid.

13.2) Determine the %w/w of Cu and Zn in alloy.

problems.title: Spectrophotometric Determination of Iron
problems.problem:
Problem 14. Spectrophotometric Determination of Iron

To study in vitro gastric digestion of iron, the following procedure is carried out. Dried and homogeneously ground supplement tablet of $0.4215\,\mathrm{g}$ is accurately weighed, mixed with $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water, adjusted to pH 2.0 with $6\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{HCl}$, $0.375\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of pepsin solution (16% w/v) added, and adjusted to $12.50\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ with $0.01\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{HCl}$. This mixture was quantitatively transferred into a dialysis bag of a fixed volume, which is further immersed for 2 hours in a $20.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ solution containing $0.01\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{HCl}$. Iron released by gastric digestion is dialyzed until the concentration of iron inside and outside the dialysis bag are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-14-fig1.png

To determine the gastric digestible iron from the supplement tablet, colorimetric measurement after complex formation between ferrous ion (M) and complexing agent (L) is carried out at pH 5.0. The resulting $\mathrm{ML_3}$ complex exhibits light absorption at $520\,\mathrm{nm}$, whereas M and L do not absorb light at this particular wavelength. Within the visible wavelength region, ferrous ion (M) does not absorb light, the complex ML absorbs light at X nm with the molar absorptivity of $50\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$, and the complex $\mathrm{ML_2}$ absorbs light at Y nm with the molar absorptivity of $200\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$.

14.1) The stepwise constants, $K_1$, $K_2$ and $K_3$, refer to the formation of the complexes one step at a time.

(i) At equilibrium, the absorbance of the solution (in 1.0-cm cuvette) at X nm is 0.400. This solution also contains $1\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of M and $2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of L. Calculate the stepwise formation constant of ML ($K_1$).

(ii) Then, L is added into the solution. At equilibrium, the absorbance of the solution (in 1.0-cm cuvette) at Y nm is 0.400. This solution also contains $2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of ML and $2\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of L. Calculate the stepwise formation constant of $\mathrm{ML_2}$ ($K_2$).

(iii) In an excess of L, all of iron is in the form of $\mathrm{ML_3}$.

Consider the following table:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} [\mathrm{M}],\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} & [\mathrm{L}],\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} & \text{Abs (at 520 nm), pathlength (b) = 1 cm} \\ \hline 6.25\times10^{-5} & 2.20\times10^{-2} & 0.750 \\ 3.25\times10^{-5} & 9.25\times10^{-5} & 0.360 \end{array}$$

a) Calculate the molar absorptivity ($\varepsilon$) of $\mathrm{ML_3}$ complex

b) Calculate the overall formation constant ($K_f$) of $\mathrm{ML_3}$ complex

c) Calculate the stepwise formation constant ($K_3$) of the complex

14.2) The CHN analysis shows that the complexing agent (L) contains 80% C, 4.44% H, and 15.56% N. The molar mass of this compound is $180\,\mathrm{g}$. Determine the molecular formula of L.

14.3) The $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ complexes, ML, $\mathrm{ML_2}$ and $\mathrm{ML_3}$, adopt the octahedral structure (assume perfect octahedral geometry for each isomer of these three complexes). Sketch the d-orbital splitting diagram for $\mathrm{ML_3}$. Draw all possible isomers of $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ complexes. Order the magnitudes of $\Delta_\mathrm{o}$ (crystal field splitting) of these three complexes and explain. (Spectrochemical series: $\ce{I-} < \ce{Br-} < \ce{Cl-} \approx \ce{SCN-} < \ce{F-} \approx \text{urea} < \ce{ONO-} \approx \ce{OH-} < \ce{H2O} < \ce{NCS-} < \text{pyridine} \approx \ce{NH3} < \text{en} < \text{bipy} < o\text{-phen} < \ce{NO2-} < \ce{CN-} \approx \ce{CO}$)

14.4) To determine the dialyzable iron concentration (iron outside the dialysis bag), $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the solution outside the dialysis bag is added with a reducing agent to ensure that all of dissolved iron is in the ferrous ion form. Then, the solution is adjusted to the suitable pH, followed by addition of excess amount of complexing agent (L) and deionized water added to make up the volume to $50.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ in a volumetric flask. The absorbance measured at $520\,\mathrm{nm}$ is 0.550. Calculate the concentration of dialyzable iron (in unit of $\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$).

14.5) Presume all of the iron in the supplement tablet is completely digestible in the gastric condition. Determine in mg the iron in $1.0000\,\mathrm{g}$ of supplement tablet.

Problem 23. Natural Chelator from Shrimp Shell

Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide composed of $\beta$-(1-4)-linked D-glucosamine (deacetylated unit) and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (acetylated unit). It is made by treating the chitin shells of shrimp or other crustaceans with a strong base, like sodium hydroxide. The deacetylation of chitin by a strong base yields partially-acetylated chitosan as shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-23-fig1.png

Chitosan can be used for a variety of purposes like helping plants to fight off fungal infections, preventing spoilage in wine, helping deliver drugs through the skin, being applied to reduce bleeding, and as an antibacterial agent. In the environmental aspect, chitosan can be used as an effective metal ion adsorbent. The adsorption capacities of chitosan for Cu(II), Hg(II), Pb(II) and Zn(II) are 79.94, 109.55, 37.2, $47.15\,\mathrm{mg\,(g\ chitosan)^{-1}}$, respectively.

23.1) Suggest the preferred binding sites in completely-deacetylated chitosan for metal ion.

The selectivity of chitosan towards $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ can be increased by modification with $\ce{CS2}$ yielding partially modified chitosan (PMCS) as in the structure below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-23-fig2.png

To increase the sensitivity of the chitosan toward metal ion, the dye like meso-tetra(p-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin is chemically bonded with chitosan matrix. After the two acidic protons are removed, the four nitrogen atoms will bind with metal ion. The two axial sites of the metal ion normally bind with water molecules yielding the octahedral complex. Problem 1. Synthesis of hydrogen cyanide

Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) is a colourless liquid with a characteristic almond-like odour. It can be produced when sufficient energy is supplied to numerous systems containing hydrogen, nitrogen, and carbon. Today, only the processes starting from hydrocarbons and ammonia are of economic importance. Two main HCN production processes are:

• Degussa (BMA) process: $\ce{CH4(g) + NH3(g) -> HCN(g) + 3 H2(g)}$

• Andrussow process: $\ce{CH4(g) + NH3(g) + 3/2 O2(g) -> HCN(g) + 3 H2O(g)}$

Both processes take place at temperatures above $1\,000\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at near standard pressure. Both of them require the use of special platinum catalysts.

1.1 Calculate a change in enthalpy $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H_\mathrm{m}$ at $1\,500\,\mathrm{K}$ for the reactions which take place in the Degussa process (BMA process) and in the Andrussow process, respectively. Use the data on the enthalpy of formation $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H_\mathrm{m}$ given in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Compound} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H_\mathrm{m}(1\,500\,\mathrm{K}),\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{CH4(g)} & -90.3 \\ \ce{NH3(g)} & -56.3 \\ \ce{HCN(g)} & 129.0 \\ \ce{H2O(g)} & -250.1 \\ \ce{H2(g)} & 0 \\ \ce{O2(g)} & 0 \end{array}$$

1.2 Which process (Degussa BMA or Andrussow) requires the use of an external heater to keep the reaction system at $1\,500\,\mathrm{K}$? Why?

1.3 Calculate the equilibrium constant $K$ of the reaction which takes place in the Degussa process (BMA process) at the temperatures of $1\,500\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1\,600\,\mathrm{K}$. The standard change in Gibbs free energy for this reaction at $1\,500\,\mathrm{K}$ is $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G_\mathrm{m}(1\,500\,\mathrm{K}) = -112.3\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Assume that the reaction enthalpy at $1\,500\,\mathrm{K}$ is constant over a temperature range from $1\,500\,\mathrm{K}$ to $1\,600\,\mathrm{K}$. Is the result in accordance with Le Chatelier's principle?

1.4 Referring to the Le Chatelier's principle, estimate whether the equilibrium constant $K$ of the reaction in the Andrussow process increases or decreases when the temperature changes from $1\,500\,\mathrm{K}$ to $1\,600\,\mathrm{K}$.

problems.title: Thermochemistry of rocket fuels
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Thermochemistry of rocket fuels

Common rocket engines that power spacecraft used for the transportation of space probes to Earth's orbit or to leave its gravitational field rely on simple nitrogen-based fuels. Methylhydrazine and 1,1-dimethylhydrazine (also known as unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine) are commonly used in combination with nitrogen dioxide (or fuming nitric acid) for this purpose. Despite the relatively high toxicity of the given hydrazine derivatives, these compounds possess several beneficial characteristics which make them most suitable for powering rocket engines in the outer space. First, all hydrazine derivatives form hypergolic (spontaneously ignitable) mixtures with nitrogen dioxide, making it possible for the engine to work without any additional ignition system. Next, the melting temperatures of both methylhydrazine and 1,1-dimethylhydrazine are sufficiently low, so these species remain liquid even at extreme conditions.

To investigate the thermochemical properties of selected derivatives of hydrazine, the following calorimetric experiments were performed. Samples of liquid hydrazine, methylhydrazine, and 1,1-dimethylhydrazine, each weighing 1 gram, were combusted in an adiabatic bomb calorimeter operating at a constant volume, in a stoichiometric amount of oxygen. The temperature in the calorimeter was initially $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$, and it increased by $8.25\,\mathrm{K}$, $12.55\,\mathrm{K}$ and $14.76\,\mathrm{K}$ during the experiments with the respective individual compounds. By calibration, the heat capacity of the calorimeter was determined to be $2.04\,\mathrm{kJ\,K^{-1}}$.

2.1 Assuming that all three hydrazine derivatives react with oxygen to yield molecular nitrogen, water vapour and, if relevant, carbon dioxide at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and $101\,325\,\mathrm{Pa}$, calculate the enthalpies of combustion for the reactants at the given conditions. Consider all gaseous species participating in the reaction to behave as ideal gas, and neglect any differences between the enthalpy and internal energy of all condensed phases.

2.2 Calculate the reaction enthalpies for combustion reactions of the three selected fuels with dinitrogen tetroxide at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and $101\,325\,\mathrm{Pa}$ (again, water vapour is produced). Consider all of the reacting hydrazine species to be liquid, mimicking the chemical processes occurring in rocket engines. Dinitrogen tetroxide enters the reaction in gaseous state. Use the standard enthalpies of formation of gaseous water ($-241.83\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$), carbon dioxide ($-393.52\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) and dinitrogen tetroxide ($9.08\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).

Extensive calorimetric experiments were performed for the relevant low-temperature phases of all chemical compounds present in the given systems at temperatures ranging from the vicinity of absolute zero up to ambient temperature. From these measurements, the absolute values of the standard molar entropies (at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and $101\,325\,\mathrm{Pa}$) were evaluated according to the third law of thermodynamics:

$$\begin{array}{cc|cc} \textbf{Compound} & S^\circ,\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} & \textbf{Compound} & S^\circ,\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{N2H4 (l)} & 121.92 & \ce{N2 (g)} & 191.61 \\ \ce{CH3N2H3 (l)} & 166.35 & \ce{CO2 (g)} & 213.79 \\ \ce{(CH3)2N2H2 (l)} & 199.60 & \ce{H2O (l)} & 69.95 \\ \ce{N2O4 (g)} & 209.46 & & \end{array}$$

2.3 Calculate standard reaction Gibbs energies for the three combustion reactions with dinitrogen tetroxide, estimate the corresponding equilibrium constants and predict qualitatively the extent of reactions occurring at $101\,325\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$. Assume that the reactions start from stoichiometric amounts of reactants, and water is produced in its standard state – liquid. Use the given standard entropy values and the molar vaporization enthalpy of water at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$, which amounts to $40.65\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

2.4 In which direction do the total pressure and temperature affect the given chemical equilibria? In other words, does an increase in pressure or in temperature lead to an increase or a decrease in the extent of the reaction?

2.5 Within the adiabatic approximation, calculate the flame temperature for a 1:1:1 molar mixture of the three fuels reacting with 3.75 moles of $\ce{N2O4}$ for the case when the reactants enter a combustion chamber at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ in the liquid state. The flame temperature can be calculated, assuming that the combustion reaction formally occurs at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and all of the heat released by the reaction (enthalpy) is then consumed to warm up the gaseous products (including water vapour) to the resulting temperature of the flame. Approximate the isobaric heat capacities of the relevant compounds with the following constants.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Compound} & C_p,\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{N2 (g)} & 35.26 \\ \ce{CO2 (g)} & 59.83 \\ \ce{H2O (g)} & 52.29 \end{array}$$

2.6 Compare the calculated flame temperature obtained above for the mixture of fuels, using an analogous value corresponding to burning pure liquid 1,1-dimethylhydrazine in an oxygen atmosphere.

2.7 The critical temperature of oxygen is $154.6\,\mathrm{K}$ and the melting temperature of 1,1-dimethylhydrazine is $216.0\,\mathrm{K}$. Is there a temperature range in which the same liquid–fuel engine could be used for this alternative fuel setup?

2.8 Explain the extraordinarily high thermodynamic efficiency of rocket engines when compared to the other representatives of thermal engines (e.g. steam or Diesel engine) and support your answer with a quantitative argument.
