1. Calculate the wavenumber of the absorption peak of deuterium fluoride (DF) in an IR spectrum recorded using the Ar matrix technique. Let the spring constant of D–F be the same as that of H–F. The atomic masses of F, H, and D are 18.998, 1.0079, and 2.0141, respectively.

The quantized energy levels of molecular vibration, $E_v$, are defined by:

$$E_v = \left(v + \frac{1}{2}\right)h\nu \qquad (v = 0,\ 1,\ 2,\ \cdots).$$

Here, $v$ is the quantum number of vibration.

The molecular vibrational energy is distributed over the quantized energy levels, and the distribution ratio is proportional to the following factor:

$$\exp\left(-\frac{E_v}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right).$$

This factor is known as the Boltzmann factor. Here, $k_\mathrm{B}$ and $T$ are the Boltzmann constant and absolute temperature, respectively. Although this factor is proportional to the distribution ratio, it is not equal to the probability for each level. Therefore, when all the Boltzmann factors are summed up, the sum is not unity, but instead yields $q_\mathrm{vib}$, i.e., the ‘distribution function’. The actual distribution ratio at each level can be determined using the distribution function as the normalization constant.

2. Write the equation for the distribution function at a temperature, $T$, as the summation of a geometric series using the vibrational temperature, $\theta$, which is defined as $\theta = h\nu/k_\mathrm{B}$.

3. Calculate the vibrational temperature of HF.

When the substrate temperature is raised to 26 K, the HF molecules begin to move in the Ar matrix, which yields a molecular associate of two HF molecules, $\ce{(HF)2}$, via hydrogen bonding as observed via a hydrogen-bonding-specific absorption peak in the IR spectrum. The hydrogen bond is generated from the overlapping wave functions of the electron of a lone pair and of a hydrogen atom. The molecule donating the hydrogen is called the ‘donor’, whereas the molecule receiving the hydrogen on the lone pair is called the ‘acceptor’. The hydrogen bond between two HF molecules is most stabilized when the lone pair of the acceptor and the H–F bond of the donor are aligned linearly. In this situation, the hydrogen atom is shared by the two fluorine atoms.

4. Based on this description, draw a chemical scheme for the molecular associate $\ce{(HF)2}$. Use a dotted line to represent the hydrogen bond, and show apparently the lone pairs of the accepter fluorine atom.

5. In the IR spectrum, a new absorption peak corresponding to the hydrogen-bonded acceptor is encountered. Does this new peak appear at a lower or higher wavenumber relative to the IR peak of the isolated HF molecule? Choose the correct shift with the most appropriate reason. Consider the fact that the H–F vibration becomes an F–H–F vibration with a different apparent mass, and that the bond order of the H–F bond is reduced when the hydrogen atom is shared by the two fluorine atoms.

(1) $k$ becomes smaller and $\mu$ becomes smaller; a prediction of the peak shift is difficult.

(2) $k$ becomes smaller and $\mu$ becomes larger, which results in a shift to a lower wavenumber.

(3) $k$ becomes larger and $\mu$ becomes smaller, which results in a shift to a higher wavenumber.

(4) $k$ becomes larger and $\mu$ becomes larger; a prediction of the peak shift is difficult.

Active IR absorption modes are those with a vibrational energy transition of $\Delta v = +1$; such transitions are observed between various energy levels. At low temperature, however, only the $v = 1 \leftarrow v = 0$ transition needs to be considered. Here, the leftward arrow indicates an upward energy transition. This approximation is allowed because the occupation number at $v = 1$, $g_1$, is much lower than that at $v = 0$, $g_0$. As a result, higher energy transitions such as $v = 2 \leftarrow v = 1$ can be ignored.

6. Calculate the ratios $g_1/g_0$ at temperatures of 12 K and 25 °C for an absorption peak at $3953.8\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The occupation number for a given level is proportional to the distribution ratio at that level.

problems.title: Quantum chemistry of aromatic molecules
problems.problem:
Problem 8. Quantum chemistry of aromatic molecules

The behavior of π-electrons is of paramount importance for understanding the reactivity and photophysical properties of aromatic compounds. In the electronic theory of organic chemistry, the electronic structure is considered to be a superposition of several ‘resonating’ electronic states.

1. Following the example below, draw all possible resonance structures for the compounds listed below. It should be noted that the positions of the atoms (nuclei) must remain unchanged. As only the skeletons of the structures are shown, add bonds as appropriate according to the chemical formulae. Do not include resonance structures with separated charges or unpaired electrons.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-8-fig1.png

2. In real benzene, all carbon–carbon bonds have the same bond length (1.399 Å), which means that the two cyclohexatriene resonance structures are extremes, and their superposition represents the real molecule. With this in mind, we will consider the bond lengths $R_1$, $R_2$, and $R_3$ in anthracene. Assuming that $R_\mathrm{S}$ is the typical length of a carbon–carbon single bond (1.53 Å) and $R_\mathrm{D}$ that of a typical C=C double bond (1.34 Å), arrange $R_\mathrm{S}$, $R_\mathrm{D}$, $R_1$, $R_2$, and $R_3$ in order of length.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-8-fig2.png

Following Questions are optional:

The properties of molecules are governed by their wavefunctions. Although resonance structures are useful for discussing various physical properties, it is difficult to use them to predict reactivity. The frontier orbital theory, proposed by Fukui and co-workers, is suitable for discussing reactivity based on molecular orbitals. For example, the six molecular orbitals of benzene are shown in the figure below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-8-fig3.png

The π-orbitals consist of p-orbitals perpendicular to the molecular plane of each atom (left panel); the white and black parts of each correspond to positive and negative values of the wavefunction. The right panel shows the same information more simply.

3. Give the number of orbitals occupied by π-electrons in benzene, naphthalene, and pyrrole.

4. Based on the following facts, choose the right pyrrole HOMO (highest occupied molecular orbital) from the options (a)-(c) below. The positive and negative values of wave functions are represented with white and black in the upper panel. In the lower panel, the circles on the atoms are drawn with a size proportional to the electron density.

• The reaction readily takes place at the position with the largest electron density in the HOMO.

• The electrophilic substitution reaction of pyrrole occurs faster at the 2 position than at the 3 position.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-8-fig4.png

5. Arrange these orbitals in order of their energy, from lowest energy to highest energy. The diagram of benzene can be used as a guide.

problems.title: Protic ionic liquids
problems.problem:
Problem 9. Protic ionic liquids

Water undergoes autoprotolysis according to:

$$\ce{2 H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-} \qquad (1)$$

The product of the concentration of dissociated ions is constant and known as the autoprotolysis equilibrium constant.

$$[\ce{H3O+}][\ce{OH-}] = K_\mathrm{w} = 1.00\times10^{-14}\ \ (25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}) \qquad (2)$$

The negative decadic logarithm of the concentration of $\ce{H3O+}$ is known as the pH value, which is used as a scale of the acidity of an aqueous solution:

$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\ce{H3O+}] \qquad (3)$$

When the concentration of the cations and the anions generated by autoprotolysis is the same, the solution is said to be neutral. In the case of water at 25 °C, the neutral condition, i.e., $[\ce{H3O+}] = [\ce{OH-}]$, holds when pH = 7.

1. Autoprotolysis also occurs in liquids other than water. For example, the autoprotolysis equilibrium constant of methanol is $10^{-16.7}$ at 25 °C.

1-1. Write the chemical equation for the autoprotolysis of methanol.

1-2. Calculate the concentration of the cation of methanol under neutral conditions at 25 °C.

Substances composed of ionic bonds, such as sodium chloride, usually exist in solid form at room temperature. In 1914, ethylammonium nitrate was reported as a unique salt that exists as a liquid even at room temperature. Such salts are known as ionic liquids, and these have attracted considerable attention recently.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig1.png

1-Ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (hereafter denoted as $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$) is a commonly used ionic liquid.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig2.png

1-Ethylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (hereafter denoted as $\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$), which has a similar structure to $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$ except that the methyl group on the imidazole ring is replaced by a proton, is also an ionic liquid.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig3.png

$\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$ shows an equilibrium that is similar to autoprotolysis:

$$\mathrm{CH^+/B^-} \rightleftarrows \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{HB} \qquad (4)$$

$$K_\mathrm{s} = [\mathrm{C}][\mathrm{HB}] \qquad (5)$$

To determine the $K_\mathrm{s}$ of $\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$, electrochemical measurements have been conducted (Figure 1). Using $\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$ as a solvent, a $0.35\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide solution (henceforth: HB solution) and a $3.2\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ 1-ethylimidazole solution (henceforth: C solution) were prepared.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig4.png

Figure 1. Schematic illustration of the experimental setup.

7.3 mL of the HB solution was titrated with the C solution, and the electromotive force was measured during the titration using an electrode that responds to HB. The obtained electric voltage, $E_i$, can be expressed by:

$$E_i = E^\circ + RT/F\,\ln[\mathrm{HB}] \qquad (6)$$

The resulting electric voltages as a function of the amount of the C solution added, $V_i$, are shown in Figure 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig5.png

Figure 2. Electric voltages during the titration of the HB solution as a function of the amount of the C solution added ($V_i$).

The total concentration of protons, $C_\mathrm{H}$, and the total concentration of imidazole, $C_\mathrm{im}$, can be expressed by:

$$C_\mathrm{H} = [\mathrm{HB}] + [\mathrm{CH^+}] \qquad (7)$$

$$C_\mathrm{im} = [\mathrm{C}] + [\mathrm{CH^+}] \qquad (8)$$

In the following problems, assume that the temperature of the solutions is 25 °C.

2. First, let us consider the case where there is an excess of HB. At the point of neutralization, the observed electric voltage changes drastically. This indicates that $K_\mathrm{s}$ is very small, and therefore almost all C added prior to the point of neutralization is protonated ($[\mathrm{C}] \ll [\mathrm{CH^+}]$).

2-1. Consider the case where the initial concentration of HB solution is $[\mathrm{HB}]_0$ ($= 0.35\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$), the concentration of C solution is $[\mathrm{C}]_0$ ($= 3.2\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$), the concentration of $\mathrm{CH^+}$ originating from the solvent is $[\mathrm{CH^+}]_\mathrm{sol}$, and the volume of HB solution before the titration is $V_0$ (= 7.3 mL). Write an expression for $C_\mathrm{H}$ and $C_\mathrm{im}$ in terms of $V_0$, $V_i$, $[\mathrm{HB}]_0$, $[\mathrm{C}]_0$, and $[\mathrm{CH^+}]_\mathrm{sol}$. Assume that $[\mathrm{CH^+}]_\mathrm{sol}$ does not change during the titration.

2-2. When 0.50 mL of the C solution was added, $E_i$ was 0.796 V. Calculate the value of $E^\circ$. Note that the concentration of HB can be approximated as $[\mathrm{HB}] = C_\mathrm{H} - C_\mathrm{im}$.

To analyze the obtained result, Figure 2 is replotted with $(V_0+V_i)\exp(\pm E_iF/RT)$ as the vertical axis (Figure 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig6.png

Figure 3. Replotted graphs of Figure 2. (Left) Before the point of neutralization. (Right) After the point of neutralization.

3. When the C solution is added beyond the point of neutralization, there is an excess of C. In this case, almost all the protons bind to C, and there are few protons that exist in the form of HB.

3-1. Write an expression for [HB] beyond the point of neutralization in terms of $C_\mathrm{H}$, $C_\mathrm{im}$, and $K_\mathrm{s}$. Assume that $C_\mathrm{H} = [\mathrm{HB}] + [\mathrm{CH^+}] \simeq [\mathrm{CH^+}]$, which holds when there is an excess of C.

3-2. The slope of $(V_0+V_i)\exp(-E_iF/RT)$ as a function of $V_i$ is 0.0271 beyond the point of neutralization. Calculate $K_\mathrm{s}$.

Let us consider how to control the reaction rate of the following chemical reaction.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig7.png

(S1)

An amide bond is produced by the reaction between the amine and the active ester. In the following problems, assume that all of the produced N-hydroxysuccinimide ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ = 6.0 in water) exists in the deprotonated form ($\mathrm{NHS^-}$). Ignore the degradation reaction of the active ester. The temperature of the solutions is 25 °C.

First, let us consider reaction S1 in a buffered aqueous solution. In an aqueous solution, the acid–base equilibrium of $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ is expressed by:

$$\ce{R^1-NH3+ + H2O <=> R^1-NH2 + H3O+} \qquad (9)$$

$$K_\mathrm{a} = [\ce{R^1-NH2}]\,[\ce{H3O+}]\,/\,[\ce{R^1-NH3+}] = 10^{-9.27} \qquad (10)$$

The reaction rate of S1 is expressed as a second-order reaction:

$$d[\text{–NH–CO–}]/dt = k\,[\ce{R^1-NH2}][\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}] \qquad (11)$$

The variation of [–NH–CO–] over time is obtained by integrating eq. 11, which gives:

$$[\text{–NH–CO–}] = ([\ce{R^1-NH2}]_0 + [\ce{R^1-NH3+}]_0)(1 - \exp(-k[\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}]\,f_a\,t)) \qquad (12)$$

$[\ce{R^1-NH2}]_0$ and $[\ce{R^1-NH3+}]_0$ represent the initial concentrations of $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ and $\ce{R^1-NH3+}$, respectively, while $f_a$ represents the ratio of the deprotonated form of the amine, which is defined by:

$$f_a = [\ce{R^1-NH2}]\,/\,([\ce{R^1-NH2}] + [\ce{R^1-NH3+}]) \qquad (13)$$

When the reaction occurs in a buffered aqueous solution, $f_a$ remains constant during the reaction because the pH of the solution is constant.

4. The reaction progress in a mixture of 20 μmol of $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ in 10 mL of the buffer solution and 200 μmol of $\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}$ in 10 mL of the buffer solution is monitored via the absorption of $\mathrm{NHS^-}$ in the ultraviolet region. In this case, the concentration of $\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}$ is regarded constant during the reaction, because it is significantly higher than that of $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ (pseudo-first-order reaction). Reaction S1 proceeds only for the deprotonated amine, $\ce{R^1-NH2}$. The protonated amine, $\ce{R^1-NH3+}$, does not react with the active ester.

4-1. Calculate the time at which half of the added $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ will have reacted when $k' = k[\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}] = 5.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and pH = 9.27.

4-2. In a differently buffered solution, the time at which one-third of the added $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ has reacted is 500 s when $k' = 5.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Calculate the pH of the buffer solution in this case.

Then, let us consider reaction S1 in the ionic liquid $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$. In $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$, the acid–base equilibrium of $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ is expressed as follows:

$$\ce{R^1-NH3+ + B- <=> R^1-NH2 + HB} \qquad (14)$$

$$K_\mathrm{a}^\mathrm{A} = [\ce{R^1-NH2}]\,[\mathrm{HB}]\,/\,[\ce{R^1-NH3+}] = 10^{-16.40} \qquad (15)$$

The reaction rate of S1 is expressed as a second-order reaction:

$$d[\text{–NH–CO–}]/dt = k_I\,[\ce{R^1-NH2}][\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}] \qquad (16)$$

5. As shown in Q4, to control the reaction rate of S1, the ratio of $[\ce{R^1-NH2}]$ should be set to the appropriate value by adjusting the proton concentration in the solution. However, the ionic liquid $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$ does not contain a proton. To solve this problem, let us use the ionic liquid $\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$, which was considered in Q2 and Q3, as a proton source for $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$. The acid–base equilibrium of $\mathrm{CH^+}$ in $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$ can be expressed by:

$$\mathrm{CH^+} + \mathrm{B^-} \rightleftarrows \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{HB} \qquad (17)$$

$$K_\mathrm{a}^\mathrm{C} = [\mathrm{C}]\,[\mathrm{HB}]\,/\,[\mathrm{CH^+}] = 10^{-14.90} \qquad (18)$$

5-1. Calculate the [HB] of a $6.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$ solution dissolved in the ionic liquid $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$.

5-2. A $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ solution is prepared using the solution from Q5-1 as the solvent. The [HB] of the solution of 100 μmol $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ in 10 mL of the solvent is $5.39\times10^{-17}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$. Calculate the concentrations of $\mathrm{CH^+}$, C, $\ce{R^1-NH3+}$, and $\ce{R^1-NH2}$.

As shown in Q5-2, most of the protons added as $\mathrm{CH^+}$ are transferred to $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ and exist in the form of $\ce{R^1-NH3+}$. Similarly, the protons produced in reaction S1 also bind to $\ce{R^1-NH2}$. As the resulting chemical species, $\ce{R^1-NH3+}$, does not react with the active ester, the reaction rate decreases as the reaction proceeds.

5-3. Reaction S1 is started once 100 μmol of $\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}$ have been dissolved in the solution from Q5-2. Calculate the concentrations of HB, $\mathrm{CH^+}$, C, $\ce{R^1-NH3+}$, and $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ when the concentration of $\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}$ become $8.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.

5-4. To avoid a decrease in the reaction rate, the concentration of HB should remain constant. When $\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$ and C are dissolved together, the concentration of HB is determined by the ratio of the concentrations of C and $\mathrm{CH^+}$. Express [HB] in terms of [C], $[\mathrm{CH^+}]$, and $K_\mathrm{a}^\mathrm{C}$.

A buffer solution is prepared by adding the appropriate amount of C to $0.10\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ of $\mathrm{CH^+/B^-}$ solution using $\mathrm{CM^+/B^-}$ as the solvent. The reaction progress of a mixture of 20 μmol $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ in 10 mL of the buffer solution and 200 μmol of $\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}$ in 10 mL of the buffer solution is monitored. The variation in [–NH–CO–] over time can be expressed by:

$$[\text{–NH–CO–}] = ([\ce{R^1-NH2}]_0 + [\ce{R^1-NH3+}]_0)(1 - \exp(-k_I'\,f_a\,t)) \qquad (19)$$

5-5. The time at which one third of the added $\ce{R^1-NH2}$ will have reacted is 2000 s when $k_I' = k_I[\ce{R^2-CO-NHS}] = 8.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Calculate the concentration of C in the buffer solution.

[Note] The reaction control technique explained above has already been applied to the condensation of the two polymers shown in Figure 4. As a result, high-strength gels with homogeneous network structures were prepared from both aqueous solutions and ionic liquids (for an example, see: T. Sakai et al., Macromolecules 2008, 41, 5379).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-9-fig8.png

Figure 4. Conceptual illustration of the controlled synthesis of high-strength gels.

problems.title: The Yamada universal indicator
problems.problem:
Problem 10. The Yamada universal indicator

In this problem, assume that the optical path length of the cell is 1.0 cm. Ignore the absorption of the cell and the solvent.

1. The acid dissociation constant of bromothymol blue (BTB) is $10^{-7.10}$. The absorbance values of $200\,\mathrm{\mu mol\,L^{-1}}$ BTB aqueous solutions with different pH values (2.00, 12.00) were measured, and the results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1. Absorbance values of $200\,\mathrm{\mu mol\,L^{-1}}$ BTB solutions

$$\begin{array}{llll} \text{Wavelength} & 420\,\mathrm{nm} & 501\,\mathrm{nm} & 520\,\mathrm{nm} \\ \hline \mathrm{pH} = 2.00 & 1.74 & 0.70 & 0.36 \\ \mathrm{pH} = 12.00 & 0.60 & 0.70 & 1.06 \end{array}$$

1-1. Calculate the molar absorption coefficients of the protonated/deprotonated forms of BTB at 420 nm, 501 nm, and 520 nm.

1-2. At a certain pH value, the absorbance values of an aqueous solution containing a small amount of BTB at 420 nm and 520 nm were 1.13 and 0.52, respectively. Calculate the pH of this aqueous solution.

1-3. The aqueous solution used in Q1-2 was diluted 5 times using hydrochloric acid with pH = 1. Calculate the absorbance value of the diluted solution at 501 nm.

1-4. The aqueous solution used in Q1-2 was diluted 5 times using aqueous sodium hydroxide with pH = 12. Calculate the absorbance value of the diluted solution at 501 nm.

To estimate the pH of a solution using indicators, appropriate indicators that show a clear color change in the target pH region should be used. Universal indicators have been developed as easy-to-use indicators. Universal indicators can be prepared by mixing several kinds of indicators so that the resulting mixture shows color changes over a wide pH region. As a representative universal indicator, let us consider the Yamada universal indicator, which was developed by a Japanese researcher, Shinobu Yamada, in 1933.

The components of the Yamada universal indicator, its color under various pH conditions, the molar absorption coefficients of each indicator, and the acid dissociation constants of each indicator are summarized in Tables 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively.

Table 2. Components of the Yamada universal indicator dissolved in 100 mL ethanol

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{Indicators} & \text{Molecular weight} & \text{Weight [mg]} \\ \hline \text{Thymol blue (TB)} & 466.6 & 5.00 \\ \text{Methyl red (MR)} & 269.3 & 12.5 \\ \text{Bromothymol blue (BTB)} & 624.4 & 50.0 \\ \text{Phenolphthalein (PP)} & 318.3 & 100.0 \end{array}$$

Table 3. Color of the Yamada universal indicator under various pH conditions

$$\begin{array}{llllll} \text{pH} & -3 & 3-6 & 6-8 & 8-11 & 11- \\ \hline \text{Color} & \text{Red} & \text{Yellow} & \text{Green} & \text{Blue} & \text{Purple} \end{array}$$

Table 4. Molar absorption coefficients of each indicator (unit: $\mathrm{mol^{-1}\,L\,cm^{-1}}$)

$$\begin{array}{lllllll} \text{Wavelength [nm]} & 400 & 450 & 500 & 550 & 600 & 650 \\ \hline \text{TB, }\ce{H2A} & 5500 & 2500 & 6000 & 18000 & 1500 & 0 \\ \text{TB, }\ce{HA-} & 6000 & 7000 & 3000 & 500 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{TB, }\ce{A^{2-}} & 3500 & 1500 & 3500 & 10000 & 17500 & 2500 \\ \text{MR, }\ce{HA-} & 1000 & 10000 & 35000 & 35000 & 1500 & 0 \\ \text{MR, }\ce{A^{2-}} & 15500 & 16000 & 4000 & 500 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{BTB, }\ce{HA-} & 7500 & 9000 & 3500 & 500 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{BTB, }\ce{A^{2-}} & 5000 & 1000 & 3500 & 10000 & 20000 & 10000 \\ \text{PP, }\ce{HA-} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \text{PP, }\ce{A^{2-}} & 1000 & 1000 & 6000 & 21000 & 1000 & 0 \end{array}$$

Table 5. Acid dissociation constants of each indicator (In this problem, ignore all acid dissociation constants except for these.)

$$\begin{array}{lllll} \text{Indicator} & \text{TB} & \text{MR} & \text{BTB} & \text{PP} \\ \hline \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} & \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} = 1.7,\ \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2} = 8.9 & 5.1 & 7.1 & 9.7 \end{array}$$

2. The Yamada universal indicator (1.0 mL) was added to aqueous solutions (29.0 mL) with various pH values, and the absorbance of these solutions was measured. The measured absorbance values and the colors of the solutions are shown in Table 6. Calculate the pH of solutions (1), (2), and (3) after the addition of the Yamada universal indicator up to one decimal place.

Note that under each pH condition, only one of the four indicators exhibits a drastic change in the ratio of its protonated/deprotonated forms by the slight change of its pH value.

Table 6. Measured absorbance values and colors of the solutions

$$\begin{array}{llllllll} & & \text{Wavelength [nm]} & & & & & \\ & \text{Color} & 400 & 450 & 500 & 550 & 600 & 650 \\ \hline \mathrm{pH} = 1.0 & \text{Red} & 0.236 & 0.407 & 0.655 & 0.609 & 0.028 & 0.000 \\ (1) & \text{Yellow} & 0.323 & 0.455 & 0.460 & 0.352 & 0.018 & 0.002 \\ (2) & \text{Green} & 0.435 & 0.440 & 0.176 & 0.121 & 0.179 & 0.089 \\ (3) & \text{Blue} & 0.466 & 0.360 & 0.645 & 1.979 & 0.673 & 0.275 \\ \mathrm{pH} = 12.0 & \text{Purple} & 0.490 & 0.384 & 0.793 & 2.498 & 0.701 & 0.276 \end{array}$$

problems.title: Silver electroplating
problems.problem:
Problem 11. Silver electroplating

Silver electroplating, in which silver is deposited on a metal surface, has been used to decorate objects and to increase their electrical conductivity. In silver electroplating, usually an aqueous alkaline solution containing $\ce{Ag+}$ and $\ce{CN-}$ is used. The metal to be plated is used as the cathode, and silver ions are deposited on the metal surface by reductive deposition. Pure silver is used as the anode, from which silver ions are supplied to the solution by oxidative dissolution. The half reaction and standard electrode potential $E^\circ$ of the reductive deposition/oxidative dissolution of $\ce{Ag+}$ are as follows:

$$\ce{Ag+ + e- <=> Ag(s)} \qquad E^\circ = 0.799\,\mathrm{V}$$

In the solution, $\ce{Ag+}$ forms several kinds of complexes with $\ce{CN-}$ and $\ce{OH-}$. The complex formation reactions and formation constants are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Ag+ + CN- + OH- <=> Ag(OH)(CN)-} & K_\mathrm{OHCN} = 10^{13.20} \\ \ce{Ag+ + 2CN- <=> Ag(CN)2-} & \beta_2 = 10^{20.40} \\ \ce{Ag+ + 3CN- <=> Ag(CN)3^{2-}} & \beta_3 = 10^{21.40} \\ \ce{Ag+ + 4CN- <=> Ag(CN)4^{3-}} & \beta_4 = 10^{20.80} \end{array}$$

where the overall formation constants $\beta_i$ are defined as $\beta_i = \dfrac{[\mathrm{Ag(CN)}_\mathrm{i}^{-}]}{([\ce{Ag+}][\ce{CN-}]^\mathrm{i})}$.

Answer the following questions. Unless otherwise noted, $[\ce{CN-}] = [\ce{OH-}] = 1.00\,\mathrm{M}$, and the total concentration of Ag-related dissolved species is 1.00 mM. Use the absolute temperature $T = 298.2\,\mathrm{K}$.

1. Write the five Ag-related dissolved species in this solution in order of concentration. Calculate the concentration of the species with the highest concentration.

$$\square > \square > \square > \square > \square$$

2. Write the half reaction in which the Ag-related dissolved species with the highest concentration in Q1 is reduced to Ag(s). Calculate the $E^\circ$ of the half reaction.

3. If $[\ce{CN-}]$ varies from 1.00 M, the relative order of the species in Q1 will also vary. Calculate the concentration range of $[\ce{CN-}]$ within which the relative order in Q1 holds.

4. Calculate the equilibrium potential of the cathode, assuming that the cathode surface is covered with Ag(s).

5. The reductive deposition reaction of silver competes with the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). The potentials at which the HER occurs depend on the pH of the solution; the higher the pH, the more negative the potentials for the HER. By comparing the equilibrium potential calculated in Q4 with that for the HER, calculate the lower pH limit above which the reductive deposition reaction of silver is more thermodynamically favorable than the HER.

6. Because HCN(g) is highly toxic, the evolution of this gas should be minimized, even when using a fume hood. Calculate the pH requirements for the solution to keep the equilibrium partial pressure of HCN(g) below 10 ppm ($= 10^{-5.0}$ bar). Use the following equilibrium equations for the calculation.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{HCN(g) <=> HCN(aq)} & K_\mathrm{H} = 10^{1.0} \\ \ce{HCN(aq) <=> H+ + CN-} & K_a = 10^{-9.2} \end{array}$$

problems.title: How does CO2 in the atmosphere affect the pH value of seawater?
problems.problem:
Problem 12. How does $\ce{CO2}$ in the atmosphere affect the pH value of seawater?

Let us consider the chemical equilibrium of carbonic acid in ocean acidification, which is caused by an increase in the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Use the following equilibrium equations and constants:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \ce{CO2(g)} & \ce{<=> CO2} & K_\mathrm{gas} = 10^{-1.46} \\ \ce{CO2 + H2O} & \ce{<=> H2CO3} & K_\mathrm{hyd} = 10^{-2.70} \\ \ce{H2CO3} & \ce{<=> H+ + HCO3-} & K_\mathrm{a1} = 10^{-3.65} \\ \ce{HCO3-} & \ce{<=> H+ + CO3^{2-}} & K_\mathrm{a2} = 10^{-10.33} \\ \ce{H2O} & \ce{<=> H+ + OH-} & K_\mathrm{w} = 10^{-14.00} \end{array}$$

where (g) denotes a species in the gaseous state, and all species other than $\ce{CO2(g)}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ are dissolved in an aqueous solution. Let the current value of the molar fraction of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, $x_{\ce{CO2}}$, be 410 ppm ($= 410\times10^{-6}$ bar).

1. When pure water is left exposed to the atmosphere, it absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which changes its pH. Calculate the pH of water in equilibrium with the atmosphere using the following charge balance equation:

$$[\ce{H+}] = [\ce{OH-}] + [\ce{HCO3-}] + 2[\ce{CO3^{2-}}]$$

2. To the water in equilibrium with the atmosphere in Q1, a strong base or strong acid was added such that the pH changed by ±1 ($\Delta\mathrm{pH} = \pm1$). The solution was then left exposed to the atmosphere again. What is the change in the amount of absorbed carbon dioxide relative to that before the addition? Choose the pH change for each scenario from the following Options. Assume that there is no change in the liquid volume due to the acid/base addition.

(a) Strong base ($\Delta\mathrm{pH} = +1$)

(b) Strong acid ($\Delta\mathrm{pH} = -1$)

Options

(1) The amount of absorbed carbon dioxide increases to more than double the initial value.

(2) The amount of absorbed carbon dioxide decreases to less than half the initial value.

(3) The magnitude of the increase or decrease is less than described in Options (1) and (2).

3. Currently, $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ continues to rise. A report has predicted that $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ will exceed 800 ppm by 2070 (cf. IPCC RCP 8.5). Calculate the pH of water in equilibrium with the atmosphere if $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ were twice its current value ($x_{\ce{CO2}} = 2\times410 = 820$ ppm) and evaluate the pH shift relative to the pH found in Q1 where the current $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ value was used.

As $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ rises, the oceans, like pure water, become more acidic. The current pH of the oceans is 8.05 on average, although it varies spatially and temporally. Compared to the pre-industrialization value in the 18th century, the current pH of the oceans has decreased by 0.1. If the pH decreases a further 0.2 to 7.85 in the future, the decrease in $[\ce{CO3^{2-}}]$ will result in $\ce{CaCO3}$ (aragonite), which is a component of the shells of corals and phytoplankton, being dissolved at low temperatures, causing severe damage to the marine biota. Let us estimate how much a rise in $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ would reduce pH.

4. First, let us estimate the ocean acidification due to the rise in $x_{\ce{CO2}}$, ignoring chemical equilibria other than those of carbonic acid. A variety of ions are dissolved in the ocean. The difference in the concentration of the cations and anions originating from strong electrolytes, $C_\mathrm{C-A}$, appears as a constant in the charge balance equation.

$$[\ce{H+}] + C_\mathrm{C-A} = [\ce{OH-}] + [\ce{HCO3-}] + 2[\ce{CO3^{2-}}]$$

Calculate the pH shift when $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ increases from 410 to 820 ppm, with $C_\mathrm{C-A} = 0.72$ mM.

5. In real seawater, chemical equilibria other than those of carbonic acid affect this pH shift. Let us calculate the pH shift taking into account the following ion-pair formation constant for $\ce{MgCO3}$ (dissolved species):

$$\ce{Mg^{2+} + CO3^{2-} <=> MgCO3} \qquad K_\mathrm{f} = 10^{2.88}$$

The charge balance equation can be written as:

$$2[\ce{Mg^{2+}}] + [\ce{H+}] + C_\mathrm{C-A} = [\ce{OH-}] + [\ce{HCO3-}] + 2[\ce{CO3^{2-}}]$$

where $C_\mathrm{C-A} = -105.0$ mM. Use $C_\mathrm{Mg} = 53.0$ mM as the total concentration of Mg-related species. Calculate the pH when $x_{\ce{CO2}}$ changes from 410 to 820 ppm. It may be helpful to use an approximation, $(1-x)^{-1} \sim 1 + x$, for $x \ll 1$. Can corals survive?

Let us consider the meaning of the pH shift evaluated in Q3 and Q4 using a virtual weak acid HA which dissociates as follows:

$$\ce{HA <=> H+ + A-}$$

with the acid dissociation constant $K_\mathrm{a} = 10^{-3.00}$ (note that this constant is different from that of carbonic acid). A solution is prepared using a given concentration of HA, $C_\mathrm{HA}$, and a given concentration of its conjugate base salt NaA, $C_\mathrm{NaA}$. The pH of the solution depends on these concentrations. The dependence of the pH on $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA}$ ($= -\log_{10}C_\mathrm{HA}$) and $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{NaA}$ ($= -\log_{10}C_\mathrm{NaA}$) is shown as a contour map below. A doubling in $C_\mathrm{HA}$ corresponds to a –0.30 shift of $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA}$ to the left in this contour map.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-12-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Contour map of pH for an HA/NaA solution.

6. In the situation described in Q3, i.e., pure water in equilibrium with the atmosphere, $C_\mathrm{NaA}$ is ideally zero and can be neglected. In the above contour map, this situation corresponds to either Region A, B, or C, where $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{NaA}$ is large and the following inequalities for $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA}$ hold:

(Region A) $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA} < \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$

(Region B) $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} < \mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA} < \frac{\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{w}}{2}$

(Region C) $\frac{\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{w}}{2} < \mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA}$

Derive analytical solutions for the pH as a function of $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA}$ using the charge balance equation:

$$[\ce{H+}] = [\ce{OH-}] + [\ce{A-}]$$

combined with the above inequalities for each Region. Because doubling $C_\mathrm{HA}$ corresponds to a –0.30 shift in $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{HA}$ as described above, the pH shift can be determined from the derived analytical solutions. Calculate the pH shift when $C_\mathrm{HA}$ is doubled for Regions A, B, and C, respectively. The situation in Q3 corresponds to Region $\boxed{\phantom{A}}$. Fill in this blank with either A, B, or C.

7. In the solution with pH = 8.05 in Q4, in which we ignored any chemical equilibria other than that of carbonic acid, $\ce{HCO3-}$ is the main component among the carbonic-acid-related dissolved species. This solution can be regarded as an aqueous solution of $\ce{NaHCO3}$, which corresponds to Region D with a large $C_\mathrm{NaA}$, i.e., a small $\mathrm{p}C_\mathrm{NaA}$, in the contour map. In Region D, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation holds, in which the equilibrium equation $K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{[\ce{H+}][\ce{A-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$ is approximated using $[\mathrm{HA}] = C_\mathrm{HA}$ and $[\ce{A-}] = C_\mathrm{NaA}$. Calculate the pH shift using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation when $C_\mathrm{HA}$ doubles in Region D.

problems.title: How to produce sulfuric acid and dilute it without explosion
problems.problem:
Problem 13. How to produce sulfuric acid and dilute it without explosion

Japan is a country rich in sulfur resources. Sulfuric acid can be synthesized from sulfide-based mineral resources such as copper sulfide, iron sulfide, and lead sulfide.

1. When a mixture of chalcopyrite ($\ce{CuFeS2}$) and silica sand ($\ce{SiO2}$) is melted at high temperature in the presence of oxygen in a blast furnace, sulfur dioxide is generated along with $\ce{Cu2S}$ and $\ce{FeSiO3}$ (Reaction 1). The $\ce{Cu2S}$ obtained in Reaction 1 reacts with oxygen at high temperature to form copper and sulfur dioxide (Reaction 2). Write the reaction formulae for Reaction 1 and Reaction 2.

2. Calculate how many kg of copper and how many liters of sulfur dioxide (at 25 °C, 1.00 bar) will be obtained from 100 kg of pure chalcopyrite by the process described in Q1. Assume that all the reactions proceed completely and that all gases are ideal gases.

3. Sulfur dioxide is oxidized to sulfur trioxide by air using a catalyst such as vanadium(V) oxide. This oxidation proceeds exothermically, and the reaction reaches an equilibrium state as it is a reversible reaction. Which of the following conditions is most appropriate to increase the production ratio of sulfur trioxide? Choose one option from (1) to (4).

(1) Low temperature / Low pressure

(2) Low temperature / High pressure

(3) High temperature / Low pressure

(4) High temperature / High pressure

4. A mixture of sulfur dioxide (7.00 mol) and oxygen (3.00 mol) is placed in a 50.0 L heat- and pressure-resistant container together with a catalyst. When the container is heated to 350 °C, the pressure increases to 8.60 bar. Calculate how many moles of sulfur trioxide are generated in this reaction.

5. The absorption of sulfur trioxide by concentrated sulfuric acid produces fuming sulfuric acid. Subsequent dilution of the fuming sulfuric acid with dilute sulfuric acid can afford the desired concentration of sulfuric acid. Calculate how many kg of 60% sulfuric acid are needed to dilute 20.0 kg of 32% fuming sulfuric acid (32% by weight $\ce{SO3}$, 68% $\ce{H2SO4}$) to obtain 98% sulfuric acid. Assume that the volatilization of the components during the dilution is negligible.

6. 8.0 kg of 98% sulfuric acid is diluted with water to give 60% sulfuric acid. Calculate the heat of dilution $Q$ [J] released by this dilution process. Note that when 1 mol of $\ce{H2SO4}$ is diluted with $n$ mol of $\ce{H2O}$, the heat of dilution $Q_0$ [J] is expressed by the following formula:

$$Q_0\,[J] = \frac{7.47\times10^{4}\times n}{n + 1.80}$$

The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C is 4.18 J (1 cal). Calculate the increase in temperature that the released heat of dilution $Q$ [J] would cause in 10 kg of water (0 °C).

problems.title: Hydrolysis of C vs Si and the electronegativity of N vs Cl
problems.problem:
Problem 14. Hydrolysis of C vs Si and the electronegativity of N vs Cl

1. Answer the following questions based on the following values of bond-dissociation energies [$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$]. Assume that the reaction-enthalpy change can be estimated by considering only the bond-dissociation energies of the starting materials and the reaction products.

C–Cl: 335, C–O: 392, O–H: 467, H–Cl: 426, Si–Cl: 451, Si–O: 500, C–H: 413, Si–H: 318.

1-1. Carbon tetrachloride is a stable compound in water, while silicon tetrachloride undergoes facile hydrolysis in water. For reactions (1) and (2) below, which are the initial steps of hydrolysis, calculate $\Delta H$ [$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$], which can be estimated based on the bond dissociation energies.

(1) $\ce{CCl4 + H2O -> CCl3OH + HCl}$

(2) $\ce{SiCl4 + H2O -> SiCl3OH + HCl}$

In Q1-1, it cannot be anticipated whether the reaction would proceed smoothly based on only the enthalpy change of the bond-dissociation energies between the reaction substrates and the reaction products. The difference in reactivity between carbon tetrachloride and silicon tetrachloride described in Q1-1 can be explained by the one-step reaction in the carbon case and the multi-step reaction in the silicon case.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-14-fig1.png

Equation (1) is a one-step reaction that requires a very large activation energy because its transition state involves a penta-coordinated carbon species. Equation (2) is a two-step reaction through an intermediate, which is a penta-coordinated silicon species. For example, as shown in equation (3), a penta-coordinated silicon compound known as a silicate should be generated by the reaction of silicon tetrachloride with hydrogen chloride. The molecular structure of the penta-coordinated silicon compound exhibits a trigonal bipyramidal geometry with a silicon atom at the center and a bonding atom at each vertex of the trigonal bipyramidal skeleton.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-14-fig2.png

In this intermediate, the bond dissociation energies of the atoms located at the two vertices above and below silicon (apical positions) differ from those of the atoms located at the three vertices that form the triangle centered on silicon (equatorial positions). Assume that the bond-dissociation energies of the equatorial Si–Cl bonds (BE(Si–Cl$^\mathrm{e}$)) are all equal, and that the bond-dissociation energies of the apical Si–Cl bonds (BE(Si–Cl$^\mathrm{a}$)) are also equal. The bond-dissociation energy between the penta-coordinated silicon and the oxygen atom of the apical $\ce{H2O}$ molecule is $400\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and the changes in the bond-dissociation energies of the O–H and Cl–H bonds upon coordination of the $\ce{H2O}$ and HCl molecules to the silicon atom to form the corresponding silicates are negligible.

1-2. Provided that $\Delta H_{2\text{-}1}$ in Eq.(2-1) is $14.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\Delta H_3$ in Eq.(3) is $50.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, calculate the bond-dissociation energies BE(Si–Cl$^\mathrm{a}$) and BE(Si–Cl$^\mathrm{e}$) between the silicon atom and chlorine atom at the apical and equatorial positions, respectively.

1-3. As described in Q1-2, it is important that silicon can adopt, in contrast to carbon, a penta-coordinate geometry in a meta-stable intermediate. This is due to the longer bond lengths of silicon relative to those of carbon; accordingly, there is a spatial margin around the central silicon atom, resulting in low repulsion between the five coordinated ligands. As can be found in Q1-2, although the bond-dissociation energy of each bond in the penta-coordinated silicon compound is smaller than that in the tetracoordinated silicon compound, the five weak bonds in the penta-coordinated silicon compounds should collectively yield sufficient stabilizing energy. Thus, the penta-coordinated silicon compound exhibits stability that is comparable to that of the corresponding tetracoordinated silicon compound. Based on the aforementioned considerations, choose the graphs that most appropriately represent the energy changes during the progress of reactions of (1) and (2), respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-14-fig3.png

Note that the vertical axes in figures (i)–(v) all have the same scale.

For certain elements A and B, the Pauling electronegativities $\chi_\mathrm{A}$ and $\chi_\mathrm{B}$ are defined according to the following equation:

$$(\chi_\mathrm{A} - \chi_\mathrm{B})^{2} = D_\mathrm{AB} - (D_\mathrm{AA} + D_\mathrm{BB})/2$$

$D_\mathrm{AB}$: Bond dissociation energy of an A–B bond [eV]

$D_\mathrm{AA}$: Bond dissociation energy of an A–A bond [eV]

$D_\mathrm{BB}$: Bond dissociation energy of a B–B bond [eV]

The Pauling electronegativities of hydrogen, nitrogen, and chlorine are as follows: $\chi_\mathrm{H} = 2.10$, $\chi_\mathrm{N} = 3.04$, $\chi_\mathrm{Cl} = 3.16$. The bond-dissociation energies [$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$] are as follows: N≡N: 945, O=O: 498, N–N: 158, H–H: 436, H–Cl: 426, Cl–O: 206, O–H: 467.

2-1. Based on these values, calculate the bond-dissociation energies $D_\mathrm{NH}$, $D_\mathrm{NCl}$, and $D_\mathrm{ClCl}$ for the N–H, N–Cl, and Cl–Cl bonds, respectively.

2-2. Write the molecular formulae that can apply to blanks $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{D}$ in the following sentence, and calculate the numerical value that applies to blank $\boldsymbol{Q}$.

The Pauling electronegativities of nitrogen and chlorine are $\chi_\mathrm{N} = 3.04$ and $\chi_\mathrm{Cl} = 3.16$, respectively, and thus, the polarity of the N–Cl bond can be considered to be $\mathrm{N^+}$–$\mathrm{Cl^-}$. For example, in the hydrolysis reaction of monochloroamine ($\ce{H2NCl}$), it would be expected that nitrogen-containing product $\mathbf{A}$ and chlorine-containing product $\mathbf{B}$ will be produced based on the $\mathrm{N^+}$–$\mathrm{Cl^-}$ polarization. In the actual reaction, however, nitrogen-containing product $\mathbf{C}$ and chlorine-containing product $\mathbf{D}$ are produced, as shown in the equation below. This result cannot be interpreted in terms of the Pauling electronegativities. The reaction between monochloroamine and water can be written as follows, and the enthalpy change in this reaction can be calculated as $\Delta H = \boldsymbol{Q}$ [kJ] based on the values of the bond-dissociation energies, suggesting that this reaction should proceed endothermically.

$$\text{(eq.)}\quad \ce{H2NCl + H2O ->}\ \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{D} \qquad \Delta H = \boldsymbol{Q}\ [\mathrm{kJ}]$$

Allred and Rochow defined electronegativity using the equation below. The Allred–Rochow electronegativity ($\chi_\mathrm{AR}$) depends on the values of the effective nuclear charge for the valence electrons ($Z^\mathrm{VE}{}_\mathrm{eff}$) and the covalent radius of the atom ($r$ [pm]), based on the idea that electronegativity should be determined by the strength of the electric field on the atomic surface.

$$\chi_{AR} = 3590\left(\frac{Z^{VE}{}_{eff} - 0.35}{r^{2}}\right) + 0.744$$

The effective nuclear charge ($Z_\mathrm{eff}$) can be estimated according to Slater’s rules as follows:

(i) Write the electron configuration for the atom using the following pattern, in which electrons in the s and p orbitals should be combined into the same group, while those in the d orbitals should be independent from those in the s and p orbitals. For example, [1s], [2s, 2p], [3s, 3p], [3d].

(ii) Identify the electron of interest and ignore all electrons in higher groups (larger “n” in [ns,np] group.). These do not shield electrons in lower groups.

(iii) Regarding the shielding experienced by an s- or p- electron, electrons within the same group contribute 0.35 to the shielding, except for 1s electrons, which contribute 0.30 to the shielding.

(iv) For the electrons in an [ns, np] group, the electrons in the n-1 group contribute 0.85 to the shielding.

(v) For the electrons in an [ns, np] group, electrons in the n-2 or lower groups contribute 1.00 to the shielding.

(vi) For the electrons in an [nd] or [nf] group, electrons within same group contribute 0.35 to the shielding. All electrons in higher groups of [nd] and [nf] orbitals are ignored.

(vii) For the electrons in an [nd] or [nf] group, the electrons in the lower groups contribute 1.00 to the shielding.

For example, according to Slater’s rule, in the case of silicon ($\ce{_{14}Si}$), which exhibits an electron configuration of $(1s)^2(2s)^2(2p)^6(3s)^2(3p)^2$, the effective nuclear charge for the valence electrons $Z^\mathrm{VE}{}_\mathrm{eff}$(Si) can be estimated as 4.15 [= 14–(0.35×3)–(0.85×8)–(1.00×2)].

2-3. The covalent radii of nitrogen and chlorine are $r$(N) = 70.0 [pm] and $r$(Cl) = 99.0 [pm], respectively. Using the effective nuclear charge $Z^\mathrm{VE}{}_\mathrm{eff}$ estimated with Slater’s rules, calculate the Allred–Rochow electronegativities $\chi_\mathrm{AR}$(N) and $\chi_\mathrm{AR}$(Cl) of nitrogen and chlorine.

The electronegativity values based on the Allred–Rochow definition can explain the products in the hydrolysis reaction of monochloroamine. Thus, ‘electronegativity’ is a concept that was qualitative in nature and whose numerical values vary depending on the definition.

problems.title: Sulfur in hot springs and volcanoes
problems.problem:
Problem 15. Sulfur in hot springs and volcanoes

Japan is known as a volcanic country, and the hot springs that are widely distributed throughout the country are deeply beloved. Hot springs exhibit different characteristics regarding e.g. temperature, acidity (pH), color, and smell, and are classified according to the chemical components they contain. Interestingly, many hot springs contain sulfur components.

1. Water from a certain hot spring (density: $1.00\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$) contains both thiosulfate ions and hydrogen sulfide. An excess of cadmium acetate is added to 100 mL of this hot spring water, and the resulting precipitate (9.50 mg) is separated by filtration. A small amount of starch is added as an indicator to the filtrate, and an aqueous $\ce{I2}$/KI solution (effective $\ce{I2}$ concentration: $2.50\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) is slowly added dropwise. After the addition of 7.30 mL of the aqueous $\ce{I2}$/KI solution to the analyte, the coloration due to iodine came to appear. Calculate the total sulfur (S) content [$\mathrm{mg\,kg^{-1}}$] in the initial hot spring water. Assume that sulfur is only derived from the thiosulfate ions and hydrogen sulfide and that no other species are involved in these reactions..

2. Hot springs that contain more than 2 mg of sulfur (S) derived from $\ce{H2S}$, $\ce{HS-}$, $\ce{S^{2-}}$, and $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$ in 1.00 kg of hot spring water are known as ‘sulfur springs’. In a water sample from a hot spring, the density is $1.00\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, the pH is 8.000, $[\ce{S^{2-}}]$ is $1.00\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, and $5.26\times10^{-5}$ mol of thiosulfate ion is present in 1.00 kg of the water. Calculate the total sulfur content [$\mathrm{mg\,kg^{-1}}$] of this hot spring.

The first and second acid dissociation constants of hydrogen sulfide are $K_1 = 9.50\times10^{-8}$ and $K_2 = 1.30\times10^{-14}$, respectively.

3. To investigate the content of hydrogen sulfide and sulfur dioxide contained in volcanic gas, 10.0 L of volcanic gas are sampled. The gas is absorbed into 500 mL of an aqueous $\ce{I2}$/KI basic solution (effective $\ce{I2}$ concentration: $2.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) under basic conditions. The generated elemental sulfur is removed by filtration, and the volume of the filtrate is adjusted with water to give a total volume of 1.00 L. Two 100 mL aliquots of this solution are placed in two beakers, which are referred to as beakers $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. Barium chloride is added to the solution in beaker $\mathbf{A}$ until no further precipitate appears, and 41.5 mg of white precipitate is isolated by filtration. The solution in beaker $\mathbf{B}$ is titrated with $2.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ sodium thiosulfate solution using starch as an indicator. After dropping 73.0 mL of the titrant into the solution, the coloration due to iodine disappears. Calculate the concentrations of hydrogen sulfide and sulfur dioxide in the volcanic gas [$\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$]. Assume that the only sulfur-containing components in this volcanic gas are hydrogen sulfide and sulfur dioxide, and that during the series of experiments described above, the hydrogen sulfide does not react with the sulfur dioxide directly, since they are present under dilute conditions. Additionally, assume that the only substances that react during this series of experiments are hydrogen sulfide, sulfur dioxide, and the related substances generated from them.

problems.title: Identification of unknown compounds and allotropes
problems.problem:
Problem 16. Identification of unknown compounds and allotropes

Part 1. Identification of inorganic compounds

$\boxed{\text{A}}$ is a crystalline solid of a binary compound. It contains a metal ion $\mathrm{X}^{n+}$ and is grayish-white in color. $\boxed{\text{A}}$ slowly reacts with water at room temperature to form $\boxed{\text{B}}$, which is scarcely soluble in water; the generation of a gas is observed during this reaction. Dehydration reaction occurs upon heating $\boxed{\text{B}}$ at approximately 350 °C to form the white compound $\boxed{\text{C}}$, which contains 39.7 weight% of oxygen atoms. Heating $\boxed{\text{A}}$ generates gas of an amount of 7.6 weight% based on $\boxed{\text{A}}$, and the elemental metal X is formed. $\underline{\text{(i) Heating a mass } M \text{ [g] of X under an } \mathrm{N_2} \text{ atmosphere provides a yellow-green metal nitride}}$. $\underline{\text{(ii) This metal nitride reacts with a large amount of water to generate } \boxed{\text{D}}}$. The amount of $\boxed{\text{D}}$ corresponds to the gas of volume 120 mL at 1 bar and 25 °C.

1-1. Write the chemical formulae of compounds $\boxed{\text{A}}$, $\boxed{\text{B}}$, $\boxed{\text{C}}$, and $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

1-2. Write the chemical reactions corresponding to the underlined parts (i) and (ii).

1-3. Calculate the weight $M$ [g].

Part 2. Allotropes

The term “allotrope” refers to one or more physical forms of a chemical element that occur in the same physical state. Allotropes generally exhibit different physical properties and may also differ in their chemical reactivity. For example, graphite and diamond have long been known as allotropes of carbon, and more recently, fullerenes and carbon nanotubes have been discovered as further carbon allotropes. One of the allotropes of phosphorus is a solid composed of $\ce{P4}$ molecules, which is called white phosphorus. It has a low melting point of 44 °C and is highly toxic, so care must be taken in its storage.

2-1. The solution $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectrum of fullerene $\ce{C60}$ (Figure 1) exhibits $\boxed{\text{E}}$ peak(s). X-ray diffraction measurements have revealed $\boxed{\text{F}}$ different covalent carbon–carbon bond length(s) in the crystal structure of fullerene $\ce{C60}$. Write the appropriate integer values for $\boxed{\text{E}}$ and $\boxed{\text{F}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-16-fig1.png

Figure 1. Structure of fullerene $\ce{C60}$.

2-2. Fullerene $\ce{C60}$ forms a crystal via van der Waals forces. The crystal structure of fullerene $\ce{C60}$ at room temperature is composed of a cubic unit cell with dimensions of 1.41 nm on each side. The molecules are located at all vertices and at the centers of all faces of the cubic unit cell. Calculate the density [$\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$] of the crystal of fullerene $\ce{C60}$.

2-3. The $\ce{P4}$ molecule has high structural symmetry, and all the P–P–P bond angles are 60°. Draw the steric structure of $\ce{P4}$.

Dioxygen and ozone are the allotropes of oxygen. Ozone acts as a strong oxidizing agent. For example, $\underline{\text{(iii) the oxidation reaction of potassium iodide by ozone in aqueous solution is accompanied with the generation of dioxygen, and the reaction}}$ is used for the quantitative determination of ozone. Ozone also exists in the stratosphere and acts as a filter that absorbs harmful ultraviolet light from sunlight. Dioxygen in the stratosphere is irradiated with ultraviolet light of wavelengths < 240 nm, where a dioxygen molecule is split into two oxygen atoms that react with another dioxygen molecule to produce ozone. On the other hand, ozone decomposes into dioxygen molecule and an oxygen atom when exposed to ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 240–315 nm. When these formation and decomposition reactions of ozone are in equilibrium, the concentration of ozone in the stratosphere is maintained at a constant level, blocking short-wave ultraviolet rays that are harmful to humans on the ground. In contrast, $\underline{\text{(iv) atmospheric nitric oxide reacts with ozone}}$, and $\underline{\text{(v) nitrogen dioxide reacts with oxygen atoms}}$, resulting in $\underline{\text{(vi) a reaction that converts ozone into dioxygen}}$. This creates an ozone hole that can allow harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun to reach the surface on the earth.

2-4. Write the reaction formula for the underlined part (iii).

2-5. $N$ [mol] of ozone is bubbled through 15 mL of an aqueous solution of potassium iodide with a concentration of $1.0\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$; we assume that the ozone reacts completely. The solution is then titrated with an aqueous solution of sodium thiosulfate with a concentration of $0.20\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$; the titration requires 3.5 mL of the sodium thiosulfate solution. Calculate $N$ [mol].

2-6. Write the reaction formulae for the underlined parts (iv)–(vi).

problems.title: Metal oxides
problems.problem:
Problem 17. Metal oxides

1. In the crystal structures of most metal oxides, the oxide ions ($\ce{O^{2-}}$) form a close-packed structure, wherein the metal ions occupy the voids created by $\ce{O^{2-}}$. Figure 1(a) shows the cubic close-packed structure created by $\ce{O^{2-}}$. Note that the ionic radius of $\ce{O^{2-}}$ is 0.140 nm. Answer the following questions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-17-fig1.png

Figure 1. (a) Cubic close-packed structure formed by $\ce{O^{2-}}$ in metal oxides, (b) octahedral void, (c) tetrahedral void. ● [red] $\ce{O^{2-}}$ ions, ● [grey] voids.

1-1. Considering $\ce{O^{2-}}$ as solid spheres in contact with each other, calculate the percentage volume of the voids in a cubic close-packed structure.

1-2. With reference to Figure 1(b) and (c), calculate the maximum radii of the spheres that can be placed in the octahedral and tetrahedral voids of a cubic close-packed structure composed of $\ce{O^{2-}}$, respectively.

1-3. Write the chemical formula for a ternary metal oxide $\mathrm{A}_x\mathrm{B}_y\mathrm{O}_z$ wherein one metal ion (A) occupies 1/8 of the tetrahedral voids in a cubic close-packed structure composed of $\ce{O^{2-}}$, and a second metal ion (B) occupies 1/2 of the octahedral voids.

1-4. Regular arrays of atoms, ions, or molecules in solids are represented by a repeating unit known as the unit cell. In $\ce{SrTiO3}$, which adopts a perovskite structure, the ionic radii of $\ce{Sr^{2+}}$ and $\ce{O^{2-}}$ are comparable, and a cubic close-packed structure is formed by $\ce{Sr^{2+}}$ and $\ce{O^{2-}}$. The $\ce{Ti^{4+}}$ ions occupy all octahedral voids formed by $\ce{O^{2-}}$. Based on this information, draw the unit cell of $\ce{SrTiO3}$ with reference to Figure 2, assuming $\ce{Ti^{4+}}$ (● [gold]) is located at the center of the cube. Draw $\ce{Sr^{2+}}$ as ● and $\ce{O^{2-}}$ as ×.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-17-fig2.png

Figure 2. Unit cell of $\ce{SrTiO3}$ showing only $\ce{Ti^{4+}}$ at the center.

Most divalent metal oxides (MO) crystallize in a rock salt structure wherein $\ce{M^{2+}}$ occupies the octahedral voids created by $\ce{O^{2-}}$ (Figure 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-17-fig3.png

Figure 3. Unit cell of CaO. Blue and red spheres represent $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\ce{O^{2-}}$, respectively. (● [blue] $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$, ● [red] $\ce{O^{2-}}$)

The thermodynamic properties of metal oxides can be discussed in terms of the standard molar enthalpy change ($\Delta H_\mathrm{Lexp}$) associated with the formation of gaseous ions from the ionic solid:

$$\ce{MO(s) -> M^{2+}(g) + O^{2-}(g)} \qquad \Delta H_\mathrm{Lexp} \qquad (1)$$

$\Delta H_\mathrm{Lexp}$ is known as the lattice enthalpy; although it cannot be measured directly, it can be determined from enthalpy data (Table 1) using a Born–Haber cycle, which is a closed path of steps that includes lattice formation as one stage.

Table 1. Enthalpy changes of reactions involved in the Born–Haber cycle

$$\begin{array}{lc} \text{Steps} & \text{Enthalpy change } [\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}] \\ \hline \text{Sublimation of Ca(s): } \ce{Ca(s) -> Ca(g)} & +193 \\ \text{Ionization of Ca(g) to } \ce{Ca+(g)}\text{: } \ce{Ca(g) -> Ca+(g) + e^-(g)} & +590 \\ \text{Ionization of } \ce{Ca+(g)} \text{ to } \ce{Ca^{2+}(g)}\text{: } \ce{Ca+(g) -> Ca^{2+}(g) + e^-(g)} & +1010 \\ \text{Dissociation of } \ce{O2}\text{: } \ce{O2(g) -> 2 O(g)} & +498 \\ \text{Electron gain by O(g): } \ce{O(g) + e^-(g) -> O^-(g)} & -141 \\ \text{Electron gain by } \ce{O^-(g)}\text{: } \ce{O^-(g) + e^-(g) -> O^{2-}(g)} & +878 \\ \text{Formation of CaO(s): } \ce{Ca(s) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CaO(s)} & -635 \end{array}$$

2-1. Calculate the $\Delta H_\mathrm{Lexp}$ [$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$] of CaO using the enthalpy data in Table 1 and the Born–Haber cycle.

The lattice enthalpy of an ionic crystal can be calculated theoretically ($\Delta H_\mathrm{Lcalc}$) from the sum of the Coulomb energies between the constituent ions as point charges. The Coulomb energy $E$ between ions is expressed by the following equation:

$$E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Z_1Z_2e^{2}}{r} \qquad (2)$$

where $\varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of the vacuum, $e$ the elementary charge, $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ the charge numbers of the ions, and $r$ the distance between the ions. $E$ is attractive (i.e., negative) between an anion and a cation, while $E$ is repulsive (i.e., positive) between two anions or two cations.

$\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ is surrounded by six $\ce{O^{2-}}$ in an octahedral arrangement (Figure 4).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-17-fig4.png

Figure 4. A unit cell of a rock salt structure to calculate the Madelung constant.

For a distance $d$ between $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\ce{O^{2-}}$ in the rock salt structure depicted in Figure 4, the Coulomb energy ($E_1$) between a $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and six $\ce{O^{2-}}$ is formulated as follows:

$$\boxed{\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad (3)}$$

In the structure depicted in Figure 4, twelve $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ are located at a distance of $\sqrt{2}d$ from a given $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$. The Coulomb energy ($E_2$) between the $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and the twelve surrounding $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ is formulated as follows:

$$\boxed{\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad (4)}$$

Similarly, for any given $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$, there are 8 $\ce{O^{2-}}$, 6 $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$, 24 $\ce{O^{2-}}$, and 24 $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ at distances of $\sqrt{3}d$, $\sqrt{4}d$, $\sqrt{5}d$, and $\sqrt{6}d$, respectively. The overall Coulomb energy $E_\mathrm{all}$, obtained by the summation of $E_\mathrm{n}$ converges to the following equation:

$$E_\mathrm{all} = \frac{N_\mathrm{A}Z^{+}Z^{-}e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d}M \qquad (5)$$

where $Z^{+}$ and $Z^{-}$ are the charge numbers of the cation and anion, respectively; $N_\mathrm{A}$ is Avogadro’s constant, and $M$ is the Madelung constant, which is 1.748 for the rock salt structure. The theoretical lattice enthalpy $\Delta H_\mathrm{Lcalc}$ is calculated using the Born–Mayer equation below, which takes into account the electron–electron and nucleus–nucleus repulsion of nearby ions:

$$\Delta H_\mathrm{Lcalc} = \frac{N_\mathrm{A}|Z^{+}Z^{-}|e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d}\left(1 - \frac{d^*}{d}\right)M \qquad (6)$$

where $d^*$ is a constant (typically: 0.0345 nm).

2-2. Fill in the blanks (3) and (4) with the appropriate equations.

2-3. Calculate $\Delta H_\mathrm{Lcalc}$ [$\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$] for CaO using equation (6); use $d$ = 0.240 nm.

problems.title: Coordination chemistry and its application to solid-state catalysts
problems.problem:
Problem 18. Coordination chemistry and its application to solid-state catalysts

Transition-metal complexes are formed by the coordination of ligands (e.g., $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{NH3}$) to transition metals or their ions. Most transition-metal complexes exhibit beautiful colors that cannot be explained by the classical theory of chemical bonding. Therefore, crystal-field theory has been developed; the repulsion between the d-electrons and the lone pairs of the ligands as negative point charges splits the energy of the five degenerate d-orbitals. Transition-metal complexes exhibit color because this energy separation and the corresponding transitions coincide with the energy of visible light.

Consider an octahedral transition-metal complex with the metal ion at the origin of a three-dimensional coordinate system and a total of six ligands as negative point charges equidistant from the origin on the $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes (Figure 1a). The energies of the five degenerate d-orbitals are split into two groups called the $\mathrm{e_g}$ and $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals, which are oriented along and between the axes, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-18-fig1.png

Figure 1. Arrangement of the metal ion ($\mathrm{M^{n+}}$) and ligands (L) in (a) octahedral and (b) tetrahedral complexes. Blue solid lines represent the coordination bonds. The metal ion is located at the origin (0, 0, 0) of the three-dimensional coordinate system. The coordinates of the four ligands in the tetrahedral complex are indicated for clarity.

1. Classify the five d-orbitals into $\mathrm{e_g}$ and $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals.

Let the energy separation between the $\mathrm{e_g}$ and $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals (i.e., the crystal-field splitting parameter) be $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$, where the subscript O signifies an octahedral arrangement. The barycenter of the energies of the $\mathrm{e_g}$ and $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals is equal to the energy of the five degenerate d-orbitals.

2. Write the energies of the $\mathrm{e_g}$ and $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals relative to the barycenter in units of $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$.

The energetically split d-orbitals, caused by the repulsion between the transition metal ion and the ligands, accommodate electrons according to Hund’s rule. For example, $\ce{Ti^{3+}}$ with one d-electron ($\mathrm{d^1}$) forms an octahedral complex $\ce{[Ti(H2O)6]^{3+}}$; this complex is energetically more stable than $\ce{Ti^{3+}}$ without ligands. This additional stability relative to the barycenter is known as the ‘crystal field stabilization energy’ (CFSE). The first through third d-electrons ($\mathrm{d^1}$ to $\mathrm{d^3}$) are exclusively accommodated in the $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals. However, there are two possible ground-state electron configurations for $\mathrm{d^4}$ to $\mathrm{d^7}$. Namely, Hund’s rule applies when the CFSE is small, resulting in a ‘high-spin’ ground state with a large number of unpaired electrons. On the other hand, Hund’s rule does not apply when the CFSE is large, resulting in a ‘low-spin’ ground state with a smaller number of unpaired electrons. In general, the CFSE depends on the type of ligands (cf. spectrochemical series).

3. Draw the high-spin electron configurations of octahedral complexes for $\mathrm{d^4}$-$\mathrm{d^7}$ by referring to the electron configuration of $\mathrm{d^3}$ shown below, and calculate each CFSE in units of $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-18-fig2.png

While six-coordinate octahedral complexes are the most common among the transition-metal complexes, four-coordinate complexes are also very frequently encountered. There are two types of four-coordinate complexes, tetrahedral and square planar complexes. Of these two, tetrahedral complexes have a lower steric repulsion between the ligands, and similarly to octahedral complexes, the energy splitting of their d-orbitals can be considered using crystal-field theory. In the tetrahedral crystal field (Figure 1b), the energy of the five degenerate d-orbitals is split into two sets of orbitals, e and $\mathrm{t_2}$ orbitals.

4. Draw the energy separation between the e and $\mathrm{t_2}$ orbitals with $\Delta_\mathrm{T}$ as the crystal-field splitting parameter, where the subscript T signifies a tetrahedral arrangement. Classify the five d-orbitals into e and $\mathrm{t_2}$ orbitals. Write the energies of e and $\mathrm{t_2}$ orbitals relative to the barycenter in units of $\Delta_\mathrm{T}$.

When an aqueous solution containing the octahedral complex $\ce{[Ti(H2O)6]^{3+}}$ is irradiated with visible light, a d-electron is excited from the $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ to the $\mathrm{e_g}$ orbital, which is accompanied by the absorption of green light ($\lambda$ = 500 nm). Consequently, the aqueous solution takes on a red-purple color, which is the complementary color of green.

5. Calculate the energy separation $\Delta_\mathrm{O}$ ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) between the $\mathrm{e_g}$ and $\mathrm{t_{2g}}$ orbitals in $\ce{[Ti(H2O)6]^{3+}}$.

Transition-metal complexes with carbon monoxide (CO) as a ligand are called metal carbonyls. Representative examples are the octahedral $\ce{Cr(CO)6}$ and tetrahedral $\ce{Ni(CO)4}$ complexes. The total number of electrons provided by the metal and ligands in a transition-metal complex is called the effective atomic number (EAN), and the 18-electron rule states that a complex is stable when the EAN is equal to the atomic number of noble gases. For instance, Cr and the CO ligands in $\ce{Cr(CO)6}$ supply 6 and 2 × 6 = 12 electrons, respectively; similarly, Ni and the CO ligands in $\ce{Ni(CO)4}$ supply 10 and 2 × 4 = 8 electrons, respectively, satisfying the 18-electron rule for each metal carbonyl. In addition to mononuclear metal carbonyls with one metal atom, there are also multinuclear metal carbonyls with multiple metal atoms and metal–metal bonds.

6. Draw the molecular structure of $\ce{Mn2(CO)10}$ and $\ce{Ir4(CO)12}$ and show that the EAN per metal atom is 18.

The coordination bonds formed between carbon monoxide (CO) and metals can be used to estimate the size of metal nanoparticles loaded on catalyst support such as $\ce{Al2O3}$. Figure 2a shows a schematic illustration of a platinum catalyst supported on alumina ($\ce{Pt/Al2O3}$), which is used as an automotive catalyst.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-18-fig3.png

Figure 2. Schematic illustrations of (a) the $\ce{Pt/Al2O3}$ catalyst and (b) the CO molecules adsorbed on the Pt surface. The Pt metal particles in (a) are the same size.

1.0 g of $\ce{Pt/Al2O3}$ catalyst that contains 0.010 g of Pt metal is prepared. Upon exposure to CO gas, 0.55 mL (1.0 bar, 273 K) of CO was adsorbed per 1.0 g of catalyst. The Pt metal particles on $\ce{Al2O3}$ are spherical, and their surfaces can be regarded as being covered with Pt atoms without gaps. As shown in Figure 2b, one CO molecule coordinates to one Pt atom exposed on the surface. The density of the Pt metal is $21.45\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, and the area occupied by each Pt atom is $8.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{nm^{2}}$.

7. Answer the following questions.

7-1. Calculate the ratio [%] of Pt atoms exposed on the surface to the total number of Pt atoms in the spherical Pt metal particles.

7-2. Calculate the number of CO molecules adsorbed per 1.0 g of Pt metal dispersed on the $\ce{Al2O3}$ support.

7-3. Calculate the surface area [$\mathrm{m^{2}}$] per 1.0 g of Pt metal.

7-4. Calculate the diameter of the Pt metal particles.

problems.title: Acids and bases
problems.problem:
Problem 19. Acids and bases

In 1923, Brønsted and Lowry defined an acid–base reaction as the transfer of a proton ($\ce{H+}$) from the proton donor (acid) to the proton acceptor (base).

$$\ce{HF + H2O <=> H3O+ + F-} \qquad (1)$$

$$\ce{H2O + NH3 <=> NH4+ + OH-} \qquad (2)$$

Hydrogen fluoride (HF) is an example of a Brønsted acid, ammonia ($\ce{NH3}$) is an example of a Brønsted base, while water ($\ce{H2O}$) is amphoteric, i.e., it can behave as both a Brønsted acid and a Brønsted base. When acid–base reactions are in chemical equilibrium, the reactions are indicated by two one-sided arrows as in (1) and (2). When HF donates a proton to $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{F-}$ and $\ce{H3O+}$ are formed as the conjugate base and conjugate acid, respectively. Brønsted acidity can be evaluated quantitatively using the acidity constant, or qualitatively using the $\underline{\text{(a) stability of the conjugated base}}$.

1. Arrange the following Brønsted acids in order of increasing acidity by referring to the underlined part (a).

$$\ce{HClO}\quad \ce{HClO2}\quad \ce{HClO3}\quad \ce{HClO4}$$

The Brønsted acidity of hydrogen halides (HX, X = F, Cl, Br, I) can be evaluated by the standard enthalpy change ($\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HX}$) of the protonation reaction of their conjugate bases ($\ce{X-}$):

$$\ce{X^-(g) + H^+(g) -> HX(g)} \qquad \Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HX} \quad (3)$$

This reaction can be divided into three steps:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{Electron loss from } \ce{X-}\text{: } \ce{X^-(g) -> X(g) + e^-(g)} & \Delta H^\circ_1 & (4) \\ \text{Electron gain by } \ce{H+}\text{: } \ce{H^+(g) + e^-(g) -> H(g)} & \Delta H^\circ_2 & (5) \\ \text{Combination of H and X: } \ce{H(g) + X(g) -> HX(g)} & \Delta H^\circ_3 & (6) \end{array}$$

Therefore, $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HX}$ is calculated as $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HX} = \Delta H^\circ_1 + \Delta H^\circ_2 + \Delta H^\circ_3$.

2. Calculate the absolute value of $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HF}$ ($|\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HF}|$ in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) by drawing a thermodynamic cycle for the protonation reaction of $\ce{F-}$. Use the following values if necessary: H–F bond dissociation enthalpy: $567\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; ionization enthalpy of hydrogen: $1312\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; enthalpy of electron gain by fluorine: $-328\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

3. Calculate the absolute value of $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HI}$ ($|\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HI}|$ in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) by drawing a thermodynamic cycle for the protonation reaction of $\ce{I-}$. Use the following values if necessary: H–I bond dissociation enthalpy: $298\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; enthalpy of electron gain by iodine: $-295\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

4. According to Q2 and Q3, $|\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HI}|$ (a)__ $|\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{HF}|$; therefore, the Brønsted acidity of hydrogen halides is arranged in the following order, HF (b)__ HCl (b)__ HBr (b)__ HI. Choose which inequality sign, ‘>’ or ‘<’, should be placed in blanks a and b.

Metal ions are hydrated in aqueous solutions, and generally, the first hydration shell of metal ions consists of six water molecules. When the oxygen atom of a water molecule is strongly coordinated to a metal ion, the coordinated water acts as a proton donor as shown in (7).

$$[\mathrm{M(OH_2)_6}]^{n+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \ce{H2O(l)} \rightleftharpoons [\mathrm{M(OH_2)_5(OH)}]^{(n-1)+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \ce{H3O+(aq)} \qquad (7)$$

5. Arrange the following aqua acids in order of increasing acidity.

$$\ce{[Na(H2O)6]+}\quad \ce{[Ca(H2O)6]^{2+}}\quad \ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^{3+}}\quad \ce{[Zn(H2O)6]^{2+}}$$

Lewis introduced a more general concept of acids and bases, which includes reactions that do not involve protons. Lewis defined an acid–base reaction as the transfer of an electron pair from the electron-pair donor (Lewis base) to the electron-pair acceptor (Lewis acid). Note that the Brønsted acid HA is a complex formed by the Lewis acid $\ce{H+}$ with the Lewis base $\ce{A-}$. All Brønsted acids and Brønsted bases exhibit Lewis acidity and Lewis basicity, respectively.

6. Identify the Lewis acids and bases in each of the following reactions.

(i) $\ce{BF3 + NH3 -> BF3NH3}$

(ii) $\ce{Ni + 4 CO -> [Ni(CO)4]}$

(iii) $\ce{CO2 + OH- -> HCO3-}$

(iv) $\ce{SiF4 + 2 F- -> SiF6^{2-}}$

7. Phosphoric acid ($\ce{H3PO4}$) and boric acid ($\ce{H3BO3}$) are both acids with three hydrogens. While phosphoric acid reacts as a triprotic Brønsted acid, boric acid reacts as a monoprotic acid. Draw the Lewis structure of the conjugate base of boric acid by considering the reaction with water.

problems.title: Semiconductors
problems.problem:
Problem 20. Semiconductors

In molecules that exist as gases or liquids, the molecular orbitals are formed by the overlap between the atomic orbitals of individual atoms. In contrast, in the electronic state of a solid composed of an infinite number of atoms, many atomic orbitals are overlapping; therefore, many molecular orbitals with close energy levels are formed. As the gap between their energy levels is very narrow, these orbitals are for practical reasons represented as an energy band. Insulators have a wide energy gap between the valence band (VB), which is completely filled with electrons, and the conduction band (CB), which does not contain electrons (Figure 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-20-fig1.png

Figure 1. Schematic view of the electronic band structure in solid-state materials.

In insulators, the electrons are bound within the VB. On the other hand, in semiconductors, some electrons ($\mathrm{e^-}$) in the VB can be transferred to the CB by thermal energy, as the energy gap between the VB and CB is relatively small. An electron transition in a semiconductor creates a hole in the VB; this hole behaves like a positively charged particle. The hole is commonly referred to as $\mathrm{h^+}$. The electrons and holes formed in the semiconductor can move, which results in electrical conductivity.

1. With reference to Figure 1, illustrate the band structure of a metallic conductor, which shows electrical conductivity even when the temperature is lowered.

Semiconductors are classified as either intrinsic or extrinsic semiconductors. An intrinsic semiconductor is composed of a pure material, and the same number of electrons and holes are produced by thermal energy and other factors. The electrical conductivity is not very high. On the other hand, there are two types of extrinsic semiconductors, n-type and p-type, whose electrical conductivity is generally higher than that of intrinsic semiconductors. In n-type semiconductors, small amounts of electrons are added to a pure material (electron doping), while in p-type semiconductors, small amounts of holes are added to a pure material (hole doping). For example, adding a small amount of P to pure Si, a typical intrinsic semiconductor, results in the doping of an extra electron (Figure 2). Accordingly, P-doped Si exhibits n-type semiconductor properties.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-20-fig2.png

Figure 2. Schematic view for electron states of (a) Si and (b) P-doped Si.

2. Indicate which elements in the following list could be used to produce p-type semiconductor properties in Si.

Ga, Ge, As, B

$\ce{TiO2}$, a representative oxide semiconductor, is capable of inducing the water-splitting reaction at room temperature using light energy as a driving force. The water-splitting reaction, which generates hydrogen ($\ce{H2}$) from water, is expected to be a significant source of renewable energy in the near future. The discovery of the following phenomena is one reason for the development of photocatalysts such as $\ce{TiO2}$. $\underline{\text{(1) The electrolysis of water occurs when a voltage is applied.}}$ In contrast, $\underline{\text{(2) when } \mathrm{TiO_2} \text{ and platinum electrodes are arranged as shown in Figure 3 and the } \mathrm{TiO_2} \text{ side is exposed to light irradiation, oxygen and hydrogen are generated from each electrode.}}$ This phenomenon is called the Honda–Fujishima effect and was discovered in 1972. Electrons and holes are produced by irradiating $\ce{TiO2}$ with light, which leads to the reduction and oxidation of water, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2021-20-fig3.png

Figure 3. Schematic illustration of the photoelectrochemical water-splitting reaction.

3-1. When $\ce{TiO2}$ is subjected to a thermal treatment under an $\ce{H2}$ flow, it exhibits n-type semiconductor properties. Explain the reasons for this phenomenon.

3-2. Regarding the underlined part in (1), calculate the voltage at which water can be thermodynamically electrolyzed. The standard Gibbs energy change for the splitting of 1 mole of water is 237 kJ.
