problems.title: Recyclable Plastic—Turning Waste into Treasure
problems.problem:
Problem 22. Recyclable Plastic—Turning Waste into Treasure

White pollution creates serious damage to the environment and ecosystems, and the topic about recyclable plastic and degradable polymers has gained widespread attention in recent years. Polyethylene (PE) is the largest-volume plastic in the world, with annual production exceeding 100 million metric tons. In contrast to other plastics, PE is remarkably inert with necessitating pyrolysis temperature above 400 °C, which is due to all atoms of PE being connected by strong single C-C and C-H bonds, leading to tremendous stability. Therefore, to endow PE with degradability, we need to start with activation of C-H bond or C-C bond.

Part A

A strategy for PE degradation has been developed by Chinese scientist, based on a tandem catalytic cross alkene metathesis shown below. First, the dehydrogenation catalyst removes hydrogen from both PE and a light alkane to form unsaturated species and [Ir-$\ce{H2}$], then the alkene metathesis catalyst scrambles the alkenes, and finally hydrogenation of the newly formed alkenes with [Ir-$\ce{H2}$] affords saturated alkanes. Consequently, the PE chain is cut into two pieces, and after multiple cycles with light alkanes, PE will be eventually converted to short hydrocarbons for industrial use as oil and waxes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig1.png

22-1 The dehydrogenation and hydrogenation process require a coordination catalyst [Ir], the synthetic route of which is shown below, draw the structures of $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$. Known that $\mathbf{2}$ contains two five-membered cycles.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig2.png

22-2 To investigate the exact reaction site, PE is represented as

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig3.png

and the light alkane added is represented as

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig4.png

(assume $m_1 > m_2 \gg n_1 > n_2 > 0$), then the process can be simplified as follow (the symbol ‘>>’ means ‘far more than’):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig5.png

Assuming that in the first step, there are 3 different kinds of $\mathbf{A}$, the dehydrogenation product of PE (the possible dehydrogenation site:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig6.png

). Similarly, there are 4 different kind of $\mathbf{B}$, the dehydrogenation product of light alkane (regardless of geometric isomerism, assuming that $n_1$ and $n_2$ are too small for being regarded as polymers).

After one cycle of reactions, there are at most ______ possible kinds of polymers in mixture $\mathbf{C}$.

22-3 In question 1.2, if in the real reaction $m_1 = 40$ and $m_2 = 38$ (also with 3 possible dehydrogenation site), the light alkane added is n-hexane ($\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3}$), and the hexane may dehydrogenate anywhere to form C=C double bond, then after one cycle of reactions, there are at most ______ possible kinds of polymers in mixture $\mathbf{D}$.

22-4 Actually most of the polymer materials contain side chain or heteroatoms, which are not that ‘stubborn’ as PE and more suitable for other degradation methods. Choose the polymer material from below that is the most suitable for degradation by alkene metathesis.

(a) Polypropylene (b) Phenolic Resin (c) Polyamide (d) Polyurethane

22-5 The early polymer degradation mainly relies on thermolysis. At certain temperature, firstly the C-C bond in the polymer main chain breaks into free radicals, and then comes to other reactions. Think about why thermolysis of PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate) mainly produces monomers (MMA, methyl methacrylate), while thermolysis of PE produces only 1% of monomer and a lot of fragments with large molecular weight? According to the following polymer structure, choose the most appropriate reason.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig7.png

(a) PMMA doesn’t melt when heated, but PE melts first when heated.

(b) PMMA contains hydrolyzable ester side groups, but PE is non-hydrolyzable.

(c) PMMA has lower thermolysis temperature, but that of PE is higher.

(d) PMMA side groups stabilizes free radicals, but free radicals from PE is unstable.

Part B

It is reported that by introducing low density of oxygen-containing functional groups into the hydrocarbon chain, the crystalline structure and the desirable material properties of PE can be fully retained with great recyclability (recovery rate > 96%). These so called “PE” are actually polyesters, which can be synthesized by monomers from biorefining of plant oils:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig8.png

(b) The polymer materials have great mechanical properties.

(c) The polymer chain contains ester bonds, which can be nucleophilic attacked.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-22-fig9.png

22-9 Polymer $\mathbf{P1}$ and $\mathbf{P2}$ can be almost completely degraded, and their degradation products can be recycled for synthesis of new materials. Choose the correct degradation mixture under different conditions and mark whether they are $\mathbf{R1}$, $\mathbf{R2}$ and $\mathbf{R3}$.

problems.title: The combustion of water gas

Problem 23. The combustion of water gas

Water gas is a mixture of $\ce{H2}$ (g) and CO (g) with the molar ratio of 1:1. In order to achieve its complete combustion, the amount of $\ce{O2}$ provided in the form of air (21% $\ce{O2}$ and 79% $\ce{N2}$) should be twice of the amount needed from the reaction. At 298 K, the thermodynamic data of the species involved in the reactions are listed in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c} & \ce{H2O(g)} & \ce{CO(g)} & \ce{N2(g)} & \ce{O2(g)} & \ce{CO2(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}H_\mathrm{m}^\circ\,(298\,\mathrm{K})\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & -241.83 & -110.52 & & & -393.51 \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}G_\mathrm{m}^\circ\,(298\,\mathrm{K})\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & & -137.27 & & & -394.38 \\ \hline C_{p,\mathrm{m}}^\circ\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & 33.58 & 29.14 & 29.12 & 29.36 & 37.13 \end{array}$$

Assume that $C_{p,\mathrm{m}}^\circ$ does not change with temperature.

23-1 Calculate the highest temperature that the system can reach if the initial temperature is 298 K, the pressure is maintained constant at $10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, and the combustion proceeds in an adiabatic manner.

23-2 The enthalpy and entropy changes with temperature are given by the equations:

$$\Delta_\mathrm{r}H_\mathrm{m}^\circ(T_2) = \Delta_\mathrm{r}H_\mathrm{m}^\circ(T_1) + \Delta_\mathrm{r}C_p^\circ\,(T_2 - T_1)$$

$$\Delta_\mathrm{r}S_\mathrm{m}^\circ(T_2) = \Delta_\mathrm{r}S_\mathrm{m}^\circ(T_1) + \Delta_\mathrm{r}C_p^\circ \ln\frac{T_2}{T_1}$$

Calculate the $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G_\mathrm{m}^\circ$ of the reaction $\ce{CO(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CO2(g)}$ at 310 K.

Problem 25. The condensation of 1-butanol vapor

In order to condense the vapor of 1-butanol at 273 K, the supersaturation ratio (the ratio between the actual vapor pressure needed for the condensation and the saturated vapor pressure on top of a flat liquid surface) has to be 4. At 273 K, the surface tension of 1-butanol, $\sigma$, is $2.61\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, density, $\rho$, is $0.81\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and molar mass, $M$, is $74\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}$. The relationship between the saturated vapor pressure on top of a curved surface, $p$, and the saturated vapor pressure on top of a flat surface, $p_0$, is given by the Kelvin equation: $\ln\dfrac{p}{p_0} = \dfrac{2\sigma M}{\rho R T r}$, where R is the ideal gas constant, $T$ is the temperature, and $r$ is the radius of liquid droplet.

25-1 Calculate the radius of the droplet when the supersaturation ratio is 4.

25-2 Calculate the number of molecules in the 1-butanol droplet.

The decomposition reaction of a compound $\ce{A2B}$ proceeds with the chemical equation $\mathrm{2A_2B} \xrightarrow{k} \mathrm{2A_2 + B_2}$, and the reaction rate equation follows $r = kc_{\mathrm{A_2B}}^2$. The kinetic data of the system is given in the table below:

26-3 The reaction, $\ce{A -> C}$, can occur by two different mechanisms (Fig. 26):

(a) The reaction $\mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{k_a} \mathrm{C}$ occurs directly, and the half-life is not related to the initial concentration. At 294 K, the half-life is 1000 min, and at 340 K, the time needed for the concentration of A decreases to 1/1024 of the original concentration is 0.10 min.

(b) The reaction proceeds in two steps:

$$\mathrm{A} \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \mathrm{A^*} \qquad \mathrm{A^*} \xrightarrow{k_2} \mathrm{C}$$

problems.title: π-conjugated systems
problems.problem:
Problem 28. $\pi$-conjugated systems

Particle in a box and Hückel molecular orbital (HMO) theory are the two simple models to describe the state of $\pi$ electrons in conjugated molecules.

The $\pi$ electrons in linear polyenes can be viewed as particles moving in a one-dimensional box. Assuming that a linear polyene molecule is composed of $2k$ C atoms, the lengths of all the C=C double bonds and C-C single bonds are $d$, the length of the one-dimensional box $l$ is $(2k + 1)d$, and the energies of the electrons in the box are defined by the formula $E_n = \dfrac{n^2h^2}{8ml^2}$ ($n$ = 1, 2, …), where $m$ is the mass of electron and $h$ is Planck’s constant.

28-1 Calculate the energy differences of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO), i.e. $\Delta E = E_\mathrm{LUMO} - E_\mathrm{HOMO}$, of (a) 1, 3-butadiene, (b) 1, 3, 5-hexatriene, (c) 1, 3, 5, 7-octatetraene.

28-2 Sort the max. wavelengths of the absorption spectra, $\lambda_\mathrm{a,\,max}$, $\lambda_\mathrm{b,\,max}$ and $\lambda_\mathrm{c,\,max}$, of these three molecules in increasing order.

Based on experimental evidence, the $\lambda_\mathrm{max}$ calculated from the above model has non-negligible errors, thus the $\Delta E$ should further be modified by the formula:

$$\Delta E' = E_\mathrm{LUMO} - E_\mathrm{HOMO} + 3.25\times10^{-19}\left(1 - \frac{1}{2k}\right)\,\mathrm{J}$$

28-3 Assuming that the $\lambda_\mathrm{max}$ of 1, 3, 5-hexatriene is 268 nm, calculate $d$.

The electrons in anthracene can be viewed as particles moving in a two-dimensional box whose length is $a$ and width is $b$. The energies of the $\pi$ electrons in the box are defined by:

$$E_{n_x,n_y} = \frac{h^2}{8ml^2}\left(\frac{n_x^2}{a^2} + \frac{n_y^2}{b^2}\right)\quad (n_x = 1, 2, \ldots;\ n_y = 1, 2, \ldots;).$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2022-28-fig1.png

28-4 The $\lambda_\mathrm{max}$ of its absorption spectrum is 357 nm. Assuming $a = 3b$, calculate $b$.

When treating linear polyenes with the HMO theory, the energies of the $\pi$ electrons are defined by $E_n = \alpha + 2\beta\cos\dfrac{n\pi}{2k+1}$ ($n$ = 1, 2, …2$k$), where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are negative numbers, and $\alpha$ represents the energy of an electron in an isolated $2p_z$ orbital, and $\beta$ is the interaction energy between two neighboring $2p_z$ orbitals.

28-5 Calculate the energy levels of all the occupied orbitals and HOMO of 1, 3, 5-hexatriene.

The energy levels of the $\pi$ molecular orbitals of polyacenes include $E = \alpha + \beta$ and $E = \alpha - \beta$, and the rest of the $4N$ energy levels are given by

$$E = \alpha \pm \frac{\beta}{2}\left[1 \pm \sqrt{9 + 8\cos\left(\frac{p\pi}{N+1}\right)}\right]\quad (p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, N)$$

28-6 The $\lambda_\mathrm{max}$ of its absorption spectrum is 357 nm, calculate the value of $\beta$.

problems.title: The Sun-to-Fuel Project
problems.problem:
Problem 1. The Sun-to-Fuel Project

There are many approaches being investigated for the conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ to syngas or higher fuels, as these conversions would close the anthropogenic carbon cycle. A promising “sun-to-fuel” approach, being developed by Prof. A. Steinfeld from ETHZ, uses cerium dioxide and solar irradiation to generate syngas (a mixture of $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{CO2}$) at an industrial scale. $\ce{CO2}$ thereby can be obtained through direct air capture (DAC). The whole approach then comprises three essential units: the DAC, the solar redox unit using non-stoichiometric $\ce{CeO2}$, and the gas-to-liquid (GTL) unit that produces methanol or kerosene depending on the syngas composition.

The solar redox unit relies on a two-step catalytic cycle: in the first step $\ce{CeO2}$ is non-stoichiometrically reduced by losing oxygen, using sunlight energy. In the second step it is re-oxidized by $\ce{CO2}$ to produce $\ce{CO}$, or by $\ce{H2O}$ to produce $\ce{H2}$, at far lower temperatures than the reduction step. The non-stoichiometry after reduction is denoted by $\delta$ and it contributes to the oxygen exchange capacity of $\ce{CeO2}$.

The process starts with the non-stoichiometric reduction of $\ce{CeO2}$ as well as the re-oxidation by $\ce{CO2}$ or by $\ce{H2O}$ can be expressed by the equation:

$$\mathrm{CeO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta} + \tfrac{\delta}{2}\,\mathrm{O_2} \qquad (1)$$

This is followed by re-oxidation by $\ce{CO2}$ and/or $\ce{H2O}$:

$$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta} + \delta\,\mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CeO_2} + \delta\,\mathrm{CO} \\ \mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta} + \delta\,\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{CeO_2} + \delta\,\mathrm{H_2} \end{array}$$

In an initial experiment, the $\ce{O2}$ evolution and the syngas formation were measured after the injection of $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$. The following data were obtained (with a margin of error of about 15%).

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Total } \mathrm{O_2} \text{ release} & 1.52\ \mathrm{mL\,g^{-1}_{CeO_2}} \\ \hline \text{Total syngas production} & 3.15\ \mathrm{mL\,g^{-1}_{CeO_2}} \\ \hline \text{Total } \mathrm{H_2} \text{ production} & 2.21\ \mathrm{mL\,g^{-1}_{CeO_2}} \\ \hline \text{Total CO production} & 0.94\ \mathrm{mL\,g^{-1}_{CeO_2}} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

1.1 Calculate the $\delta$ of equation (1) per mole ceria. (Note that throughout the task, you can assume that gases have a molar volume of 22.4 L).

Later on, it became clear that complete re-oxidation is not achieved in the cyclic process. Thus, the reduction equation has to be re-written as:

$$\mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta_{ox}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta_{red}} + \alpha\,\mathrm{O_2}$$

where $\delta_{red}$ is the non-stoichiometry after the reduction reaction and $\delta_{ox}$ is the non-stoichiometry after re-oxidation.

$\alpha$ signifies the oxygen exchange capacity of $\ce{CeO2}$ and therefore also the fuel yield per cycle.

1.2 Provide the balanced equations for i) the reduction of $\mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta_{ox}}$ to $\mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta_{red}}$ so that exactly 1 mol of O-atoms is produced and for the re-oxidation by ii) $\ce{CO2}$ and iii) $\ce{H2O}$ to $\mathrm{CeO}_{2-\delta_{ox}}$, respectively.

$\alpha$ depends on the temperature and the partial pressure of $\ce{O2}$. $\Delta_R H$ for the reduction process is 950 kJ per mole of released $\ce{O2}$.

1.3 Choose the most suitable conditions for the reduction process.

☐ Low $\ce{O2}$ partial pressure and low temperature

☐ Low $\ce{O2}$ partial pressure and high temperature

☐ High $\ce{O2}$ partial pressure and low temperature

☐ High $\ce{O2}$ partial pressure and high temperature

Using thermodynamic data, $\alpha$ can therefore be calculated as a function of the $\ce{O2}$ partial pressure at different temperatures. The relevant equations are given below:

$$\begin{array}{l} \log 2\alpha_{1673\,\mathrm{K}} = -(0.2105 \log p(\mathrm{O_2})/\mathrm{bar} + 2.613) \\ \log 2\alpha_{1723\,\mathrm{K}} = -(0.2168 \log p(\mathrm{O_2})/\mathrm{bar} + 2.4585) \\ \log 2\alpha_{1773\,\mathrm{K}} = -(0.2231 \log p(\mathrm{O_2})/\mathrm{bar} + 2.3040) \end{array}$$

1.4 Calculate $\alpha$ of the system at 1500 °C and $p\mathrm{O_2}$ = 0.1 mbar and show that its oxygen exchange capacity is bigger than for the system in question 1.

1.5 Determine the percentage by which $\alpha$ drops, when the reduction is run at 1400 °C instead of 1500 °C. Assume that $p\mathrm{O_2}$ = 0.1 mbar for both temperatures.

In a typical run using $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{CO2}$ simultaneously for the re-oxidation, the following data for a 20-minute and an 8-minute run under the same conditions (1500°C and $p(\mathrm{O_2})$ = 0.1 mbar) were obtained:

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \text{Cycle time} & 20.0\ \text{min} & 8.0\ \text{min} \\ \hline \text{Collected Gas} & 18.5\ \text{L} & 9.4\ \text{L} \\ \hline \text{Gas composition} & 40.7\%\ \mathrm{H_2},\ 4.3\%\ \mathrm{CO},\ 22.4\%\ \mathrm{CO_2},\ 32.6\%\ \mathrm{Ar} & 59.9\%\ \mathrm{H_2},\ 6.0\%\ \mathrm{CO},\ 17.2\%\ \mathrm{CO_2},\ 16.9\%\ \mathrm{Ar} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Argon, Ar, is used to repressurize the solar redox unit to 1 bar.

1.6 For the 20.0 min run, calculate the $\ce{H2}$ : $\mathrm{CO}_x$ ratio where $\mathrm{CO}_x$ = CO + $\ce{CO2}$.

1.7 Calculate the yield of conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ to CO for the 20-minute run.

1.8 Depending on when the reaction is ended, different compositions are obtained. Repeat the calculations of questions 6 and 7 for the 8.0 min run.

The final step (Gas to Liquid, GTL) is the synthesis of methanol or of liquid alkanes according to the Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process. The FT synthesis works with CO and $\ce{H2}$ whereas the methanol synthesis can also process $\ce{CO2}$.

1.9 Provide the general reaction equations for the production of alkanes and for the production of alkenes, starting from syngas.

The process producing methanol works both with $\ce{H2}$ + CO, and with $\ce{H2}$ + $\ce{CO2}$.

1.10 Provide the reaction equations for both substrate mixtures.

1.11 Comparing the 20.0 min and 8.0 min runs, decide which one is more suitable for methanol synthesis and which one for the FT process.

In a typical long run 96.2 L of syngas was collected. Its composition was 59.5% $\ce{H2}$ and 4.6% CO, and the rest was $\ce{CO2}$ and Ar. The ratio of $\ce{H2}$ to $\mathrm{CO}_x$ was 2.69. In the last step of the sun-to-fuel process, methanol can be synthesized by the processes studied above.

1.12 The yield of methanol production was 85%. Calculate how many grams of methanol were produced.

problems.title: Many-faceted Oxides of Carbon
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Many-faceted Oxides of Carbon

The trapping and conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ has become a major challenge in modern society. Whereas nature converts $\ce{CO2}$ elegantly into carbohydrates via the Calvin cycle with the help of solar energy, industry uses the Sabatier reaction to convert $\ce{CO2}$ to methane. Along this path, partially reduced products such as formic acid represent important intermediates. Conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ requires its activation, and modern research in homo- and heterogeneous catalysis for this reaction is steadily growing. Essentially any conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ requires $\ce{H2}$, as a co-reactant. Thus, the activation of $\ce{CO2}$ also requires the activation of $\ce{H2}$ at the same time. This leads to very interesting chemistry that includes catalyst design, mechanistic studies and biomimetic chemistry.

2.1 Complete the following reaction sequence with 2 $\ce{H+}$ and 2 $\ce{e-}$ in each step and the eventual side products. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

$$\ce{CO2} \longrightarrow \mathbf{A} \longrightarrow \mathbf{B} \longrightarrow \ce{H3COH + H2O}$$

2.2 To activate $\ce{CO2}$, it must be polarized through non-covalent interactions. Describe the chemical properties associated with polarity of potential activators as indicated in the following scheme.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-2-fig1.png

$\ce{CO2}$ and ammonia ($\ce{NH3}$) react to form urea ($\ce{CO(NH2)2}$), which is a widely used fertilizer in agriculture. Before $\ce{NH3}$ was available in large quantities, $\ce{CaCO3}$ was reacted with carbon to get calcium carbide (acetylide, $\ce{CaC2}$). $\ce{CaC2}$ reacts at high temperatures with $\ce{N2}$ to give $\ce{CaCN2}$. $\ce{CaCN2}$ was used as a fertilizer since it forms urea with water in the soil.

2.3 Draw the full reaction sequence from $\ce{CaCO3}$ to urea.

2.4 Cyanamid $\ce{H2CN2}$ exists in two tautomeric forms. Draw the Lewis structures of both forms.

2.5 Sequestering $\ce{CO2}$ from the atmosphere is commercially done with different trapping agents. Draw the products obtained from reacting $\ce{CO2}$ with the following compounds.

1. primary amines $\ce{R-NH2}$

2. 1,2-diamines

3. glycerol

4. butadiene (catalyzed)

$\ce{CO2}$ is used by plants to eventually form sugar. The first steps of the process of $\ce{CO2}$ fixation are described in the following.

Starting from ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate RuBP (compound C), by action of the enzyme rubisco, a proton at C3 of RuBP is abstracted to form an endiolate D, which then in a nucleophilic attack binds $\ce{CO2}$. The resulting $\beta$-ketoacid E is immediately attacked by a water molecule at C3 to form a labile adduct that is split into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate $\mathbf{F}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-2-fig2.png

2.6 Draw the structures $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ for this reaction sequence.

Besides $\ce{CO2}$, there are a number of other neutral binary oxides of carbon, namely $\ce{CO3}$, $\ce{C3O2}$, and $\ce{C12O9}$. The latter is the anhydride of a hexacarbonic acid.

1. $\ce{CO3}$

2. $\ce{C3O2}$

3. $\ce{C12O9}$

Carbon monoxide CO binds very well to low valent transition metals. The highest stability in such complexes is achieved when all available orbitals are filled.

2.8 Draw a complex with elementary $\mathrm{Ni}^0$ and CO. Draw its structure according to VSEPR.

2.9 Draw a complex with $\mathrm{Fe}^0$ instead of $\mathrm{Ni}^0$. Draw its structure according to VSEPR.

Squaric acid is an uncommon acid, which liberates 4 equivalents of CO after a two-electron oxidation.

2.10 Draw the structure of squaric acid.

2.11 Squaric acid is a rather strong organic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_{a1}$ = 1.5, $\mathrm{p}K_{a2}$ = 3.4). Explain this observation.

problems.title: What to do with CO2
problems.problem:
Problem 3. What to do with $\ce{CO2}$

The electrochemical reduction of $\ce{CO2}$ (in the following denoted $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$) has the great potential to substantially contribute to the closing of the so-called anthropogenic carbon cycle.

What renders the $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ particularly appealing is that value-added products such as high energy density fuels (e.g. methanol, ethanol, and n-propanol) or chemical feedstock (e.g., formic acid, ethylene, and syngas ($\ce{CO/H2}$)) can be produced using the surplus of renewable electricity originating from solar, hydro and wind sources. The counter reaction to the $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ taking place on the anode side of the electrolysis cell is typically the oxidative oxygen evolution reaction (OER).

Key to the $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ process is the use of specific catalyst materials which control both the overall $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ rate and the resulting product distribution. The product distribution of an electrolysis event is typically expressed in terms of the so-called Faradaic efficiency ($FE_{product}$ in %). This quantity can be derived from the ratio of the charge consumed for the production of a specific electrolysis product ($Q_{product}$) and the total charge ($Q_{total}$) transferred at the electrode surface during the electrolysis reaction:

$$FE_{product} = \frac{Q_{product}}{Q_{tot}} \cdot 100\%$$

The sum of Faradaic efficiencies of all formed products adds to 100%.

Silver (Ag) is among the most efficient $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ catalysts for the production of carbon monoxide (CO). A recently developed fabrication method of high surface area catalysts is based on the simultaneous release of $\ce{H2}$ and the electrodeposition of metals on the cathode producing metal foam. A prime example of such novel porous catalyst material is presented at various length scales in Figure 1a-d for a silver catalyst.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-3-fig1.png

Figure 1: a-d) Scanning electron microscopy of a novel Ag foam.

The effective surface area of this foam can be calculated using electrochemical techniques. A peak current $i_p$ in mA is measured against the potential sweep rate $v$ in V/s. The peak current $i_p$ is proportional to the surface area $A$ and the potential sweep rate $v$ measured in V/s.

This relationship is represented by the Randles-Sevcik equation valid for reversible systems at room temperature.

$$i_p = 2.69 \cdot 10^5 \cdot n^{3/2} \cdot A\ c\ D^{1/2} \cdot v^{1/2}$$

with:

$n$ = number of electrons transferred ; $A$ = reactive surface area ; $c$ = concentration $D$ = diffusion coefficient; $v$ = potential sweep rate

The constant values are:

$c = 5 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol/cm^3}\ ;\ D = 5.50 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm^2/s}\ ;\ n = 1$

Putting together the constant values the equation can be simplified to $i_p = kA\sqrt{v}$.

3.1 Calculate k.

In a run of a silver foam after 20 seconds the following data were obtained:

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Scan rate (V/s)} & \text{Peak current (mA)} \\ \hline 0.005 & 0.45 \\ \hline 0.01 & 0.84 \\ \hline 0.025 & 1.53 \\ \hline 0.05 & 2.34 \\ \hline 0.1 & 4.21 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

3.2 Plot the graph and draw the fitting line. Then calculate the slope and A in $\mathrm{cm^2}$. Hint: For this calculation you need the slope in $\mathrm{A}/\sqrt{\mathrm{V/s}}$ instead of $\mathrm{mA}/\sqrt{\mathrm{V/s}}$.

Potentiostatic (constant electrolysis potential) $\ce{CO2}$ electrolysis reactions were carried out over the Ag foam and, for comparison purposes, over a planar Ag foil using a $\ce{CO2}$-saturated 0.5 M $\ce{KHCO3}$ aqueous solution as the electrolyte. Figure 2a-b displays plots of the experimentally determined Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) as function of the electrolysis potential applied to the cathode (potential values are displayed versus the Reversible Hydrogen Electrode (RHE)). The comparison of panel a and b clearly demonstrates that the resulting $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ product distribution is not only dependent on the chemical nature of the catalyst material (e.g., Ag) but also on its morphology on various length scales.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-3-fig2.png

Figure 2: a) Potential-dependent product distribution of the $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ carried out over the Ag foam catalyst shown in figure a-d. b) Product distribution of the $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ carried out over the Ag foil catalyst (reference).

We consider a water/$\ce{CO2}$ co-electrolysis taking place in a classical three-electrode arrangement using a divided electrolysis cell (anolyte and catholyte compartments are separated from each other by a membrane). In the following we focus, however, only on the cathode side of the electrolysis cell where the CO2RR takes place. As electrolyte we use a $\ce{CO2}$-saturated 0.5 M $\ce{KHCO3}$ aqueous solution. The electrolysis potential applied to the cathode was -1.0 V vs. RHE. A silver foil ($A = 10\,\mathrm{cm^2}$) served as the catalyst (see Figure 1a). The only products formed over the Ag foil during electrolysis were CO ($FE_{CO} = 76\%$) and hydrogen ($FE_{H2} = 24\%$).

3.3 Write the balanced equations for the production of CO from $\ce{CO2}$ ($\mathrm{CO_2RR}$) and for the parasitic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) through water splitting. For the $\mathrm{CO_2RR}$ consider water as the proton source.

3.4 Calculate the (total) current density ($j_{tot}$; current normalized to the surface area) when 5 mmol carbon monoxide (CO) were produced within 10 hours of electrolysis.

3.5 Consider the electrolysis current density as constant. Calculate the partial current density for the parasitic hydrogen evolution reaction ($j_{H_2}$).

Consider a $\ce{CO2}$ reduction over the improved Ag foam electrocatalyst. A product distribution analysis revealed that the total current density of the electrolysis reaction at -1.5 V vs RHE is composed of partial current densities of methane formation ($j_{CH_4} = -18.8\,\mathrm{mA\ cm^2}$), ethane formation ($j_{C_2H_6} = -1.8\,\mathrm{mA\ cm^2}$), CO formation ($j_{CO} = -4.8\,\mathrm{mA\ cm^2}$), and hydrogen evolution ($j_{H_2} = -8.5\,\mathrm{mA\ cm^2}$).

3.6 Calculate the corresponding Faradaic efficiencies (FEs). Of note, by convention cathodic currents have a negative sign.

problems.title: Two Transition Metals - Many Oxidation States
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Two Transition Metals - Many Oxidation States

Among the ruthenium (Ru) isotopes formed during nuclear fission there are two relatively long-lived isotopes, $^{103}$Ru and $^{106}$Ru, both of which form part of the Highly Active (HA) waste raffinate during spent nuclear fuel reprocessing. Especially the volatile $[\ce{RuO4}]$ is a cause for serious concern. In order to investigate the possible mobilization of this metal in nature, the redox properties are intensively studied. The figure below shows the Latimer diagram of ruthenium for acidic conditions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-5-fig1.png

Latimer diagram of Ru for acidic conditions (pH=0) vs SHE (standard hydrogen electrode).

5.1 Calculate the missing potentials a) and b).

Ru forms a number of well-known chloro-complexes. Scheme 2 below shows a choice of the reactions that lead to some of these chloro-complexes starting from $[\ce{RuO4}]$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-5-fig2.png

All compounds $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{E}$ have 6 ligands, either Cl or $\ce{H2O}$ or O or a combination of them. Furthermore, the following information about the different species is given:

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|} \hline \textbf{Species} & \textbf{Oxidation State of Ru} & \textbf{Charge of the complex} & \textbf{Molecular Mass (g/mol)} \\ \hline \mathbf{A} & +\mathrm{VI} & -2 & 540.69 \\ \hline \mathbf{B} & +\mathrm{III} & & 261.48 \\ \hline \mathbf{C} & +\mathrm{III} & -2 & \mathrm{MM} > 260 \\ \hline \mathbf{D} & +\mathrm{IV} & -2 & \\ \hline \mathbf{E} & +\mathrm{III} & -3 & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

5.2 Give the formula of compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{E}$.

5.3 $\mathbf{F}$ contains a Ru-O-Ru unit, give the structure of $\mathbf{F}$.

5.4 Give the equation for the reaction of $[\ce{RuO4}]$ to compound $\mathbf{A}$.

Besides the problem for nuclear waste management, ruthenium today is very important for catalysis and bioinorganic chemistry. problems.title: Useful Radioactivity
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Useful Radioactivity

[$^{68}$Ga]GaPSMA-11 is a radiolabelled compound used in PET imaging (PET = Positron Emission Tomography) of prostate cancer ($t_{1/2}$($^{68}$Ga) = 67.7 min).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-6-fig1.png

6.1 A sample containing [$^{68}$Ga]GaPSMA-11 has an activity of 100 MBq at 10:00 in the morning.

• a) Find the activity at 12:00.

• b) Find the activity at 17:30.

• c) If the minimum activity required to record a PET image in a patient is 15 MBq at administration, find the latest time that the radiopharmaceutical can be injected.

• d) What is the specific activity (GBq/g) of $^{68}$Ga?

6.2 The figure below is a schematic representation of the Chart of the Nuclides. Name the decay modes of the parent nucleus that give daughter nuclides shown in the yellow squares (1), (2) and (3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-6-fig2.png

Nuclear fuel is material used in nuclear power stations to produce heat to power turbines. Most nuclear fuels contain heavy fissile actinide elements that can undergo nuclear fission and sustain the chain reaction. The three most relevant fissile isotopes are uranium-233, uranium-235 and plutonium-239. The plutonium isotope 239 is inevitably produced in nuclear power plants operating with $^{238}$U-rich isotope mixtures, due to neutron capture.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-6-fig3.png

6.3 Find the isotopes $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

A complex enrichment process is required for U-235-based nuclear fuel. U-233, on the other hand, can be produced in a reactor by neutron capture from a naturally occurring stable element. The production follows an analogous reaction path as for Pu-239 production.

6.4 State what naturally occurring element must be added to a nuclear reactor to produce U-233. Write out all nuclear reactions and decays that are part of U-233 production.

Geochronology is the science of determining the age of rocks, fossils, and sediments using signatures in the rocks themselves. Absolute geochronology can be accomplished through radioactive isotopes such as the Rb-Sr and the Sm-Nd system. In such “chronometer” systems the amount of daughter nuclide as a function of the amount of mother nuclide and time is given by:

$$N_D = N_M \cdot (e^{\lambda \cdot t} - 1) \qquad (1)$$

and can be derived from the law of radioactive decay.

6.5 Derive equation (1) from above.

An interesting chronometer system is based on the decay of K-40. In addition, K-40 (natural abundance 0.012%) has a favorable half-life ($1.25\times10^9$ years) for radiometric dating, which corresponds to 1/4 of the age of the earth. K-40 has a nuclide with an odd proton and neutron number, which leads to special decay properties. K-40 decays by $\beta^-$ decay (89.14%, $\lambda_b$ = $4.962\times10^{-10}\cdot\mathrm{a^{-1}}$ (=per year)) to Ca-40 (decay energy 1.32 MeV) and by electron capture (0.2%) to Ar-40 (ground state, decay energy 1.51 MeV). Furthermore, the electron capture yields Ar-40 in an excited state (10.66%, decay energy 0.05MeV). By $\gamma$-emission ($\gamma$-energy 1.461 MeV) the excited state of Ar-40 relaxes to the ground state. The decay constant for the overall electron capture process has been determined as $\lambda_e$ = $0.581\times10^{-10}\cdot\mathrm{a^{-1}}$

6.6 Draw the generic decay scheme of K-40.

The isotopic composition of Ar in rocks is not constant, but a function of their K content, age and thermal history. Provided that at time $t$ = 0 (magmatic or metamorphic age), the sample contained no Ar-40 and from $t$ = 0 to the present, the sample was a closed system for K and Ar, the ratio of K-40 / Ar-40 can indicate the age of the rock.

The analysis of 1 kg volcanic rock showed a total potassium content of 0.14 kg. The amount of Ar-40 has been determined as $7.638\times10^{-4}$ mg.

6.7 Based on the generic decay scheme of K-40, estimate the age of this sample.

problems.title: Heavy Metal Detoxification

Problem 7. Heavy Metal Detoxification

2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) is a medication for metal poisoning, such as lead (Pb), mercury (Hg), and arsenic (As), with the formula $\ce{HO2CCH(SH)CH(SH)CO2H}$. Its mechanism of action is based on chelating by which the drug, called a chelating agent, strongly binds the metal ion, forming a water soluble 1:1 complex that is then excreted via the urinary system.

Dicarboxylicacetylene $\mathbf{A}$ is reacted with thioacetic acid to give compound $\mathbf{B}$ to yield the product DMSA.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2023-7-fig1.png

7.1 Write this reaction sequence with structures of all compounds and the reagent $\mathbf{X}$.

7.2 DMSA has several stereoisomers. Draw all of them, give them a number, and state the absolute configuration of each chiral center. Are there sets of enantiomers within the possible isomers? If yes, indicate which of them.

7.3 The active substance in the medication is only one isomer. This isomer reveals a rotation angle of zero under the polarimeter. Give the isomer that represents the active substance in the pharmaceutical.

7.4 DMSA is a tetraprotic acid. Its acid dissociation constants are:

• $\mathrm{p}K_{a_1}$: 2.71

• $\mathrm{p}K_{a_2}$: 3.48

• $\mathrm{p}K_{a,\mathrm{SH1}}$: 9.65

• $\mathrm{p}K_{a1,\mathrm{SH2}}$:12.05

Calculate the pH of a 0.1 mol/L solution of uncoordinated DMSA (The autoprotolysis of water may be neglected and the deprotonation steps can be considered decoupled).

The acid dissociation constants of the uncoordinated groups in the $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ chelates of mono-O-methyl DMSA are given:

$$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{PbLH} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbL^-} + \mathrm{H^+},\ \mathrm{p}K_a = 5.28 \\ \mathrm{HgLH} \rightarrow \mathrm{HgL^-} + \mathrm{H^+},\ \mathrm{p}K_a = 3.38 \end{array}$$

The IR spectrum of HgLH shows the presence of a protonated carboxylic group, that of PbLH the presence of a carboxylate group.

7.5 Draw the structure of the Pb and of the Hg complex.

7.6 Explain the different $\mathrm{p}K_a$ values.

A person was diagnosed with Pb-poisoning when a blood test revealed a blood lead level (BLL) of 85 µg/dL. The patient was treated with intravenously administered DMSA and the given dose corresponded to 5 mg/kg. Assume an average body weight of 75 kg and blood volume of 5 L.

7.7 Assuming that the equilibrium concentration of DMSA is 99.5% of the administered dose, determine the free Pb concentration after equilibrium has been reached (t = 0).

The clearance of the Pb(DMSA) complex was then monitored by the concentration change in free Pb over a period of 6 hours. The results are shown in the table below:

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline t\ /\ \text{min} & 0 & 60 & 120 & 180 & 240 & 300 & 360 \\ \hline c\ /\ \mathrm{\mu mol/L} & c\text{ from task 7} & 1.66 & 1.34 & 1.08 & 0.87 & 0.70 & 0.56 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

(The values are simplified)

7.8 Calculate the apparent $t_{1/2}$ and $k$ for the clearance of free Pb from the patients blood.

7.9 Calculate how long it will take until the limiting value of 90 µg/L free Pb is reached.

To test the interaction of the DMSA complex with $\ce{Cd^{2+}}$, another toxic metal ion that binds to this ligand, the following experiment was carried out:

To 0.1 mmol DMSA-Pb in 1 L of neutral water, 0.05 mmol of a Cd(II) salt was added. Assume that the volume did not change and no acid/base reaction occurred.

7.10 Write the reaction equation and the expression for the resulting equilibrium.

7.11 Calculate the equilibrium constant. The stability constant for DMSA-Pb is $K_1 = 10^{17.6}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}}$ and for DMSA-Cd $K_2 = 10^{16.5}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}}$.

7.12 Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of all four species.

Poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) is a transparent polymer used, among else, in heat-resistant tiles. Industrial synthesis starts from dichlorodimethylsilane. By vacuum-UV (VUV) irradiation in presence of oxygen, PDMS coatings can be modified to hard and transparent $\ce{SiO2}$-like coatings. The precursor polymer contains reactive silanol end groups.
