problems.problem:
Problem 5. Carbon capture

Carbon capture, storage and utilization is an important area of technological research. A few years ago, a water-fed electrolyzer was reported to achieve a current density of $420\,\mathrm{mA/cm^2}$ for $\ce{CO}$ generation without difficulty. The cell design is as follows:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-5-fig1.png

The key is the central ion exchange membrane, in which certain ions are mobile. On either side of this membrane is a GDL - a gas diffusion layer. This is a partially wettable porous material on whose surface a catalyst is deposited. Optimally, both the gas and the electrolyte enter and leave the pores and electricity is conducted through the layer.

5.1. What could be this cheap, modifiable, inert, porous, and conductive layer on the cathode side?

This carrier is activated on the cathode side by a silver nanoparticle catalyst. On the anode side, the gas diffusion layer is a porous Ti-film with an $\ce{IrO_x}$ nanoparticle catalyst on its surface.

Humidified carbon dioxide is passed through the cathode space wetted with a neutral solution, while a more concentrated (1 M) $\ce{KOH}$ solution is usually passed through the anode space.

5.2. Give the expected cathode and anode electrode reactions (in a form appropriate for the pH of solutions). Give is the net reaction of electrolysis?

The material of the ion exchange membrane is indeed crucial. Commonly used porous polymers in electrochemistry, such as Nafion or SPEEK (structures are on the figure on the right) present practical challenges in this system.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-5-fig2.png

If these membrane materials were employed, two ions could permeate them, leading to undesirable outcomes. One ion can alter the pH at the cathode, influencing product composition through an alternative electrode reaction. On the other hand, if the other ion flows through the membrane, the cathode space would maintain a near-neutral pH, but the solid filling the pores would hinder extended electrolysis.

5.3. Identify these two ions and the direction in which they could flow across the membranes. Write down the side reaction mentioned for one of them and the formula of the solid that would form in the pores due to the flow of the other ion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-5-fig3.png

If the ion-exchange membrane is made of the polymer on the left, the situation improves. Additional chemical reactions are still likely to happen in the cathode space due to the high concentration of carbon dioxide.

5.4. Name the ions and the direction in which they can flow through this separation membrane.

In the cagse of continuous operation (after one hour), steady-state operation of the system is established and the two-component gas leaving the anode space will have only 1/3 as the oxygen mole fraction.

5.5. Name the other component in the gas. Determine, based on the stoichiometry of the chemical and electrochemical processes involved, which of the various ions capable of passing through the membrane serves as the primary charge carrier.

5.6. In the case of ideal electrochemical selectivity, calculate the fraction of the $\ce{CO2}$ input that is converted to $\ce{CO}$ in this steady state?

5.7. Calculate the minimum $\ce{CO2}$ volume flow rate with a $100\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ electrode and a steady current density of $420\,\mathrm{mA/cm^2}$. The temperature of the gas at atmospheric pressure is $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

problems.title: Nanoparticles
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Nanoparticles

Nanoparticles have attracted growing scientific interest in recent decades. Physical, optical and electronic properties of nanoparticles in comparison with bulk phases of similar chemical composition are fundamentally determined by their size. However, this size is never uniform, as particles of varying sizes are present in any real sample. As a result, the size cannot be characterized by a simple number, not even by an average. Typically, the size distribution of nanoparticles needs to be determined experimentally.

A simplified model of nanoparticle size distribution is the following. Monomer unit $\mathrm{M}_1$ is assumed to be engaged in a series of equilibrium reactions in which growing nanoparticles are produced. $\mathrm{M}_i$ denotes the particle with exactly $i$ monomeric units in it. The equilibria are described by the following general reaction:

$$\mathrm{M}_i + \mathrm{M}_1 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{M}_{i+1}$$

As a first approach, the equilibrium constants ($K$) of all such processes are assumed to be equal, so independent of the value of $i$.

$$\frac{[\mathrm{M}_{i+1}]}{[\mathrm{M}_i][\mathrm{M}_1]} = K$$

Imagine an experiment in which initial concentration of $\mathrm{M}_1$ (before the formation of any nanoparticles) was $T$, and the molar mass $\mathrm{M}_1$ is $W$.

6.1. Derive a formula that gives the average molar mass of the nanoparticles formed as a function of $T$, $W$, and $K$.

Hint: you might need the formula to sum an infinite geometric series:

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a\,r^k = \frac{a}{1-r} \quad \text{for } |r| < 1$$

The size of the individual nanoparticles is not proportional to their mass. If the particle shape is assumed to be approximately spherical, then the size of a particle ($d_i$) is proportional to the cube root of the molar mass, which is directly proportional to $i$, the number of monomeric units in it. So overall:

$$r_i = r_0 \sqrt[3]{i}$$

Here, $r_0$ is a constant representing the hypothetical size of the 'nanoparticle' containing a single monomeric unit.

Distributions are frequently illustrated using histograms, which are bar diagrams. The x-axis of the histogram displays ranges of the property of interest, while the height of the bars is proportionate to the probability of finding the property within the specified range.

6.2. Utilizing spreadsheet software, create two histograms based on the outlined system. Set $T = 1\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ and $K = 10^6\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}\,dm^3}$ for the calculations. The first histogram should depict the distribution of molar masses of the nanoparticles, with a range width of $100W$. This implies the first column represents the molar mass range $0$–$100W$, the second $100W$–$200W$, and so forth. The second histogram should display the distribution of nanoparticle sizes, with $r_0$ as the width of the range.

problems.title: Adiabatic reactor
problems.problem:
Problem 7. Adiabatic reactor

A constant-volume adiabatic reactor is primarily a theoretical construct that helps in understanding the concepts of thermodynamics. In a reactor like this no heat exchange is possible with the environment, and the overall volume is constant, so if chemical reactions occur, other parameters like temperature and pressure change in response. This reactor also helps to some extent imagine what happens during gas explosions.

Imagine the burning of carbon monoxide in a constant-volume adiabatic reactor. The fixed volume is $1.00\,\mathrm{m^3}$, $50.0\,\mathrm{mol}$ carbon monoxide and $50.0\,\mathrm{mol}$ oxygen is fed into the reactor at the beginning, the initial temperature is $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

You can assume that all gases and their mixture follow the ideal gas law. Note, that the molar entropy of an ideal gas has the following temperature and pressure dependence:

$$S_m(p,T) = S_m(p_0,T_0) + C_p \ln\frac{T}{T_0} - R\ln\frac{p}{p_0}$$

Use the following data:

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|} \hline & C_p\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & S^\mathrm{o}_{298}\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\mathrm{o}_{298}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{O2}(g) & 29.4 & 205.2 & \\ \hline \ce{CO}(g) & 29.1 & 197.7 & -110.5 \\ \hline \ce{CO2}(g) & 37.1 & 213.8 & -393.5 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

The constant pressure molar heat capacities are independent of temperature above $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

7.1. Give the balanced chemical equation of the reaction and its standard enthalpy ($\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$).

The amount of carbon dioxide formed in the reaction is $n_{\ce{CO2}}$ mol.

7.2. Give the stoichiometrically possible maximum value of $n_{\ce{CO2}}$?

7.3. Using $n_{\ce{CO2}}$ as an independent variable derive expressions that give certain thermodynamic properties of the system. Where it is not possible to give an expression for the property itself, give the expression for the change in the property relative to the initial conditions.

a) the internal energy ($U$) of the system

b) the temperature ($T$) of the system

c) the pressure ($p$) of the system

d) the reaction quotient ($Q$)

e) the enthalpy of the system ($H$)

f) the entropy of the system ($S$)

g) the Gibbs free energy of the system ($G$)

h) the equilibrium constant of the reaction ($K$) at the given temperature (already obtained as $T$)

7.4. Use spreadsheet software to calculate each property for $n_{\ce{CO2}} = 1\,\mathrm{mol}$, $2\,\mathrm{mol}$, $3\,\mathrm{mol}$,

On the spreadsheet, find the $n_{\ce{CO2}}$ value at which the system is in equilibrium

Which of the previously listed properties has an extremum in the equilibrium?

problems.title: Nitrogen oxides
problems.problem:
Problem 8. Nitrogen oxides

The nitrogen oxides stand out among non-metal oxides, as there is at least one binary molecular oxide corresponding to each oxidation state between +1 and +5.

8.1. Give a molecular formula and a Lewis structure (one resonance structure is sufficient) of the simplest oxide for each oxidation state.

For some oxidation states, multiple oxides are possible. For example, when brown gas $\mathbf{A}$ is cooled down, a colorless liquid of compound $\mathbf{B}$ is formed, which is a dimer of $\mathbf{A}$. For practical calculations, the volume of the liquid is negligible as compared to the volume of the gas.

8.2. Determine $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. Give the molecular formula and a Lewis structure of $\mathbf{B}$.

Let us consider the chemical equilibrium $2\,\mathbf{A}(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{B}(\mathrm{g})$ (reaction $\mathbf{1}$) and the following data (assume them to be independent of temperature):

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\mathrm{o}\ /\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} & S^\mathrm{o}\ /\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)} \\ \hline \mathbf{B}(\mathrm{g}) & 9.16 & 304.29 \\ \mathbf{A}(\mathrm{g}) & 33.18 & 219.85 \end{array}$$

8.3. Calculate the equilibrium constant of reaction $\mathbf{1}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

1 mol of $\mathbf{A}$ is put into an empty container, it is closed with a fixed volume of $25\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ and thermostated at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

8.4. Calculate the equilibrium pressure of the system.

The standard atmospheric boiling point of $\mathbf{B}$ is at $21.69\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. $\Delta H_{vap} = 22.96\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, $\Delta S_{vap} = 77.9\,\frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{mol\cdot K}}$ for the evaporation of $\mathbf{B}$. Assume them to be independent of temperature.

8.5. Calculate the enthalpy of formation of $\mathbf{B}$(l).

8.6. Calculate the entropy change of the reaction $2\,\mathbf{A}\,(\mathrm{g}) = \mathbf{B}\,(\mathrm{l})$ (reaction $\mathbf{2}$).

We can assume that the entropy change of reaction $\mathbf{2}$ is independent of temperature between $-10$ and $22\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

8.7. Calculate the equilibrium constant of reaction $\mathbf{2}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

1 mol of $\mathbf{A}$ is put into an empty container, it is closed with a fixed volume of $25\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ and thermostated at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

8.8. Calculate the equilibrium pressure of the cooled system.

problems.title: Statin drugs
problems.problem:
Problem 9. Statin drugs

Statins are the drugs of first choice for management of many lipid disorders. All statins interfere with the conversion of 3-hydroxi-3-methyl-glutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) to the cholesterol precursor mevalonate by HMG-CoA reductase, an early and rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis. Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase by binding to the enzyme and sterically inhibiting substrate binding.

The family of statins contains some very effective pharmaceutical compounds, a few of which are shown in the drawing below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-9-fig1.png

Table 1. Thermodynamic properties of the substrates at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & K_\mathrm{I}\ /\ \mathrm{nM} & \Delta_\mathrm{r}H\ /\ \mathrm{kcal/mol} & \Delta_\mathrm{r}H\ /\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} \\ \hline \textbf{Atorvastatin} & 14 & -4.3 & -18.1 \\ \textbf{Cerivastatin} & 5.7 & -3.3 & -13.9 \\ \textbf{Fluvastatin} & 256 & \text{-} & \text{-} \\ \textbf{Pravastatin} & 103 & -2.5 & -10.5 \\ \textbf{Rosuvastatin} & 2.3 & -9.3 & -39.1 \end{array}$$

$K_\mathrm{I}$ is the equilibrium constant for the dissociation of the enzyme-inhibitor complex. $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H$ is the binding enthalpy for the inhibitor and in can be assumed to be temperature independent.

Efficacy and selectivity of the drug substance depends on the strength of binding to the target enzyme. Thus, a binding study is usually carried out for larger active substance families. In a series of experiments the initial activity of the enzyme is measured by spectrophotometry at different substrate concentrations, and the results are evaluated using the formula of initial rate according to Michaelis-Menten kinetics ($v_\mathrm{I}$ is the initial rate of the reaction, $K_\mathrm{M}$ and $v_\mathrm{max}$ are coefficients depending on the reaction between the enzyme and substrate, $c$ and $[\mathrm{I}]_0$ are the initial concentrations of substrate and inhibitor, respectively):

$$v_I = v_{max}\cdot\frac{c}{K' + c} \quad \text{where } K' = K_M\left(1 + \frac{[I]}{K_I}\right)$$

In the present study the binding of the drug molecule was characterized by the ratio $\mathrm{v_I/v_0}$, where $\mathrm{v_0}$ is the initial rate in the absence of inhibitor at the given substrate (HMG-CoA) concentration. Under the experimental conditions of the study $\mathrm{K_M} = 70\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ and all experiments were carried out at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Results of the study were present on the diagrams A, B and C ($\mathrm{v_I/v_0}$ vs. $[I]/\mathrm{\mu M}$) but unfortunately the names of the active substances disappeared from the graphs.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-9-fig2.png

9.1. Match the diagrams with the active substances taking into account that at this level of precision multiple drugs can belong to the same diagram.

9.2. Estimate the order of magnitude of substrate concentration in the spectrophotometry experiments.

Enthalpy change of the binding was determined by calorimetric titration. A solution with known concentration of the enzyme was titrated with the solution of the drug substance. In order to evaluate the results, the molar heat effect (with respect to substrate) versus molar ratio of substrate was shown on a diagram (bottom part of the next figure) but, unfortunately labelling was lost again. However, it was noted that in the case of Fluvastatin the enthalpy change was below the detection limit of the equipment (practically it is $0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-9-fig3.png

9.3. Match diagrams with the drugs above (one molecule to each diagram)

9.4. Determine the equilibrium constant for the association of each pharmaceutical compound at 25 and at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

9.5. Estimate the (overall) ratio of drug molecules necessary to obtain a solution at $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ where the concentration of free (unbound) drug molecules are equal if the enzyme is present

i. in a catalytic amount.

ii. in excess.

problems.title: Minions and berries
problems.problem:
Problem 10. Minions and berries

Dr. Nefario after getting tired of doing evil, started a new project preparing his own brand of berry juice. Unfortunately, the product was a complete flop on the market, so he started a quality check on the process.

It turned out that the flavor compound berrine coming from the fruits is oxidized to diberrine during cooking by the moxone additive they used. Their research showed that when 75% of the berrine is used up, then the juice will become unpalatable due to the bitter taste of diberrine.

The reaction takes place according to the following overall reaction:

$$\text{2 berrine} + \text{moxone} \rightarrow \text{diberrine}$$

During their experiments they changed the quantity of the fruit and the added moxone. After starting cooking, they took samples from the mixture every minute and determined the initial rate of formation of diberrine. Every batch of juice was $100\,\mathrm{dm^3}$. The fruit contains 8.0 mass% berrine, and we can suppose that all of it is liberated at the start of cooking. Moxone was added as $1.0\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ solution.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{experiment} & \text{fruit (kg)} & \text{moxone } (\mathrm{dm^3}) & \text{diberrine formation rate } (10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,min^{-1}}) \\ \hline 1 & 10.0 & 2.6 & 4.36 \\ \hline 2 & 5.0 & 2.6 & 2.19 \\ \hline 3 & 20.0 & 2.6 & 8.75 \\ \hline 4 & 10.0 & 10.4 & 17.42 \\ \hline 5 & 10.0 & 5.2 & 8.80 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

10.1. Determine the reaction order of the components and give the rate equation of the reaction, based on the initial rate data.

In a different series of experiments, a great excess of moxone was used when monitoring the formation of diberrine.

10.2. Identify the shapes of the detected kinetic curves?

The observed rate constants were the following in experiments with different oxidizer concentrations:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{moxone } (\mathrm{mol/dm^3}) & k_\mathrm{obs}\ (\mathrm{h^{-1}}) \\ \hline 0.040 & 0.180 \\ \hline 0.100 & 0.460 \\ \hline 0.160 & 0.747 \\ \hline 0.220 & 1.020 \\ \hline 0.280 & 1.320 \\ \hline 0.340 & 1.560 \\ \hline 0.400 & 1.838 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Make a diagram to determine the rate constant of the reaction.

1 kg of berries and $11\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of moxone stock solution were mixed in a $100\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ batch of juice. Berrine has a molar mass of $365\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.

10.3. Calculate the berrine concentration in this experiment when 5 minutes have passed after the start of the cooking?

10.4. Calculate the duration of cooking before the juice becomes unpalatable when using a concentration of $0.100\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ moxone (still in high excess).

Normally the cooking was run at $108\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In one experiment the minion responsible set the temperature to $120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The activation energy of the reaction is $58.60\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Moxone was also in excess here in a concentration of $0.22\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$.

10.5. Determine if the juice remained tasty after 35 minutes of cooking?

problems.title: Clock reactions
problems.problem:
Problem 11. Clock reactions

Clock reactions show a sudden change in some property (typically color) after a period of induction. In iodine clock reactions iodide containing solutions are mixed with an oxidizer in the presence of thiosulfate and starch. After some time, the solution will suddenly turn blue due to the starch-iodine complex forming.

Measuring the time needed for this reaction gives an opportunity to study the iodide – oxidizer reactions, determining reaction orders and rate constants based on initial reaction rates.

The reaction between Fe(III) ions and iodide can be studied in this way. When the blue color appears that shows that the thiosulfate present was all used up. If a small quantity of thiosulfate is used, we can suppose that the concentration of other reagents will not change. Based on this and the stoichiometry of the reactions, we can use the following:

$$v_0 \approx -\frac{\Delta[\ce{Fe^{3+}}]}{\Delta\mathrm{t}} = -\frac{\Delta[\ce{S2O3^{2-}}]}{\Delta\mathrm{t}} = \frac{[\ce{S2O3^{2-}}]_0}{\Delta\mathrm{t}} \qquad (1)$$

$$v_0 = k[\ce{Fe^{3+}}]_0^{\,\mathrm{n}}[\ce{I-}]_0^{\,\mathrm{m}} = \frac{[\ce{S2O3^{2-}}]_0}{\Delta\mathrm{t}} \qquad (2)$$

The following was found for the $\Delta t$ period when the three concentrations were changed:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline [\ce{S2O3^{2-}}]_0\ (\mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}}) & [\ce{KI}]_0\ (\mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}}) & [\ce{Fe(NO3)3}]_0\ (\mathrm{mmol\cdot dm^{-3}}) & \Delta\mathrm{t}\ (\mathrm{s}) \\ \hline \text{variable} & 20.0 & 6.5 & \Delta\mathrm{t} = 2.32\cdot10^{4}[\ce{S2O3^{2-}}]_0 \\ \hline 0.2 & \text{variable} & 8.5 & \Delta\mathrm{t} = 1.54\cdot10^{-3}\,([\ce{I-}]_0)^{-1.98} \\ \hline 0.25 & 13.0 & \text{variable} & \Delta\mathrm{t} = 5.01\cdot10^{-2}\,([\ce{Fe^{3+}}]_0)^{-1.05} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

11.1. Give the balanced equation for the reaction of Fe(III) and $\ce{I-}$.

11.2. How does the initial rate depend on the initial thiosulfate concentration?

11.3. Give the individual and the overall reaction orders? Give the rate equation.

11.4. Give the unit of the rate constant? Calculate the rate constant from the three sets of experiments. Considering that a 10% margin of error is often acceptable in reaction kinetics, assess the quality of these experiments.

The following mechanism was proposed:

$$\ce{I- + Fe^{3+} <=>[$k_1$][$k_{-1}$] FeI^{2+}} \qquad (3)$$

$$\ce{I- + FeI^{2+} <=>[$k_2$][$k_{-2}$] Fe^{2+} + I2^-} \qquad (4)$$

$$\ce{I2^- + Fe^{3+} ->[$k_3$] I2 + Fe^{2+}} \qquad (5)$$

Supposing a steady state for the $\ce{FeI^{2+}}$ and $\ce{I2^-}$ intermediates, the following rate equation was derived, but the result is not fully correct. One of the elements in the denominator is not necessary.

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{I2}]}{\mathrm{dt}} = \frac{k_1k_2k_3[\ce{I-}]^2[\ce{Fe^{3+}}]}{\dfrac{k_{-1}k_{-2}[\ce{Fe^{2+}}]}{[\ce{Fe^{3+}}]} + k_{-1}k_3 + \dfrac{k_2k_{-2}[\ce{Fe^{2+}}][\ce{I-}]}{[\ce{Fe^{3+}}]} + k_2k_3[\ce{I-}]} \qquad (6)$$

11.5. Derive the right rate equation to identify the unnecessary element.

problems.title: Crystal violet
problems.problem:
Problem 12. Crystal violet

Crystal violet (or gentian violet or methyl violet 10B), is known for its antiseptic and fungicide effects and is commonly used for staining Gram positive bacteria. In aqueous solution crystal violet (CV) dissociates into the cation shown in the figure and chloride ions. The compound has a vivid violet color. In the presence of $\ce{NaOH}$, crystal violet forms a colorless carbinol product.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-12-fig1.png

The reaction is represented by the following simple equation:

$$\mathrm{CV^+ + OH^- = CVOH}$$

Due to the compound’s intense color, the kinetic study of this reaction can be carried out by spectrophotometry at $595\,\mathrm{nm}$. The rate law can be written:

$$v = k[\mathrm{CV}]^a[\mathrm{OH^-}]^b$$

A set of experiments was carried out at $30.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ using the following mixtures:

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline \text{Exp. no.} & c(\mathrm{CV}),\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3} & V(\mathrm{CV}),\ \mathrm{cm^3} & c(\ce{NaOH}),\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3} & V(\ce{NaOH}),\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ \hline \#1 & 1.82\cdot10^{-5} & 5 & 0.08 & 5 \\ \hline \#2 & 1.82\cdot10^{-5} & 5 & 0.12 & 5 \\ \hline \#3 & 1.82\cdot10^{-5} & 5 & 0.16 & 5 \\ \hline \#4 & 1.82\cdot10^{-5} & 5 & 0.32 & 5 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Performing the measurements in a $1.000\,\mathrm{cm}$ pathlength cuvette, the following kinetic curves were recorded:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-12-fig2.png

12.1. Calculate the initial concentrations of the reactants in each reaction mixture.

12.2. Calculate the molar absorption coefficient of CV at $595\,\mathrm{nm}$ (you can assume that the products do not absorb at this wavelength).

12.3. Determine $a$ and $b$ (the partial orders of the reactants) and give the rate law of the reaction. Calculate the rate constant ($k$), using the same units as the chart and the table.

12.4. Calculate the concentration of CV in experiment #3 at 6 minutes.

The $k$ rate constant follows the Arrhenius law in this temperature range and its numeric value is 22.78 at $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, in the same unit as calculated in Part 3.

12.5. Calculate the Arrhenius parameters (pre-exponential factor ($A$) and activation energy ($E_\mathrm{a}$)).

$6\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $2.75\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ crystal violet solution is mixed with $14\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $3.86\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ $\ce{KMnO4}$ solution. The optical pathlength of the cell is $0.6\,\mathrm{cm}$, $\varepsilon_{595}(\ce{KMnO4}) = 1875\,\mathrm{M^{-1}cm^{-1}}$. Assume that the volumes are additive, no chemical reaction takes place in the cell and the solution is completely homogenized.

12.6. Calculate the absorbance of the mixture at $595\,\mathrm{nm}$ and the corresponding percentage light absorption.

Crystal violet belongs to the family of triphenyl-methyl dyes. A study revealed that triphenyl-methyl (trityl) radicals react with thiophenol producing triphenyl methane and phenyl trityl thioether according to the scheme below: (’I’: hexaphenyl ethane)

$$\ce{I <=>[$k_1$][$k_{-1}$] 2 (C6H5)3C$\cdot$} \qquad (1)$$

$$\ce{(C6H5)3C$\cdot$ + C6H5SH <=>[$k_2$][$k_{-2}$] (C6H5)3CH + C6H5S$\cdot$} \qquad (2)$$

$$\ce{(C6H5)3C$\cdot$ + C6H5S$\cdot$ ->[$k_3$] C6H5SC(C6H5)3} \qquad (3)$$

Substitution of the thiol hydrogen with tritium ($\ce{^3T}$) in thiophenol leads to a significant decrease in the overall reaction rate.

12.7. Which elementary step is expected to be most affected by the described isotope exchange? What is expected to happen with the overall reaction rate when one of the carbon atoms in the aromatic ring of thiophenol is changed to $\ce{^{13}C}$?

problems.title: Aluminium in lattices
problems.problem:
Problem 13. Aluminium in lattices

Metallic aluminium under standard conditions forms a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal with a density of $2.710\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Interestingly, it undergoes several structural changes under extreme pressures.

At a pressure of $213\,\mathrm{GPa}$ the FCC structure is still stable, but the unit cell dimension is changed to $324.6\,\mathrm{pm}$. When the sample is further compressed between diamond anvils to above $310\,\mathrm{GPa}$, a transformation to a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure with a unit cell size of $250.5\,\mathrm{pm}$ was detected.

13.1. Calculate and compare the densities ($\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) of the different modifications under extreme pressures.

13.2. Calculate the metallic radius of Al in the three structures.

The unit cell for a family of magnetic alloys is shown on the figure. If the alloys contain Al, then the Al atoms usually take up the positions labeled with Z. The other two metals in the alloy are usually transition metals.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-13-fig1.png

Interesting variations arise from the possibility that in some cases all (dark and light) blue positions are taken by X atoms, and in other cases only the dark blue positions.

13.3. Identify the lattice (primitive cubic, FCC, BCC, something else) formed by the Z atoms only. Identify the lattice formed by the blue (both dark and light) atoms only.

13.4. Determine the empirical formula of the alloy if all blue positions contain X as shown on the figure. Consider the Z atoms: How many X, how many Y and how many Z atoms are nearest neighbors with a Z atom?

13.5. Identify the lattice formed by the dark blue atoms. Determine the empirical formula of the alloy if the X atoms are only present in the dark blue positions.

An aluminium containing semiconductor has the following unit cell. The lattice constant is $613.5\,\mathrm{pm}$, the density of the material is $4.277\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-13-fig2.png

13.6. Determine the empirical formula of this semiconductor. Identify the other element.

problems.title: Sulfide minerals
problems.problem:
Problem 14. Sulfide minerals

Element substitutions and crystal defects are common in most complex sulfide minerals, resulting in variable compositions in natural samples. However, specimens with relatively pure compositions identifiable as compounds do exist. While not mined in large quantities, many complex sulfide minerals are present in copper ores and are reasonably well-documented due to the significance of copper. These minerals will be discussed in this task.

In minerals of the chalcopyrite group, which are structurally equivalent to chalcopyrite ($\ce{CuFeS2}$), iron atom substitution is most prevalent. Some variants with a pure composition in such substitution structures have only been identified in microscopic samples.

Two of these minerals/compounds, which can be derived by complete substitution of iron, have a sulfur content of 32.5 % ($\mathbf{A}$) and 26.5 % ($\mathbf{B}$) by weight.

14.1. Give the empirical formula of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

Mineral $\mathbf{C}$ can be derived from mineral $\mathbf{B}$ by an additional element substitution and has a sulfur content of 22.4%.

14.2. Give the formula of $\mathbf{C}$.

Significant copper ore minerals include enargite ($\mathbf{D}$) with a theoretical composition of $\ce{Cu3AsS4}$ and bornite ($\mathbf{E}$) with a composition of $\ce{Cu5FeS4}$. Neither structure has an S-S bond, there are no S atoms close to each other in the lattice. Each crystal has chemically equivalent atoms of the same kind (e.g., all Cu atoms in $\mathbf{E}$ are identical).

14.3. Give the conventional oxidation numbers of the elements in $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$.

14.4. Write balanced equations for the reactions of the two minerals if

• they undergo roasting in air with excess oxygen (resulting in black metal oxides, including magnetite)

• react with an excess of bleach solution.

The figure shows the structure of the elementary cell of enargite.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-14-fig1.png

14.5. Find the coordination number of Cu (brown), As (purple) and S (yellow) atoms. Find the number of formula units per elementary cell.

Two additional minerals, $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$, are derived from the same elements as enargite. Mineral $\mathbf{F}$ has an ideal composition with a sulfur content of 18.8%, featuring a relatively simple composition. On the other hand, mineral $\mathbf{G}$ presents challenges in determining the ideal composition due to wide substitution possibilities and a relatively complex structure (its empirical formula mass is close to $1500\,\mathrm{g/mol}$). Its ideal sulfur content is 28.18%. The World Mineralogical Association last fine-tuned the data and classification of this mineral in 2019.

14.6. Identify the ideal empirical formulas of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$.

In the crystal structure of $\mathbf{G}$, Cu(I), Cu(II), thioarsenite ($\ce{AsS3^{3-}}$) and sulfide ions can be identified.

14.7. Give the proportions of these ions in $\mathbf{G}$.

Lautite is a rare copper arsenosulfide. In it, the coordination number of all atoms is 4. Three projections of the elementary cell:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-14-fig2.png

14.8. Give the empirical formula of the mineral. Identify the homonuclear bonds found in the crystal. How many of these homonuclear bonds are there in an elementary cell?

problems.title: Beauty and Infinity
problems.problem:
Problem 15. Beauty and Infinity

Part I

The largest sand desert on Earth, the Rub’al Khali (ٱلرُّبْع ٱلْخَالِي) covers the southeastern part of Saudi Arabia. The most common constituents of sand grains are silica ($\ce{SiO2}$) and various silicates. Indeed, silicon and oxygen are the two main elements of Earth’s crust in various minerals. Olivine, $\ce{(Mg,Fe)2SiO4}$ and garnet, $\ce{(Mg,Fe,Mn)3Al2Si3O12}$ or $\ce{Ca3(Al,Cr,Fe)2Si3O12}$ are only two examples of the many silicate minerals. The bracketed elements signify a variable composition crystal structure with different atoms taking a certain crystal position. For olivine, this means that specimens with any $x$ = 0-1 exist for $\mathrm{(Mg_{1-x}Fe_x)_2SiO_4}$.

15.1. Express the formula of the garnet variant with the lowest silica content as a combination of oxides.

Several skeletal structures of polysilicate ions are represented on the figure, showing $\ce{SiO4}$ tetrahedra.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-15-fig1.png

15.2. Find the corresponding charge for each of the four structures in the Figure. Structures $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ can be extended to a 1D, structure $\mathbf{d}$ to a 2D polymeric ion. Find the empirical formula for the polymeric ions.

Some silicates are beautiful gemstones, displaying a spectrum of colors. Recent findings in the southwest of Saudi Arabia, in the Bisha area include beryls, belonging to the mineral family of emeralds and aquamarines.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-15-fig2.png

Emerald and aquamarine share the same beryl structure and have specific green and blue colors. Pure beryl is colorless and consists of Si, O, Al and Be. $0.2024\,\mathrm{g}$ of beryl contains $0.0635\,\mathrm{g}$ of Si and $0.0102\,\mathrm{g}$ Be. Another mineral, sky blue bazzite has the same stoichiometry as beryl, but the Al is replaced by another metal. The Si mass fraction in bazzite differs by 6.25% when compared to the Si mass fraction in beryl.

15.3. Find the formula of these two minerals: beryl and bazzite.

15.4. Identify the color of light absorbed by emerald: a) No absorption in the visible spectrum, b) Green color light, c) Red color light, d) Emerald color light.

Part II

In industrial processes, pure silicon, a primary semiconductor in the electronics industry, is derived from silane ($\ce{SiH4}$), itself obtained through the reduction of $\ce{SiO2}$. Additionally, on a smaller scale, silane can be produced from certain silicon derivatives such as silicon halides ($\ce{SiF4}$, $\ce{SiCl4}$) or metal silicides like $\ce{Mg2Si}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-15-fig3.png

15.5. Write balanced equations for the three numbered reactions of silane formation.

These reactions can yield Si containing byproducts. From the byproducts, let us consider $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$, each unique for one of the three reactions. Their molecular mass increases in order: $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{A}$. Compound $\mathbf{A}$ contains 93.3 % Si by mass. The mass spectrum of compound $\mathbf{B}$ can be used to obtain an average molar mass of $101\,\mathrm{g/mol}$. Also, $\mathbf{B}$ possesses two planes of symmetry. Finally, $\mathbf{C}$ contains 73.1% halogen by mass.

15.6. Identify the unknown compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ and assign them to their respective reactions.

15.7. Among the $\ce{SiX4}$ molecules ($\ce{SiH4}$, $\ce{SiF4}$, $\ce{SiCl4}$), determine a) the one with the lowest melting point, and b) the one with the highest Lewis acidity.

Part III

$\ce{SiH4}$ is highly flammable in $\ce{O2}$ containing atmospheres. The final product is $\ce{SiO2}$, however, in a less oxidative atmosphere like $\ce{N2O}$ gas, partial oxidation of silane can yield valuable products. Significant elementary reactions of the radical mechanism of this gas-phase reaction are below. The 1st and the 6th steps are very slow.

$$\begin{array}{l} \ce{N2O ->[$k_1$] N2 + O} \\ \ce{O + SiH4 ->[$k_2$] SiH3 + OH} \\ \ce{OH + SiH4 ->[$k_3$] SiH3 + H2O} \\ \ce{SiH3 + N2O ->[$k_4$] SiH3O + N2} \\ \ce{SiH3O + SiH4 ->[$k_5$] SiH3OH + SiH3} \\ \ce{SiH3 + SiH3O ->[$k_6$] H3SiOSiH3} \end{array}$$

15.8. Categorize steps 1, 4 and 6 with respect to their role in the chain reaction mechanism.

15.9. Write the net chemical reaction.

15.10. Find the kinetic law and reaction orders for the net reaction when $\ce{N2O}$ is in excess. Use the steady-state approximation for the intermediates.

15.11. Identify the coordinate system that would result in a linear graph:

a) $\ln[\ce{SiH4}]$ vs. $t$, b) $\log[\ce{SiH4}]$ vs. $t$, c) $1/[\ce{SiH4}]$ vs. $t$, d) $1/[\ce{SiH4}]^2$ vs. $t$, e) none of these

problems.title: Boron clusters
problems.problem:
Problem 16. Boron clusters

The chemistry of boron-based cluster anions is undergoing a revival thanks to their high stability, kinetic inertness, and easy functionalization.

A synthesis starts by heating $\ce{NaBH4}$ with equimolar amount of $\ce{B2H6}$ to produce compound $\mathbf{A}$. A reaction was accompanied by the evolution of a combustible gas equimolar with $\mathbf{A}$. After that, compound $\mathbf{A}$ was heated up to $165\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in diglyme (bis(2-methoxyethyl) ether) with 1.5 equivalent of $\ce{B2H6}$ in a sealed air-free reactor to produce a salt $\mathbf{B}$ containing a doubly charged cluster anion and the same combustible gas. Compound $\mathbf{B}$ has 1:1 B:H ratio and a 24.5% by weight Na content.

16.1. Give the formulas of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ and the balanced reactions of their formation.

Functionalizing boron clusters can be done using a wide range of reagents. One of the functionalization reactions is halogenation, forming weakly coordinating anions that activate their counter cations.

The cesium salt prepared by ion exchange from compound $\mathbf{B}$ was suspended in 1:1 water-methanol solvent mixture. Then the suspension was cooled down using an ice bath and halogen $\mathbf{C}$ was added slowly. After that, the reaction mixture was heated up to $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ under reflux. After quenching the small excess of halogen using sodium sulfite, the solvent was removed using rotary evaporator and product $\mathbf{D}$ was recrystallized using hot water, which is another cesium salt with a doubly charged anion. It has 19.6% by weight cesium and 9.6% by weight boron besides halogen.

16.2. Give the formulas of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ and the balanced reactions of the formation of $\mathbf{D}$ and the quenching of excess $\mathbf{C}$.

These clusters can serve as scaffolds for multifunctional nanomolecules with a well-defined structure. Using varied linkers and functional groups, the size and functionality of the nanomolecules can be tuned. A recent work showed great promise with covalently attached saccharides as functional groups that can bind with proteins.

The synthesis was pursued according to the synthesis scheme below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-16-fig1.png

The synthesis starts by reacting the tetrabutylammonium salt of the perhydroxylated clusters in the presence of a base with compound $\mathbf{E}$ ($\ce{C13H6BrF5}$) in a polar solvent. Compound $\mathbf{E}$ shows two doublets around 7.5 ppm and a singlet around 4.5 ppm in its $\ce{^1H}$-NMR spectrum and 3 different signals in $\ce{^{19}F}$-NMR. The attachment reaction of linker $\mathbf{E}$ is reasonably fast and complete on all cluster atoms. Subsequent functionalization is carried out on the neutral molecule $\mathbf{F}$ produced by reaction with Fe(III)-chloride.

16.3. Give the structure of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$. Use $\otimes$ to symbolize the cluster and only draw out one of the attached groups.

$\mathbf{F}$ was reacted with 1-thio-β-D-glucose tetraacetate (and other thiols) in the presence of $\ce{K3PO4}$ to introduce biologically relevant functionality. The rapid and complete functionalization reaction was monitored by $\ce{^{19}F}$-NMR because the pure product only has 2 different fluorine environments. The final product obtained after deprotecting the glucose is a dipotassium salt of the decorated cluster, $\mathbf{G}$.

Thiols were always used in excess, because they serve in another role besides the attachment of functionality to the cluster.

16.4. Determine the minimum amount of thiol needed by 1 mol of $\mathbf{F}$. What is an appropriate reagent to deprotect the glucose residue?

16.5. Draw the structure of a linker in $\mathbf{G}$ indicating only the B and S atoms from the rest of the molecule.

The glucose-coated nanomolecules show a much higher affinity towards lectin (a carbohydrate binding protein) than individual glucose molecules. Gold nanoparticles coordinated with 1-thio-β-D-glucose molecules also strongly bind to lectin.

16.6. What molecules potentially present in biological samples could affect the stability of the coordinated gold nanoparticles, but not the functionalized borate clusters?

problems.title: MOFs: The Ultimate Coordination Network
problems.problem:
Problem 17. MOFs: The Ultimate Coordination Network

Metal Organic Frameworks (MOFs) are coordination polymers typically built up from a transition metal and an organic linker featuring multiple coordinating functional groups. They play a significant role in hydrogen or ammonia storage and catalysis due to their large cavities and high porosity. The wide range of linker variations in size, shape, and coordinating functional group, coupled with the diverse metals available, results in numerous MOFs with distinct properties and applications. Their cavities make them excellent for storing various gases (hydrogen, ammonia, carbon dioxide, etc.).

The copper-based $\textbf{MOF-a}$ holds promise in ammonia storage. The synthesis of the structure starts by combining copper(II) salt $\mathbf{A}$ with an equimolar amount of the double linker $\mathbf{B}$ in DMF ($N$,$N$-dimethylformamide), resulting in a blue solution. This solution is stirred for 16 hours at $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, leading to the formation of a green-blue precipitate. After filtration, the precipitate was washed three times with DMF, followed by soaking in methanol for 24 hours. This soaking process is repeated with fresh methanol before final storage in a separate portion of methanol.

To analyze $\mathbf{A}$, slow heating was applied under a flow of inert gas, and the weight loss was monitored. Around $120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a 19.4% weight loss was observed, attributed to water loss. After reaching $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a black material $\mathbf{C}$ remained, and a reddish gas mixture evolved. The total mass loss up to this point, including water, amounted to 65.8% by weight. Switching the gas flow to hydrogen, and continuing heating, the black material lost 20.1% weight and copper was left behind.

17.1. Give the formula of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. Support your result by calculations.

Linker $\mathbf{B}$ is a symmetrical molecule containing only 3 elements and has a molar mass of $172\,\mathrm{g/mol}$. It has an inversion center, and it does not decolorize bromine water. Titrating the distinctly acidic solution of $0.500\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathbf{B}$ needed $11.6\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.500\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ solution. $\mathbf{B}$ has 3 different signals in $\ce{^{13}C}$-NMR.

17.2. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{B}$. Does it have any stereoisomers?

One method to estimate the surface area of a porous material consists of flooding nitrogen gas on the evacuated sample and monitoring pressure and adsorption. For $\textbf{MOF-a}$, the nitrogen uptake flattened out around $5.0\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol/g}$ before further increase. This region is interpreted to correspond to the formation of a monolayer on the surface.

17.3. Calculate the specific surface area of $\textbf{MOF-a}$ in $\mathrm{m^2/g}$ if we know that the cross-sectional surface area of a nitrogen molecule is $0.162\,\mathrm{nm^2}$.

$\textbf{MOF-a}$ has a unique metal coordination environment resulting in a 3D framework. Each copper atom is linked to 4 oxygen atoms from 4 different linkers in an approximately square planar way. That places two Cu atoms in each other’s vicinity, and an oxygen atom from a 5th linker is attached to each copper.

When ammonia, nitrogen, and hydrogen adsorptions were tested at room temperature, $\textbf{MOF-a}$ adsorbed significant amounts of ammonia compared to nitrogen and hydrogen as summarized on the graph below. The green solid becomes blue on exposure to ammonia (solid circles), and on desorption (empty circles) it turns purple. Two levels are marked on the graph for their importance. Level 2 corresponds to saturation with ammonia and Level 1 is the endpoint of desorption at 1 mbar pressure at room temperature. Careful heating resulted in the reconstruction of the original $\textbf{MOF-a}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-17-fig1.png

17.4. Calculate the number of ammonia molecules coordinating to each Cu atom in the structure corresponding to Level 1 and 2. $\textbf{MOF-a}$ has 27.2% by weight of copper.

X-ray measurements established that both structures are one-dimensional (i.e. have a straight linear arrangement of linked Cu atoms) and the copper atoms in both structures have two oxygen atoms from two ligands coordinated.

17.5. What are the primary coordination environments of the copper atoms in the two structures?

problems.title: Black gold
problems.problem:
Problem 18. Black gold

“Black gold” has nothing to do with the actual element Au or its compounds. It is a name which refers to oil, also known as petroleum: “black” due to the color of crude oil and “gold” as it is a very valuable resource nowadays.

Saudi Arabia has the second-largest proven petroleum reserves in the world. The country actively produces, exports, and refines petroleum crude oil. Gasoline and diesel are the products of petroleum that are used as fuels for vehicles. Due to the nature of engine combustion phenomena, burning these fuels in automotive engines contributes to the emission of air pollutants. Among them are unburned hydrocarbons (UHC), particulate carbon (C), carbon monoxide (CO), and nitrogen oxides ($\ce{NO_{$x$}}$).

18.1. Choose the major products of gasoline combustion when the air supply is $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ per $1\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of fuel. Use octane $\ce{C8H18}$ (density $\rho = 0.703\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) as the model compound for gasoline.

☐ UHC ☐ C ☐ CO ☐ $\ce{CO2}$ ☐ $\ce{H2}$ ☐ $\ce{H2O}$ ☐ $\ce{H2O2}$

The formula $\ce{NO_{$x$}}$ represents two nitrogen oxides: $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{NO2}$. These gases are formed in engines from atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen due to high temperatures achieved during the combustion of fuels. Although $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{NO2}$ are relatively simple compounds, they have rather complicated structures and bonding. First of all, both compounds are radical species, for which the commonly used octet rule doesn’t apply.

18.2. For the $\ce{NO2}$ molecule:

a) Draw the Lewis structures of two resonance forms,

b) Indicate the N–O bond order,

c) Indicate the hybridization of N atom,

d) Indicate the geometry of the molecule.

The correct N–O bond order in $\ce{NO}$ molecule can’t be determined using Lewis structures with the typical two-center two-electron bonds. Instead, the molecular orbital (MO) diagram can provide the answer.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-18-fig1.png

18.3. For the $\ce{NO}$ molecule:

a) Fill in the atomic (AO) and molecular (MO) orbitals in the provided MO diagram with the electrons.

b) Calculate the N–O bond order.

c) Compare the dissociation energies of $\ce{NO}$, $\ce{NO+}$ and $\ce{NO-}$.

It is mandatory now in most countries that all the vehicles sold are equipped with a special device that converts harmful exhaust gases from the engine into less harmful ones. This device is called a catalytic converter as it has a heterogeneous redox catalyst, which is usually a mixture of precious metals.

18.4. Give the formulas for the target products of catalytic conversion of UHC, C, CO and $\ce{NO_{$x$}}$.

More than half of metal $\mathbf{M}$ mined is used by the automotive industry to produce catalytic converters. This has a drastic influence on the price of this metal: although there are rarer elements than metal $\mathbf{M}$, some of them actually cost less because of the lower demand.

Organic compound $\mathbf{HL}$ is used to precipitate metal $\mathbf{M}$ from solutions in the form of a $\mathbf{ML_2}$ complex for recovery, purification, and gravimetric purposes. The content of metal $\mathbf{M}$ in $\mathbf{ML_2}$ is 31.61% by mass (wt.%, mass fraction, ω) and 3.23% by number of atoms (at.%, atomic percent, χ). The $\mathbf{HL}$ molecule consists of 2 nitrogen atoms, 2 oxygen atoms and 2 other elements, and has a degree of unsaturation (also known as “double bond equivalent”) of 2.

18.5. Determine the molecular formula of $\mathbf{HL}$ and metal $\mathbf{M}$.

Below is the simplified MO diagram for $\mathbf{ML_2}$ with the most important interactions shown. The interaction between d orbitals of metal cation $\mathbf{M}^{2+}$ and high-lying filled orbitals of the ligands $\mathbf{L}^-$ leads to the splitting of d orbitals.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-18-fig2.png

18.6. Fill in the MO diagram with electrons of $\mathbf{M}^{2+}$. Note: If you haven’t found metal $\mathbf{M}$ in the previous question, take any platinum group metal and note it on the diagram.

$\mathbf{ML_2}$ is a square planar complex, where $\mathbf{M}^{2+}$ is coordinated to all 4 $\mathrm{sp^2}$-hybridized N atoms. Therefore, 8 high lying filled ligand orbitals considered here are the following:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-18-fig3.png

18.7. In the table below:

a) Draw each d orbital of the metal (note the coordinate system),

b) Indicate the interacting orbital(s) $\varphi_i$ of appropriate symmetry and the type of overlap between these orbitals (σ, π, or δ).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-18-fig4.png

problems.title: Nitrogen fixation
problems.problem:
Problem 19. Nitrogen fixation

Dissociating the $\ce{N2}$ molecule requires $945\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. The high bond energy results in nitrogen being inert and not very reactive. In the early 20th century, Haber and Bosch pioneered a method involving $\ce{N2}$ reacting with $\ce{H2}$ to produce $\ce{NH3}$. However, their process requires high pressure and temperature to break the strong $\ce{N#N}$ bond. Overcoming this challenge is crucial as it would mark a significant advancement in artificial nitrogen fixation.

To understand this reaction, it's important to grasp the basics of nitrogen orbitals and bonding.

19.1. Draw the MO diagram of $\ce{N2}$. Indicate the HOMO and LUMO of the molecule.

One approach to break the $\ce{N#N}$ bond is to connect nitrogen atoms with an organometallic species that's similar in terms of electronic structure. This concept predicting interactions between metals and main group elements is called the isolobal analogy.

For instance, the $\ce{CH3}$ fragment and $\ce{Mn(CO)5}$ are isolobal because they both possess a single unpaired electron. They are also one electron away from a closed shell: 8 electrons for carbon and 18 electrons for manganese.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-19-fig1.png

The looped arrow is used to denote two species that are isolobal.

In the nitrogen fixation context, we will employ a molybdenum complex $\mathbf{D}$ that is isolobal to the nitrogen atom in $\ce{N2}$.

To synthesize this complex, we start with $\ce{MoCl5}$ based on the scheme below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-19-fig2.png

19.2. Give the oxidation state of Mo and the d-electron count in each of the three compounds.

The next schemes show the steps to synthesize the ligand for the complex and the combination of the ligand and the metal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-19-fig3.png

• Compound $\mathbf{A}$ $\ce{^1H}$ NMR: 7.69 ppm (s, 2H), 2.80 ppm (s, 6H), 2.65 ppm (s, 3H).

• Compound $\mathbf{B}$ $\ce{^1H}$ NMR: 6.36 ppm (s, 2H), 6.32 ppm (s, 1H), 3.89 ppm (br s, 1H), 2.17 ppm (s, 6H), 1.29 ppm (s, 9H).

19.3. Give the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$. Hint: $\mathbf{A}$ is aromatic.

Finally, when exposed to nitrogen gas, 2 equivalents of $\mathbf{D}$ will cleave the $\ce{N#N}$ to produce the complex $\mathbf{F}$, through the intermediate $\mathbf{E}$. (r.t. = room temperature)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-19-fig4.png

19.4. Provide the constitution (connectivity) of intermediate $\mathbf{E}$ and the structure of complex $\mathbf{F}$. Use 'L' instead of drawing the entire ligand.

19.5. Show the isolobal analogy of the $\mathbf{D}$ complex synthesized with the N atom, considering the d-electron count and the number of ligands in the complex.

problems.title: Bromination
problems.problem:
Problem 20. Bromination

The addition of bromine to alkenes occurs through a so-called bromonium ion intermediate:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-20-fig1.png

The positively charged bromine atom occupies one side of the intermediate, so the bromide ion can only attack from the other side. This means that the process is stereospecific, i.e., not all stereoisomers that are theoretically possible are formed. For example, in the case of ($E$)-pent-2-ene, only molecules with the stereostructures shown above are formed.

If the bromine atoms could not only enter from the opposite side (so-called anti-position), the other two possible stereoisomers shown below could also be formed during the bromination of ($E$)-pent-2-ene:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-20-fig2.png

In the following question, the bromine addition to hydrocarbon molecules with eight carbon atoms and only one double bond is investigated.

20.1. Give the structure of one alkene molecule that doesn’t contain a ring and one alkene molecule that does contain a ring for which the particular statement is true if such a molecule exists. If no such molecule exists, write an X. [The answer table has the columns "Does not contain ring" and "Contains ring" for each statement.]

a) During bromine addition, only one of the three possible stereoisomers is formed.

b) During bromine addition, two of the three possible stereoisomers are formed, and they are enantiomers.

c) During bromine addition, both of the two possible stereoisomers are formed, and they are enantiomers.

d) During bromine addition, both of the two possible stereoisomers are formed, and they are diastereomers.

e) The product of bromine addition has no stereoisomers.

However, other products can also result from the bromination process. If the reaction takes place in an aqueous medium, the bromonium ion produced in the first step may be attacked by a water molecule instead of the bromide ion. The resulting cation is deprotonated, and overall, a hydroxy group is incorporated into the molecule. In aqueous solution, this so-called bromohydrin is the main product, in which a bromine atom and a hydroxy group are present at the 1,2 positions.

During the formation of bromohydrin, regioselectivity plays a role in addition to stereospecificity. The water molecule is more likely to attack the higher order (more substituted) carbon atom of the bromonium ion.

20.2. Which main product(s) do you expect to be formed during the bromination of 1-methylcyclohex-1-ene in an aqueous solution? Show the stereostructure using wedge–dash notation [the two printed symbols, wedge and dash, are shown below]:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-20-fig3.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-20-fig4.png

problems.title: NMR puzzle
problems.problem:
Problem 21. NMR puzzle

One day Dr. Preping found a sealed container in his lab, filled with a white powder. The label only said has disappeared. He did not want to dispose of it, so he tried to figure out what it was. Upon dissolving the powder in water, he experienced intensive bubbling and the solution turned slightly basic afterwards. When he dissolved the powder in alcohol, he experienced gas evolution again, but less intensive than before. He could not observe melting in the range of his apparatus (up to $300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). The compound could not be dissolved in ether and was only slightly soluble in THF. He asked for the help of Prof. Speclock, who examined the filtrate of the THF suspension, and found an interesting group of signals in the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum. See the figure. (The numbers at the bottom are integrals of the respective signals.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-21-fig1.png

She immediately knew what the unknown compound could be. She showed Dr. Preping the following table.

21.1. Suggest a formula for the unknown compound $\mathbf{X}$. (Give your explanation!)

Dr. Preping was very happy because he wanted to perform the following reactions and he had been looking for the necessary reagent in his lab for a long time. Now he understood that he hadn’t been able to find it because it was labelled ‘compound $\mathbf{X}$’ the whole time. When carrying out the reactions, he was again absentminded a bit and could not remember which reactants he used for which flask. He knew only that he used all the amines and aldehydes once (see table). Prof. Speclock helped again. Based on the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectra of the amine products ($\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$) it was obvious which flask contained which compound.

21.2. Give the structures for $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$.

The next week he attempted the same synthesis using a new combination of his amines and aldehydes listed above. He obtained a colored compound $\mathbf{D}$ with totally different characteristics. It gave the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum listed below.

problems.title: Organonitrogen Compounds: The Compounds of Life
problems.problem:
Problem 22. Organonitrogen Compounds: The Compounds of Life

Nitrogen-containing compounds, such as amino acids, proteins, dyes, and medicines play a crucial role in different aspects of our everyday lives. We shall explore some of their classes in this task.

Amines are used as organic bases, for example in polymer and drug synthesis. Historically, amines were made using the Gabriel synthesis, which was developed by Siegmund Gabriel in 1887. In this reaction, a primary alkyl halide reacts with potassium phthalimide in an $\mathrm{S_N2}$ reaction, which is followed by reaction with hydrazine. Gabriel synthesis is a key step in the synthesis of the 2,3-dihydro-1$H$-indolizinium salt as shown below.

22.2. Determine the number of signals in the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum of the final compound (indolizinium salt)?

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They can be synthesized from 2-oxoacids as shown below in the synthesis of amino acid $\mathbf{E}$. The synthesis yields racemic $\mathbf{E}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-22-fig3.png

22.3. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$.

22.4. Draw the two enantiomers of $\mathbf{E}$ and assign the $R/S$ configuration of the chirality center(s).

Many commercial medicines contain nitrogen atoms. Finasteride 474 is a medicine used to treat hair loss in men. Its synthesis is shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-22-fig4.png

22.5. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$, and $\mathbf{H}$.

In the following reactions all the steps are routinely used basic transformations, so only the end product $\mathbf{X}$ was isolated, and the intermediates were not. problems.title: Neurotransmitters
problems.problem:
Problem 24. Neurotransmitters

Information is transmitted between neurons using neurotransmitters, chemicals that carry messages from one nerve cell across space to the next nerve. Catecholamines are neurotransmitters released by neurons and the adrenal gland. Dopamine, for example, induces feelings of pleasure, satisfaction and motivation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-24-fig1.png

Other examples of catecholamines include epinephrine ($\mathbf{D}$) and norepinephrine, derived from the amino acid phenylalanine. The following scheme shows a synthetic route to epinephrine ($\mathbf{D}$), starting from catechol. $\mathbf{D}$ is stable under acid/alkaline hydrolysis conditions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-24-fig2.png

24.1. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{D}$.

The synthetic route above leads to a racemic epinephrine. However, our body produces it as a single enantiomer of ($R$)-configuration. Using chiral resolution, it is possible to isolate one enantiomer from a racemic mixture.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-24-fig3.png

24.2. Explain how the chiral resolution works and draw the structure of ($R$)-$\mathbf{D}$.

Another group of neurotransmitters is derived from lipids. Anandamide is a fatty acid-based neurotransmitter, first isolated and identified by William A. Devane in 1992. It is present in the brain and binds to cannabinoid receptors. The name anandamide is derived from the Sanskrit word ananda, which means joy, bliss, delight. It is responsible for calmness and dream states.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-24-fig4.png

Anandamide has a short-duration neurological effect and has attracted scientists to use its structural variants as therapeutic agents to treat neuropathic pain. A series of anandamide analogues were synthesized by solid phase synthesis technique, in which the starting material is attached to a solid support. After a sequence of reactions building larger molecules, the product can be easily separated from the reaction mixture by a simple filtration. Then, the solid support is removed by an appropriate reagent.

The synthetic scheme below depicts the preparation of an analogue ($\mathbf{M}$) of anandamide. Solid support is represented as a black ball. CuI and NaI serve as catalysts.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-24-fig5.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-24-fig6.png

24.3. What is the role of DIC? Select all that apply.

a) Base

b) Acid

c) Catalyst

d) Coupling reagent

e) Solvent

24.4. What is the role of DMAP? Select all that apply.

a) Base

b) Acid

c) Catalyst

d) Coupling reagent

e) Solvent

24.5. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{E}$–$\mathbf{M}$.

problems.title: Henna
problems.problem:
Problem 25. Henna

Henna is an essential product in the Saudi Arabian and Middle Eastern cultures. Traditionally, women use henna to make gorgeous ornaments on their hands, arms and feet for special occasions such as weddings and the two Eid holidays. Henna is a red or brown dye that is typically obtained from dried leaves of the henna tree (Lawsonia inermis). Henna leaves contain a dye molecule that is called lawsone. This molecule binds to the keratin in the skin and hair and the colour lasts for 2 to 6 weeks.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-25-fig1.png

Lawsone exists in three tautomeric forms that are in equilibrium. The 1,4-naphthoquinone structure is the most stable form, followed by $\mathbf{A}$ and then $\mathbf{B}$, which is the least stable.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-25-fig2.png

25.1. Draw the structures of lawsone tautomers $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

A short route to lawsone and other similar naphthoquinones was described by Heerding and Moore, proceeding via 4-aryl-3-$tert$-butoxy-4-hydroxycyclobutenones as illustrated below.

25.2. Draw the missing compounds $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$ in the total synthesis of lawsone.

Hint: $\mathbf{D}$ contains a hydroquinone motif.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-25-fig3.png

Naphthoquinone-based 1,2,3-triazole $\mathbf{I}$ was shown to have potent trypanocidal and antitumor activities. This compound can be synthesized starting from lawsone according to the scheme below. $\mathbf{E}$ contains two condensed six-membered rings. The final step is the azide–alkyne cycloaddition, which proceeds according to the scheme in the box.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-25-fig4.png

25.3. Draw the missing compounds $\mathbf{F}$–$\mathbf{I}$ in the total synthesis of triazole $\mathbf{J}$.

problems.problem:
Problem 26. Natural products syntheses

Part A

Vernolepin is a highly functionalized elemanolide dilactone isolated from sweet bitterleaf (Vernonia hymenolepis) that grows in tropical Africa. Thanks to its platelet anti-aggregating and irreversible DNA polymerase inhibiting properties, it may serve as antitumor agent. Compound $\mathbf{E}$ serves as a key intermediate in the total synthesis of vernolepin. It can be prepared in several steps, starting with a series of cycloaddition reactions as shown below.

Part B

(+)-Cassaine is a toxic compound which is found in the tree genus Erythrophleum. Since ancient times, it has been used as an ordeal poison by African tribes and as an arrow poison by the Casamance people of Senegal. It inhibits $\ce{Na+}$, $\ce{K+}$-ATPase, thereby changing the force and energy of cardiac muscle contractions. One synthetic route to (+)-cassaine is depicted below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-26-fig2.png

Hints:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-26-fig3.png

problems.title: Przewalskin B: Medicine for the heart
problems.problem:
Problem 27. Przewalskin B: Medicine for the heart

(±)-Przewalskin is a diterpenoid found in a Chinese plant Salvia przewalskii, a member of the Labiatae plants family. Many species of this widely distributed genus have been used for centuries as folk medicine to treat a variety of illnesses. Przewalskin, first isolated in 2007, is used to treat cardiovascular diseases. Zhixiang Xie’s group outlined the total synthesis shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-27-fig1.png

Compound $\mathbf{A}$ is made regioselectively via a Diels–Alder cycloaddition reaction. Then, $\mathbf{A}$ is reduced using Wolff–Kishner reduction and deprotected using HCl. Aldol condensation between $\mathbf{B}$ and protected aldehyde gave $\mathbf{C}$ which, after deprotection with TBAF, afforded a bicyclic intermediate $\mathbf{D}$. The next step provided an inseparable mixture of stereoisomers $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$. The oxo group in both $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ can be reduced using $\ce{NaBH4}$ to yield stereoisomers $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$, respectively. This gives a new chirality center, which has the ($S$) configuration in both $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$.

27.1. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{G}$, and $\mathbf{H}$ (stereochemistry in $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ is not required).

27.2. What is the stereochemical relation between compounds $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$?

When the reduced functional group in in $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ is treated with the base DBU, it can form a cyclic ester if the other group is on the same face of the ring.

27.3. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{I}$. Identify which compound(s) can form a cyclic ester: $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$, both, neither?

Problem 28. Polymers

Polymerization processes play a crucial role in the petrochemical and manufacturing industries, allowing the creation of complex polymers that were previously inaccessible, thanks to techniques like olefin metathesis.
