14. Explain the concentration behaviour of [LL] and [DD] when:

a) $\varphi < \varphi_1$;
b) $\varphi_1 < \varphi < \varphi_2$;
c) $\varphi > \varphi_2$.

problems.title: Fluorescence, phosphorescence and quenching
problems.problem:
Problem 11. Fluorescence, phosphorescence and quenching

Molecules can exist in different electronic spin states known as singlet and triplet states. A singlet state has all electron spins paired (total spin, $S = 0$), while a triplet state has two unpaired electrons with parallel spins ($S = 1$). Transitions between these states govern important luminescence processes such as fluorescence (singlet → singlet) and phosphorescence (triplet → singlet). Understanding the decay kinetics of these excited states is essential for interpreting emission lifetimes, nonradiative losses, and designing efficient photonic materials.

When a molecule absorbs a photon ($hv$), an electron is promoted to a higher energy level, called an excited state ($\mathrm{S_1}$). This process is called excitation (Exc. with rate $I_\mathrm{abs}$). From this excited state ($\mathrm{S_1}$), the molecule can lose energy in different ways. It can undergo internal conversion (IC with rate constant $k_\mathrm{IC}$), where energy is lost non-radiatively as heat through changes in vibrational states. Alternatively, it can return to the ground state ($\mathrm{S_0}$) by emitting a photon ($hv$); this process is called fluorescence (Fluo. with rate constant $k_\mathrm{F}$). The excited singlet state ($\mathrm{S_1}$) can also convert to an excited triplet state ($\mathrm{T_1}$) through intersystem crossing (ISC with rate constant $k_\mathrm{ISC}$). The triplet state has a longer lifetime, and the molecule may return to the ground state ($\mathrm{S_0}$) by emitting a photon ($hv$), known as phosphorescence (Phos. with rate constant $k_\mathrm{P}$), or by losing energy as heat through non-radiative decay (Non.rad. with rate constant $k_\mathrm{N}$). If a quencher is present, it can accept the excitation energy, causing the molecule to return to its ground singlet state ($\mathrm{S_0}$) without emitting light.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-11-fig1.png

1. Choose the correct option: "For electron excitation, the wavelength of the absorbed photon must be …":

a) higher than that of the fluorescence wavelength
b) equal to that of the fluorescence wavelength
c) lower than that of the fluorescence wavelength

Internal Conversion (IC) is usually more common than Intersystem Crossing (ISC) because it is the spin allowed process (singlet → singlet).

2. Choose the correct option: "To increase $k_\mathrm{ISC}$ the energy gap between $\mathrm{S_1}$ and $\mathrm{T_1}$ states should be …":

a) higher
b) lower

To predict light emission (e.g., fluorescence) quantum yield, it is necessary to know the decay mechanism of the excited singlet state:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{Absorption:} & \mathrm{S} + hv \rightarrow \mathrm{S^*} & r_\mathrm{abs} = I_\mathrm{abs} \\ \text{Fluorescence:} & \mathrm{S^*} \rightarrow \mathrm{S} + hv & r_\mathrm{F} = k_\mathrm{F}[\mathrm{S^*}] \\ \text{Internal conversion:} & \mathrm{S^*} \rightarrow \mathrm{S} & r_\mathrm{IC} = k_\mathrm{IC}[\mathrm{S^*}] \\ \text{Intersystem crossing:} & \mathrm{S^*} \rightarrow \mathrm{T^*} & r_\mathrm{ISC} = k_\mathrm{ISC}[\mathrm{S^*}] \end{array}$$

3. Find the order of $[\mathrm{S^*}]$ and the observed rate constant ($k_\mathrm{obs}$) for the rate of decay of the excited singlet state, and the emission lifetime ($\tau_0$) after the incident light is turned off. Note: Emission lifetime ($\tau_0$) is the time required to reduce $[\mathrm{S^*}]$ by $e$ (≈ 2.72) times.

Fluorescence quantum yield ($\varphi_0$) is the fraction of the excited singlet state molecules that emit a photon (fluoresce).

4. Derive $\varphi_0$ as a function of the rate constants ($k_\mathrm{F}$, $k_\mathrm{IC}$, and $k_\mathrm{ISC}$).

To control fluorescence efficiency in devices (e.g., LEDs, sensors), quenching is very helpful. Fluorescence quenching is the promotion of non-radiative decay of the excited state. In a collision quenching, an excited fluorophore collides with a quencher, and due to the energy loss, there is no light emission:

$$\mathrm{S^*} + \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow \mathrm{S} + \mathrm{Q} \qquad r_\mathrm{Q} = k_\mathrm{Q}[\mathrm{S^*}][\mathrm{Q}]$$

5. Derive the fluorescence quantum yield ($\varphi$) as a function of the quencher concentration.

6. In the Stern–Volmer equation, the relationship between $\varphi_0/\varphi$ and [Q] is linear. Derive this relationship.

In one experiment, quenching of tryptophan fluorescence in a solution by dissolved $\ce{O2}$ gas was monitored by measuring emission lifetimes at 348 nm in aqueous solutions.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} [\mathbf{O_2}]\ /\ \mathbf{M} & 0 & 2.3\times10^{-2} & 5.5\times10^{-2} & 8\times10^{-2} & 10.8\times10^{-2} \\ \hline \boldsymbol{\tau}_\mathbf{0}\ /\ \mathbf{s} & 2.6\times10^{-9} & 1.5\times10^{-9} & 0.92\times10^{-9} & 0.71\times10^{-9} & 0.57\times10^{-9} \end{array}$$

7. Determine the quenching rate constant ($k_\mathrm{Q}$) for this process.

8. Calculate the concentration of $\ce{O2}$ at which half of the excited tryptophan molecules are quenched.

Phosphorescence can also be influenced by singlet state quenchers. There are several approaches to reducing the likelihood of collisions between quencher and phosphorescent molecules. One effective method is to increase the rigidity of the molecule. This rigidity also reduces non-radiative decay by limiting additional vibrational modes and suppressing vibrational relaxation pathways.

Phosphorescence molecule DA1 was heated at $120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ with PFMA and the product obtained suppressed the non-radiative decay ($k_\mathrm{N}$) of the triplet state.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-11-fig2.png

9. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{P}$, which is an adduct of the following [4+2] cycloaddition reaction:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-11-fig3.png

At low temperatures, the process of quenching is limited by an energy barrier:

$$\Delta E = E(T_1^\mathrm{Host}) - E(T_1^\mathrm{Guest})$$

Therefore, non-radiative decay can be suppressed by maintaining rigidity with a polymer matrix under this condition. At higher temperatures, vibrations increase and triplet energy transfer from the triplet state of the phosphorescent guest molecule to the polymer matrix (host) becomes possible:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-11-fig4.png

$\ln(k_\mathrm{N}+k_\mathrm{Q})$ as a function of (1/Temperature) is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-11-fig5.png

$k_\mathrm{N}$ – rate constant of the non-radiative decay of the triplet state.

$k_\mathrm{Q}$ – quenching of the triplet state by T–T energy transfer from the guest to the host molecule.

10. Estimate the energy barrier $\Delta E$ of T–T energy transfer.

problems.title: Photoacids
problems.problem:
Problem 12. Photoacids

Photoacids form a unique class of molecules that undergo a major change in their $\mathrm{p}K_a$ values between their ground and excited states. The loss of a proton is facilitated by light excitation. This phenomenon is also called excited state proton transfer (ESPT).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-12-fig1.png

Once, Khoja Nasreddin, who was bored with his usual routine, decided to investigate 2-naphthol, a simple molecule that exhibits the ESPT phenomenon. He prepared five 2-naphthol solutions (each of 25 mL) in different pH media, using a 2.1 mM 2-naphthol solution (solution $\mathbf{Z}$) and measured light absorbance ($l = 1.0\,\mathrm{cm}$) at 344 nm:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Solution} & \text{Composition} & \text{Absorbance} \\ \hline \mathbf{1} & 5\ \mathrm{mL}\ \mathbf{Z} + 20\ \mathrm{mL}\ 0.02\ \mathrm{M}\ \ce{HCl} & 0.219 \\ \mathbf{2} & 5\ \mathrm{mL}\ \mathbf{Z} + 20\ \mathrm{mL}\ 0.02\ \mathrm{M}\ \ce{NaOH} & 0.440 \\ \mathbf{3} & 5\ \mathrm{mL}\ \mathbf{Z} + 20\ \mathrm{mL}\ \ce{NH4Cl}/\ce{NH3}\ \text{(3:1 buffer)} & 0.256 \\ \mathbf{4} & 5\ \mathrm{mL}\ \mathbf{Z} + 20\ \mathrm{mL}\ \ce{NH4Cl}/\ce{NH3}\ \text{(2:1 buffer)} & 0.273 \\ \mathbf{5} & 5\ \mathrm{mL}\ \mathbf{Z} + 20\ \mathrm{mL}\ \ce{NH4Cl}/\ce{NH3}\ \text{(1:1 buffer)} & 0.300 \end{array}$$

1. Find the final concentration ($\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) of 2-naphthol in solutions $\mathbf{1}$–$\mathbf{5}$.

2. Calculate the molar extinction coefficients, $\varepsilon_\mathrm{ArO^-}$ and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{ArOH}$ at this wavelength.

3. Plot the graph pH vs $\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{ArO^-}]}{[\mathrm{ArOH}]}$. Estimate the $\mathrm{p}K_a$ of 2-naphthol if $\mathrm{p}K_b(\ce{NH3}) = 4.75$.

To check the ESPT phenomenon in 2-naphthol, Khoja Nasreddin recorded the fluorescence spectra of solutions $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-12-fig2.png

Dissociation of a photoacid in the ground and excited states can be described with a combined Förster and Jablonski diagram:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-12-fig3.png

$\mathrm{S_0}$, $\mathrm{S_1}$, …, $\mathrm{S_n}$ stand for different electronic states, each of them having multiple vibrational levels. $\Delta H$ and $\Delta H^*$ indicate changes in the enthalpy of dissociation in the ground and excited states, respectively. $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ are the frequencies of $\mathrm{S_1}$ to $\mathrm{S_0}$ (0–0) transitions for the photoacid and its deprotonated form, respectively. Internal conversion (IC) is a spin-allowed non-radiative transition from a higher to a lower electronic state and does not show any peak in the spectra. Fluorescence, on the other hand, is the emission of a photon during a transition between the states with the same spin quantum number (for example, $\mathrm{S_1} \rightarrow \mathrm{S_0}$). Vibrational relaxation (VR) is a non-radiative transition from a higher vibrational level to a lower one in the same electronic state of the molecule. VR is very fast, so it occurs right after light absorption and precedes other radiative processes like fluorescence.

In practice, transition wavelengths $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are commonly used instead of corresponding frequencies.

4. Assuming $\Delta H^{\circ*} - \Delta H^\circ = \Delta G^{\circ*} - \Delta G^\circ$, derive the relationship between $\Delta\mathrm{p}K_a$, $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$, and temperature. $\Delta\mathrm{p}K_a = \mathrm{p}K_a - \mathrm{p}K_a^*$.

5. Determine the $\mathrm{p}K_a^*$ of the excited state (ES) of 2-naphthol at 298 K. Calculate $[\mathrm{ArOH^*}]/[\mathrm{ArO^{-*}}]$ at $\mathrm{pH} = 5$.

Khoja Nasreddin wondered whether every acid decreases its $\mathrm{p}K_a$ in its excited state. After consulting with Prof. Beruni, Khoja found out that this might relate to Baird's rules – the analogue of Hückel's aromaticity rules for excited states. According to Baird's rules, in the excited state, planar conjugated structures with $4n$ $\pi$-electrons are considered aromatic, and $(4n + 2)$ $\pi$-electrons are considered antiaromatic. In this terminology, photoacidity is the result of Baird-antiaromatic molecules "relieving stress" through deprotonation. This is made possible because of the excess charge redistribution from the anionic centre to the ring.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-12-fig4.png

6. Classify the structures below as Baird-aromatic and Baird-antiaromatic. Identify those that could be used as potential photoacids.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-12-fig5.png

7. 2-Naphtalenecarboxylic acid behaves the opposite way when treated with light – its $\Delta\mathrm{p}K_a = \mathrm{p}K_a - \mathrm{p}K_a^* < 0$. Explain this phenomenon.

Merocyanines are an excellent example of photoacidity, turning into spiropyrans under light irradiation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-12-fig6.png

8. Draw the structure of the spiropyran.

The synthesis of a merocyanine photoacid polymer is given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-12-fig7.png

Hints:

• Hydrolysis of compound $\mathbf{A}$ results in compound $\mathbf{B}$.
• $\mathbf{C}$ can be converted into $\mathbf{C'}$ with a carboxylic acid moiety under $\ce{NaClO2}$.

9. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{X}$.

problems.title: Interested in micelles?
problems.problem:
Problem 13. Interested in micelles?

Part 1. The forms of micelles

The form of a micelle can be described by the surfactant packing parameter, $N_\mathrm{S}$. The packing parameter considers the volume and the length of the hydrophobic chain ($V_\mathrm{C}$ and $L_\mathrm{C}$, respectively), and the equilibrium hydrophilic area per molecule at the aggregate interface, $a_0$:

$$N_\mathrm{S} = \frac{V_\mathrm{C}}{a_0\times L_\mathrm{C}}$$

The table below shows the relationships between the surfactant packing parameter and the form of the structure:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \textbf{Form of micelle} & \text{Sphere} & \text{Cylinder} & \text{Bilayer} \\ \hline \boldsymbol{N}_\mathbf{S} & \le \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3} < \cdots \le \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2} < \cdots \le 1 \end{array}$$

1. If there are cone (a), rectangular wedge (b) and cylinder-shaped (c) surfactants, match them with their appropriate form of structure. Prove your answers by calculation. Note: It is only an assumption. In fact, surfactants themselves are more complicated structures and can have shapes which are different from these three below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-13-fig1.png

The phosphorus dendrons $\mathbf{G_1}$ and $\mathbf{G_2}$ act as charged surface active substances, although their structure differs from that of classical surfactants with a well-defined polar head and non-polar tail. They aggregate into clear structures and can be synthesised through the scheme below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-13-fig2.png

$\mathbf{A_1}$ is a cyclic compound with a threefold symmetry axis, with mass fractions of P, N, and Cl of 26.73%, 12.09%, and 61.18%, respectively. With the addition of an appropriate number of equivalents of 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde to $\mathbf{A_1}$, $\mathbf{A_2}$ is produced as the main product with only one Cl atom.

Note: A threefold symmetry axis is an imaginary line through an object around which it can be rotated by 120° and appear unchanged. For example, it is present in the molecule of ammonia.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-13-fig3.png

2. Identify structures $\mathbf{A_1}$–$\mathbf{A_4}$, $\mathbf{I_1}$–$\mathbf{I_2}$, and $\mathbf{G_1}$–$\mathbf{G_2}$.

3. Based on the synthesis pattern for $\mathbf{G_1}$ and $\mathbf{G_2}$ shown in the scheme, calculate how many cationic groups will be present in $\mathbf{G_{10}}$ if the same reaction stages are repeated.

4. By analysing the structure, determine which type of surfactants the $\mathbf{G_1}$ and $\mathbf{G_2}$ molecules resemble. Indicate the type of assembly they most likely show. Specify without calculations.

5. Choose the main purpose of adding HCl at the end of the synthesis:

a) to hydrolyse unreacted P–Cl bonds for purification;
b) to make the fluorescent label brighter;
c) to create a water-soluble, positively charged form that will show biological activity;
d) to rigidify the dendron structure via cyclisation.

In contrast to $\mathbf{G_1}$ and $\mathbf{G_2}$, in a series of amphiphilic polystyrene (PS)-poly(propylene imine) dendrimer diblock copolymers $\mathbf{Gen1}$–$\mathbf{Gen3}$, varying in head group size, the form of micelles within a polar medium depends on the generation number.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-13-fig4.png

6. Propose the forms of micelle in which $\mathbf{Gen1}$, $\mathbf{Gen2}$ and $\mathbf{Gen3}$ are assembled in water, if each generation forms a distinct micelle type.

Part 2. Thermodynamics of micelle formation

The micelle formation process can be seen as an equilibrium between two states:

$$n[\mathrm{M}](\text{surfactant}) \rightleftharpoons [\mathrm{M}_n](\text{micelle})$$

$$K_n = \frac{[\mathrm{M}_n]}{[\mathrm{M}]^n} = e^{\frac{-\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ_\mathrm{micelle}}{RT}}$$

where $n$ is the aggregation number, i.e. the number of surfactant molecules (further referred to as monomers) in the micelle; [M], $[\mathrm{M}_n]$ reflect the concentrations of monomers and micelles, respectively.

7. Derive the equation for the fraction of monomers present in micelles as a function of [M], $n$ and $K_n$.

8. Choose which of the suggested conditions would lead to the maximum number of monomers inside the micelles. Assume that in all conditions the equilibrium constants are the same and the monomer concentration is lower than $1\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

(a) Low concentration of monomers with low aggregation number.
(b) Low concentration of monomers with high aggregation number.
(c) High concentration of monomers with low aggregation number.
(d) High concentration of monomers with high aggregation number.

At the critical point, the monomers inside the micelles start to account for the largest fraction. This is the so-called "critical micelle concentration ($CMC$)", above which the monomers will mostly be within the micelles.

9. Describe $CMC$ as a function of aggregation number.

The dependence of specific conductivity on the concentration of surfactant monomers is shown in the picture below at temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-13-fig5.png

10. Assuming that the Gibbs energy of micelle formation, $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ_\mathrm{micelle}$, and the aggregation number remain constant, compare $T_1$ and $T_2$.

problems.title: The basics of Metal–Organic Frameworks
problems.problem:
Problem 14. The basics of Metal–Organic Frameworks

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson, and Omar M. Yaghi for the development of Metal–Organic Frameworks (MOFs). MOFs are crystalline, nanoporous coordination polymers formed by linking metal nodes (ions or metal oxide clusters – secondary building units) with multidentate organic ligands. Their hallmark is the combination of molecular-level tunability with permanent porosity, producing materials whose structural and functional diversity exceeds that of classical zeolites or activated carbons. MOFs are 3D frameworks with a complex structure. Thus, building models is useful to understand elementary units. For that, please follow the instructions from J. Chem. Educ. 2025, 102, 2, 877–881 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jchemed.4c01312). Normal paper, glue, and tape can also be used as alternatives. One of the famous materials in this field is MOF-5 constructed from zinc oxo-clusters ($\ce{Zn4O}$) and 1,4-benzenedicarboxylate (BDC) ligands.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-14-fig1.png

1. From the figure above and/or constructed model, write down the empirical formula for the repeating unit.

The first synthesis of MOF-5 was carried out by mixing $\ce{Zn(NO3)2}$, $\mathrm{H_2BDC}$ (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid), and triethylamine in a N,N-dimethylformamide/chlorobenzene mixture. Small amounts of water were added to initiate oxo-anion formation. The crystals formed were filtered and activated (dried) in a vacuum oven.

2. Write down the chemical equation of MOF-5 formation.

Elemental analysis of the crystals before activation showed elemental content (by mass): C – 44.21%, H – 5.02%, N – 7.64%. In mass spectra of crystals during heating up to $350\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, four $m/z$ signals were detected: 73, 77, 112, and 114. The relative intensity of the latter two signals was 3:1.

3. Write down the empirical formula of the crystals before activation.

MOF-5 has a high surface area of $2900\,\mathrm{m^2\,g^{-1}}$. The distance between oxygen atoms in the cluster centres was found to be 12.94 Å.

4. Find the free volume (which is not occupied by framework atoms) and experimental surface area ($\mathrm{m^2}$) of one cubic cell. Account only for Van der Waals radii of atoms ($r$), which are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \textbf{Element} & \text{Zn} & \text{H} & \text{C} & \text{O} \\ \hline \boldsymbol{r}\ \mathbf{/}\ \textbf{Å} & 1.5 & 1.2 & 1.7 & 1.5 \end{array}$$

5. To be correct, there are two pores with diameters of 11.0 Å and 15.1 Å. Find the elementary unit cell parameter $a$.

6. MOF-5 has been tested for hydrogen uptake. It was found that 10 g of the material can take up to 1 wt% of $\ce{H2}$ at 20 bar, 298 K. Assuming all the material is an ideal crystal, calculate excessive hydrogen uptake (how much excess hydrogen can be stored compared to pure hydrogen of the same volume without MOF-5 under the given conditions).

7. Suggest the ligands which might change the cubic cell volume down to 69.3%. The distance between the 1- and 4-carbons of a benzene ring is 2.69 Å.

problems.title: Microscopy in chemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 15. Microscopy in chemistry

Scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) is a microscopy method that lets us see individual atoms and molecules on the surface. It works by moving a sharp metal tip very close to the surface and applying a small voltage. In 1986, Binnig, Quate, and Gerber combined the principles of STM with a stylus profilometer to create Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM). While STM can only be used to image conductive samples, AFM does not require a current flow between the tip and the sample and can map a surface regardless of its conductivity.

In 2012, an article was published reporting that British chemists from the University of Warwick, together with a group of scientists from IBM Research, had captured an AFM image of a hydrocarbon molecule called $\mathbf{X}$ (see the image below). This image was subsequently recognised as the smallest logo for the London 2012 Summer Olympics.

The synthesis of this hydrocarbon began with pyrene-4-carbaldehyde:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-15-fig1.png

DMF – dimethylformamide, Amberlyst – protonic ion exchange resin. Initially obtained hydrocarbon molecule $\mathbf{E}$ easily isomerises to more symmetrical $\mathbf{X}$ under proton migration conditions.

1. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{X}$. Note: Molecule $\mathbf{X}$ possesses a twofold symmetry axis.

2. Compound $\mathbf{X}$ was named as ...cene. Suggest its full name.

$\mathbf{X}$-based units can be used as building blocks of 1D quantum magnet chains via the formation of stable radical centres:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-15-fig2.png

3. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{F}$–$\mathbf{I}$, based on the following information about compound $\mathbf{F}$:

• A peak with $m/z$ 411.89 was registered as the main peak in the mass spectrum;
• Only 4 types of protons exist in $\mathbf{F}$;
• Compound $\mathbf{F}$ has a twofold symmetry axis.

The beauty of such systems is that for finite chains like these, the lowest spin excitation energy, $\Delta_\mathrm{LEE}$, is inversely proportional to $L$:

$$\Delta_\mathrm{LEE} \le J\,\frac{2\pi^2S^2}{L}$$

where $J$ is an exchange coupling parameter between the nearest neighbours, $S$ is a spin number, and $L$ is the number of repeating units in the quantum chain. Therefore, for a considerably large $L$, we can design spin fluids with a very low excitation gap, which can be considered gapless.

4. Calculate the value of $L$ for which the quantum chain $\mathbf{H}$ becomes gapless at room temperature ($T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$), i.e. $\Delta_\mathrm{LEE}$ becomes comparable with the average thermal energy $k_\mathrm{B}T$. Use $J = 38\,\mathrm{meV}$ and $S = 1$.

AFM can be used to study the transformation of individual molecules during complex transformations. AFM was performed for the products of the thermally induced isomerisation reaction of $\mathbf{Q}$. It is known that compound $\mathbf{S}$ has a twofold symmetry axis, $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$ contain only 5- and 6-membered fused rings.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-15-fig3.png

5. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{R}$–$\mathbf{T}$.

The molecule $\mathbf{Q}$ itself is obtained from $\mathbf{U}$ according to the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-15-fig4.png

Additionally:

• In the mass spectrum, compound $\mathbf{U}$ has a molecular ion cluster of three peaks at $m/z$ 234, 236, and 238 in an intensity ratio of 1:2:1;
• $\mathbf{U}$ has 2 types of protons in the aromatic region.

6. Based on the given AFM image and additional hints, draw the structures of $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{U}$–$\mathbf{W}$.

problems.title: Kinase inhibitors
problems.problem:
Problem 16. Kinase inhibitors

Kinases are enzymes controlling many processes in living things, including cell growth. Kinase inhibition has become an important direction for anticancer drug development. Two synthetic approaches to the class of Lck-kinase inhibitors are discussed.

A synthesis of promising inhibitor $\mathbf{F}$ is shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-16-fig1.png

1. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{E}$. Note: Nitrogen content (by mass) in $\mathbf{B}$ is 7.40%. $\mathbf{D2}$ is separated from $\mathbf{D1}$, and only $\mathbf{D2}$ is transformed into $\mathbf{F}$.

Another promising molecule $\mathbf{M}$ was synthesised. Compound $\mathbf{M}$ has a similar core to $\mathbf{F}$ but has a molecular mass lower than that of $\mathbf{F}$ by 42 atomic mass units. The first two steps were a benzylic oxidation by N-chlorosuccinimide and oxidation by $\ce{NaClO2}$. The transformation of $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{I1}$ and $\mathbf{I2}$ proceeds in the same manner as $\mathbf{B}$ to $\mathbf{C}$, but with the formation of a mixture of isomers. The transformation of $\mathbf{I2}$ to the desired product $\mathbf{J2}$ is analogous to the conversion of $\mathbf{C}$ to $\mathbf{D2}$. However, the order of the hydrolysis and reduction steps is switched. This change in order results in the formation of additional side products $\mathbf{K1}$ and $\mathbf{K2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-16-fig2.png

2. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{G}$–$\mathbf{L}$, including all isomers shown on the scheme.

3. Explain why only one product is formed during the reaction of $\mathbf{B}$.

In the reaction of $\mathbf{I2}$ to $\mathbf{J2}$, changing the order of the reduction and hydrolysis steps compared to the previous scheme was crucial to obtain $\mathbf{J}$. The compound $\mathbf{W}$ could have formed following the sequence with the original order.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-16-fig3.png

4. Draw the structure of product $\mathbf{W}$ (21.52% nitrogen by mass).

The molecules obtained showed high potency with a specific kinase enzyme. However, two transformations of $\mathbf{F}$ were also carried out to give molecules $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, the molecular formulae of which differ only by two hydrogen atoms.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-16-fig4.png

5. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. $\mathbf{Y}$ is a homologous compound to $\mathbf{M}$. Note: The number of $sp^2$-hybridised carbons in $\mathbf{X}$ increased by one.

The synthesised molecules were evaluated by $\mathrm{IC_{50}}$ (half-maximum inhibitory concentration), which is a quantitative measure that indicates how much of a particular drug is needed to inhibit in vitro a given biological process or biological component by 50%. The results are shown in the table below:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{Compound} & \textbf{R} & \mathbf{IC_{50}}\ /\ \boldsymbol{\mu}\mathbf{M} \\ \hline \mathbf{F} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & 0.46 \\ \mathbf{F} & \text{2-Cl} & >40 \\ \mathbf{F} & \text{2,4-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & >40 \\ \mathbf{F} & \text{4-Cl} & >40 \\ \mathbf{F} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Me_2} & 0.46 \\ \mathbf{F} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Et_2} & >40 \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{Compound} & \textbf{R} & \mathbf{IC_{50}}\ /\ \boldsymbol{\mu}\mathbf{M} \\ \hline \mathbf{F}\ \text{(N3-Me)} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & 1.1 \\ \mathbf{F}\ \text{(N1-Me)} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & 12.5 \\ \mathbf{F}\ \text{(N4-Me)} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & 9.6 \\ \mathbf{Y} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & 1.1 \\ \mathbf{M} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & 0.38 \\ \mathbf{X} & \text{2,6-}\mathrm{Cl_2} & 0.026 \end{array}$$

6. Explain the effect of the substituents in the aromatic ring if the coordination of $\mathbf{F}$ in a simplified enzyme pocket looks as follows:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-16-fig5.png

problems.title: Carbohydrate chemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 17. Carbohydrate chemistry

Carbohydrates are an essential class of chemicals that fuel living organisms with energy. The common saccharide glucose (Glc) exists in either a linear or cyclic form. It can undergo some common chemical transformations:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-17-fig1.png

1. Identify products $\mathbf{I}$–$\mathbf{V}$.

In its cyclic form, glucose contains five hydroxy groups. Regioselective transformation of each position represents a challenge for chemists. Some synthetic transformations of $\alpha$-glucopyranose are shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-17-fig2.png

It is known that $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{G}$, and $\mathbf{D}$ contain the same functional groups; $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ differ in formulae by $\ce{CH2}$; $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ contain three six-membered rings in their structures; there are two different $\ce{CH3}$-groups in $\mathbf{E}$.

2. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{G}$.

However, these transformations cannot differentiate neighbouring 2,3- and 3,4-diols, since in both cases the hydroxy groups are in a trans-configuration and occupy equatorial positions. A brilliant solution to this challenge was found by using the common tetrahydropyranyl protecting group in chiral form:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-17-fig3.png

3. Based on the given example and considering that sterically bulky groups tend to occupy equatorial positions in chair conformations, draw the structures of $\mathbf{H1}$ and $\mathbf{H2}$. For drawing $\mathbf{H1}$ you need to redraw the glucopyranose ring so that the 2,3-hydroxy groups are on the right side of the drawing. Use a chair conformation of the protecting group.

A very interesting example of a glucopyranose transformation led to adamantane-type cyclic compound $\mathbf{K}$ stepwise blocking three hydroxyl groups with only one protecting group:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-17-fig4.png

4. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$.

Another class of reagents that can form cyclic acetal-type structures is boronic acids. Their chemistry was successfully used to synthesise the trisaccharide "Gal-Gal-Glc" derivative:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-17-fig5.png

5. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{L}$, $\mathbf{M}$, and trisaccharide "Gal-Gal-Glc". Do not specify the configuration of the newly formed anomeric centres.

problems.title: Inositol
problems.problem:
Problem 18. Inositol

In Uzbekistan, people greatly appreciate foods that are both rich in flavour and highly nutritious. Rice is one of the main ingredients in Uzbek cuisine and forms the basis of many traditional dishes, such as pilaf and mastava.

Cooked rice consists of approximately 29% carbohydrates by mass, primarily in the form of $\alpha$-amylose, which is a polysaccharide composed of $\alpha$-D-glucose units linked through $\alpha(1\rightarrow4)$ glycosidic bonds. Carbohydrates are the primary source of energy for humans and occur in nature in a wide variety of forms.

1. a) Draw the most stable chair conformation of D-glucose.

b) Draw the structure of the repeating unit of $\alpha$-amylose in Haworth projection.

2. Calculate the number of repeating units that one amylose chain with a molar mass of 243 kDa contains.

Glucose, which is a well-known representative of carbohydrates in living organisms, can be converted into many different biomolecules.

One such compound is myo-inositol (one of the isomers of inositol), whose biosynthesis pathway is shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-18-fig1.png

ATP = Adenosine Triphosphate, ADP = Adenosine Diphosphate

3. Draw one of the chair conformations for each of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{F}$ and myo-inositol. Note: Molecules of $\mathbf{F}$ and myo-inositol contain a plane of symmetry.

4. Draw the structures of all inositol stereoisomers and indicate which of them are chiral.

Many plants synthesise myo-inositol hexaphosphate ($\mathbf{IP6}$) as a phosphorus storage compound. Studies of various plant species have revealed that the biosynthesis of $\mathbf{IP6}$ proceeds through stepwise phosphorylation of compound $\mathbf{F}$.

Below is the biosynthesis pathway of $\mathbf{IP6}$ that occurs in Dictyostelium:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-18-fig2.png

5. Determine the maximum number of myo-inositol diphosphate ($\mathbf{G}$) isomers that can be formed in this pathway. Draw their structures and indicate which of them are chiral/achiral.

6. Determine the maximum theoretically possible number of isomers of myo-inositol diphosphate (that do not necessarily originate from $\mathbf{F}$). Draw their structures and indicate which of them are chiral/achiral.

Phosphorylation of myo-inositol occurs according to the following rule: the most distant accessible hydroxyl group relative to the previously phosphorylated hydroxyl group is phosphorylated.

7. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{G}$–$\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{IP6}$. Indicate the structures that contain a plane of symmetry.

problems.title: Carbohydrates as chiral pools
problems.problem:
Problem 19. Carbohydrates as chiral pools

Asymmetric synthesis has attracted significant attention in recent years thanks to advances in asymmetric catalysis. However, using chiral auxiliary groups in the substrate structure remains an efficient approach for chiral total synthesis, especially when chiral substrates are readily available. Different monosaccharides are handy starting materials in natural product synthesis. For example, in 1985, the first synthesis of compound $\mathbf{X}$ from L-sorbose derivative $\mathbf{A}$ was published.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-19-fig1.png

1. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and the most stable diastereomer of $\mathbf{X}$, including stereochemistry. Note: $\mathbf{X}$ contains a five-membered heterocycle, and the formation of $\mathbf{X}$ proceeds through an imine intermediate.

Thromboxane B2 (TxB2) is a stable, inactive breakdown product of Thromboxane A2 (TxA2), a potent molecule that causes blood platelets to clump (aggregate) and blood vessels to constrict. It was synthesised from D-glucose. The following scheme shows the synthesis of key intermediate $\mathbf{I}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-19-fig2.png

2. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{D}$–$\mathbf{I}$ with stereochemistry. Note: Acetal/ketal formation involves a primary alcohol when it is available.

3. Determine in what order the following combinations of reagents ($\mathrm{Z_1}$–$\mathrm{Z_4}$) must be used to obtain Thromboxane $\mathrm{B_2}$ from $\mathbf{I}$:

$\mathrm{Z_1}$ – 1) PCC ($\mathrm{PyH^+\cdot CrO_3Cl^-}$), 2) $\mathrm{Ph_3P^+CH^-C(O)(CH_2)_4CH_3}$;

$\mathrm{Z_2}$ – 1) BzCl, 2) $\mathrm{BuN_4{}^+F^-}$;

$\mathrm{Z_3}$ – 1) $\ce{NaBH4}$, 2) $\ce{K2CO3}$, 3) HCl;

$\mathrm{Z_4}$ – 1) $(i\text{-Bu})_2\mathrm{AlH}$, 2) $\mathrm{Ph_3P^+CH^-(CH_2)_3COOH}$, 3) $\ce{CH2N2}$.

Using compound $\mathbf{D}$, it is possible to synthesise other chiral molecules. (+)-Actinobolin, isolated from the culture fluid of Streptomycin, has a broad antibacterial spectrum and moderate antitumor activity. In the synthesis of (+)-Actinobolin, overall, five new stereocentres were formed using the chiral auxiliary.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-19-fig3.png

4. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{J}$–$\mathbf{O}$, including stereochemistry.

Swainsonine, an indolizidine alkaloid, was synthesised using benzyl-$\alpha$-D-mannopyranoside. It is a potent inhibitor of Golgi apparatus alpha-mannosidase II, an immunomodulator, and a potential chemotherapeutic agent. The synthesis of (–)-Swainsonine is given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-19-fig4.png

Hint: $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ are epimers.

5. Determine the configurations of all stereocentres in (–)-Swainsonine and the starting material.

6. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{P}$–$\mathbf{U}$, including stereochemistry.

7. Indicate which stereocentres are preserved and which centres are newly formed.

problems.title: Pacman, Hangman, Cageman
problems.problem:
Problem 20. Pacman, Hangman, Cageman

Scientists often look for analogies in culture to explain their discoveries. One example of such a comparison was the arcade video game Pacman, popular in the 1980s and 1990s, where the main task of the yellow ball (Pacman) is to eat all the dots on the map.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-20-fig1.png

The same task must be performed by the molecules $\mathbf{Pacman\ 1}$ and $\mathbf{Pacman\ 2}$, which must "eat" small molecules such as $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{N2}$, or $\ce{O2}$, catalysing their transformations. Pacman molecules are two catalytically active structural fragments connected by a linker at a certain angle. Inspiration for such molecules comes from the active site of natural cytochrome P450, which contains a porphyrin macrocycle. Porphyrin is a macrocycle with an 18 $\pi$-electron Hückel aromatic system, which can coordinate metal ions in the middle. The synthesis of $\mathbf{Pacman\ 1}$ is shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-20-fig2.png

Note: C–H bonds of porphyrin rings are not involved in chemical transformations in this problem.

1. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$, if it is known that neither of these compounds, nor $\mathbf{Pacman\ 1}$–$\mathbf{2}$ contain oxygen. The nitrogen content (by mass) in compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ is 11.12% and 9.70%, respectively.

Unfortunately, it was impossible to isolate $\mathbf{Pacman\ 1}$. As a result, another approach to the stable $\mathbf{Pacman\ 2}$ with two different porphyrin rings was suggested. In the mass spectrum of this compound, the molecular ion peak was at $m/z$ 1535.04.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-20-fig3.png

2. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{D}$–$\mathbf{F}$, and $\mathbf{Pacman\ 1}$–$\mathbf{2}$. All molecules can be drawn flat. $\mathbf{Pacman\ 2}$ contains 7.678% of the metal by weight.

3. Calculate the distance between the two metals in $\mathbf{Pacman\ 2}$, if the distance from carbon atoms a and b to the corresponding metals is the same and equals 4.7 Å. Assume that porphyrin and benzene rings are coplanar, and bond lengths and angles on benzene rings are ideal. Note: The carbon–carbon bond distance in the benzene ring is 1.39 Å.

4. Draw a 3D schematic structure of $\mathbf{Pacman\ 2}$ binding an oxygen molecule. Note: You can simplify the macrocycle as a quadrilateral, only drawing out the linker and metals.

Another version of a binuclear complex was synthesised as follows to yield $\mathbf{Pacman\ 3}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-20-fig4.png

5. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{G}$–$\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{Pacman\ 3}$.

In the catalytic centre of cytochrome c oxidase, heme (a porphyrin-based iron-containing compound which forms the non-protein part of haemoglobin) and Cu atoms are placed in close proximity to ease the reduction of oxygen to water. Scientists attempted to mimic this pocket by synthesising a salt called $\mathbf{Hangman}$, bearing two different metal ions:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-20-fig5.png

6. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{Hangman}$.

Another type of binuclear porphyrin complexes can be called $\mathbf{Cageman}$. One of the examples of a $\mathbf{Cageman}$ synthesis is shown below. In the mass spectrum of the compound $\mathbf{K}$, a series of signals at $m/z$ 2667.0, 1261.0, 792.3, 558.0, and 417.4 were detected.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-20-fig6.png

7. Calculate the molecular weight of $\mathbf{Cageman}$ (use integer values of atomic mass).

problems.title: Catalyst C
problems.problem:
Problem 21. Catalyst C

Compound $\mathbf{A}$ is a trihydrate which contains a metal of the 5th period, $\mathbf{M}$, with a mass fraction of 39.09%. A 2.00 g sample of $\mathbf{A}$ was dissolved in ethanol. This ethanolic solution of $\mathbf{A}$ was added to an ethanolic solution of 7.96 g $\mathbf{B}$. Compound $\mathbf{B}$ is a well-known ligand, which is composed of three elements: C, H, and P. It has 11.81% of P by mass and a threefold symmetry axis. The resulting mixture was refluxed for about two hours, yielding 6.18 g of a dark red compound $\mathbf{C}$ with 88% yield.

Note: A threefold symmetry axis is an imaginary line through an object around which it can be rotated by 120° and appear unchanged. For example, a threefold symmetry axis is present in the molecule of ammonia:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-21-fig1.png

1. Identify the formulae of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{M}$, if each coefficient in the synthesis reaction is lower than 5.

2. Write the equation for the synthesis of compound $\mathbf{C}$.

Compound $\mathbf{C}$ is a well-known catalyst in the hydrogenation of alkenes:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-21-fig2.png

One example of the product [structure printed inline, reproduced below] has a maximum of one plane of symmetry.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-21-fig3.png

Note: A plane of symmetry is an imaginary plane that divides an object into two mirror-image halves. For example, the molecule of water has two planes of symmetry:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-21-fig4.png

The mass spectrum of this product is shown below. The three peaks at $m/z$ 41, 91, and 119 are noticeably more intense than the others, and two of them correspond to fragments containing different aromatic rings.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-21-fig5.png

3. Draw the structures of the cations that correspond to those 3 peaks.

4. Draw the structure of the product.

5. Find the intensity ratio $[\mathrm{M}]^+:[\mathrm{M}+1]^+$ in the mass spectrum if the relative atomic mass of carbon is 12.011 and it consists of two stable isotopes.

In the catalytic system, a minor product $\mathbf{D}$ can be formed according to the reaction:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-21-fig6.png

6. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{D}$ (you do not have to show stereochemistry).

After several catalytic cycles, the catalyst loses its activity due to the decomposition of $\mathbf{C}$, forming products $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{M}$. $\mathbf{F}$ is produced by the oxidation of $\mathbf{B}$ with atmospheric $\ce{O2}$.

7. Identify the formulae of $\mathbf{F}$ and write the equation for the oxidation reaction of $\mathbf{B}$.

Catalyst $\mathbf{C}$ can catalyse other types of reactions. For example, $\mathbf{C}$ was used to catalyse a [2+2+2] cycloaddition reaction in the synthesis of Heilonine:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-21-fig7.png

8. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{H}$–$\mathbf{J}$ (you do not have to show stereochemistry).

problems.title: Transition metals in organometallic catalysis
problems.problem:
Problem 22. Transition metals in organometallic catalysis

Organometallic chemistry studies various aspects of compounds containing a metal–carbon bond. Many transition metal (TM) complexes are of fundamental importance due to their role in industrial catalytic processes.

There are many parameters that should be considered when choosing a TM complex for a particular process, and four significant ones are:

• oxidation state (OS) of the metal in the complex,
• coordination number (CN),
• total number of valence electrons (VE), which is the sum of the number of the metal d-electrons and electrons provided by the ligands coordinated to the metal,
• overall net charge of the species that contains the transition metal.

1. For complexes $\mathbf{1}$–$\mathbf{4}$, calculate OS, CN, and VE.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig1.png

These parameters can change every time a TM complex undergoes different transformations. Below you can find the most important elementary steps that are essential for most TM-catalysed reactions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig2.png

2. Find the unknown parameters (OS, CN, VE) for complexes that underwent the mentioned elementary steps.

The parameters mentioned are quite important for catalytic transformations mediated by TM complexes. As such, $\mathbf{3}$ can catalyse the transformation of n-octene to n-octane via the catalytic cycle depicted below. S is a solvent that can coordinate to a metal with a pair of electrons.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig3.png

3. Decipher the structures $\mathbf{5}$–$\mathbf{10}$ and specify the unknown parameters (OS, CN, VE) for them if the overall charge is zero for all the metal species.

4. Determine the structure of molecule $\mathbf{11}$.

Oxidative addition of hydrogen can occur not only from complex $\mathbf{3}$, but also from another complex. This complex is a neutral 14-electron species (which are generally more reactive), and it is obtained after one ligand leaves complex $\mathbf{3}$. Thus, an alternative catalytic cycle can be proposed for the above transformation.

5. Suggest an alternative catalytic cycle that involves the aforementioned 14-electron complex. Specify the unknown parameters (OS, CN, VE) for the intermediates in your catalytic cycle (VE should be equal or greater than 14 for all the intermediates).

Some ligands can coordinate to metals in different ways. One example of such a case is the coordination of alkenes to a metal. Specifically, alkene $\mathbf{12}$ can coordinate to complex $\mathbf{13}$ without much disturbance of the C=C bond to produce $\mathbf{14}$ or via a metallacyclopropane mode to produce $\mathbf{15}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig4.png

6. Find the unknown parameters (OS, CN, VE) for complexes $\mathbf{14}$ and $\mathbf{15}$ if the OS, CN, and VE are given for $\mathbf{13}$ in the scheme above.

The geometry of complex $\mathbf{16}$ $\mathrm{RhCp(H_2CCH_2)(F_2CCF_2)}$ is shown below. The colour codes of the atoms are as follows: Rh – violet, C – grey, F – green, H – white.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig5.png

7. Based on this geometry, find the unknown parameters (OS and VE) for complex $\mathbf{16}$. Hint: the C–C bond lengths for free olefins are shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig6.png

8. Specify which mode of coordination is utilised by ethylene and tetrafluoroethylene in structure $\mathbf{16}$. Choose from the following options:

a) alkene coordination (similar to structure $\mathbf{14}$);
b) metallocyclopropane coordination (similar to structure $\mathbf{15}$);
c) no coordination.

Sometimes, the transition metal complex carries an overall charge (positive or negative).

9. Compare the following two complexes: $\mathrm{IrCl(PPh_3)_3}$ ($\mathbf{17}$) and $\mathrm{Ir(COD)(py)(PCy_3)(PF_6)}$ ($\mathbf{18}$). Calculate the unknown parameters (OS, CN, VE) for $\mathbf{18}$ if OS, CN, and VE are the same for $\mathbf{17}$ and $\mathbf{18}$. Specify the overall charge of the metal part with the charge as presented in the example below for $\ce{AlCl4-}$ and $\ce{AlCl3}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig7.png

SET is a single electron transfer process and it it known that metal complexes can take part in it. An example of SET is shown below where donor D has a lone pair and during SET it gives one electron to acceptor A. This process produces a radical cation and a radical anion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig8.png

10. Find the unknown parameters (OS, CN, VE) for complexes below that underwent SET process. Specify overall charges $k$ and $m$ for the new complexes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig9.png

Some of metal complexes are useful photocatalysts. For instance, previously discussed complex $\mathbf{4}$ can be applied for C–H-functionalisation of tertiary amines such as $\mathbf{20}$ with electron poor arenes such as $\mathbf{19}$. The catalytic cycle for the synthesis of $\mathbf{21}$ is shown below and it consists of two SET processes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-22-fig10.png

12. Determine the unknown structures $\mathbf{22}$–$\mathbf{25}$. Intermediate $\mathbf{4^*}$ is an excited state of complex $\mathbf{4}$. Calculate OS, CN, and VE for $\mathbf{22}$, and show the overall charge of $\mathbf{22}$.

problems.title: HAT and XAT (HalAT)
problems.problem:
Problem 23. HAT and XAT (HalAT)

Note: Natural abundances of some isotopes are given at the end of the problem.

Transition metal-catalysed reactions can be versatile and unique. As such, nickel complex $\mathbf{4}$ can catalyse the transformation of compounds $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$ into product $\mathbf{3}$ as described below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-23-fig1.png

1. The mass spectra (MS) of $\mathbf{2}$ and $\mathbf{3}$ are shown (electron impact ionisation method). Determine the structures of $\mathbf{2}$ and $\mathbf{3}$.

MS of $\mathbf{2}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-23-fig2.png

MS of $\mathbf{3}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-23-fig3.png

Complex $\mathbf{4}$ can be obtained via the following reaction. OS is the oxidation state of a metal in a complex; CN is the coordination number, and VE is the total number of valence electrons.
