problems.title: Anticancer complexes
problems.problem:
Problem 24. Anticancer complexes

The World Health Organisation reports that 20% of population will suffer from cancer in their lifetime. Today, cancer treatment is increasingly personalised being a combination of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy with biomarker-guided targeted drugs and immunotherapies that can give long-lasting responses for some cancers. In this problem, we will consider some types of drugs used in cancer treatment.

Part 1. Platinum complexes

Platinum complexes show antitumor activity by covalently binding to DNA, thus preventing its replication. The first-generation platinum drug, cis-diaminedichloroplatinum(II) (cisplatin), is efficient against cancer, whereas its trans-isomer (transplatin) is not. One reason for this difference is that cisplatin and transplatin form different types of crosslinks with DNA strands.

There are two possibilities for a complex to bind DNA: intrastrand and interstrand crosslinks through the N7 position of guanine. Intrastrand crosslinks form between two bases of the same DNA strand, while interstrand crosslinks connect one base from one strand to a base on the opposite strand.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-24-fig1.png

1. Using the dot notation shown below, draw the intrastrand and interstrand crosslinks on the given DNA template. State the kind of crosslink that is formed by a) cisplatin; b) transplatin.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-24-fig2.png

2. Deduce the effect of the formation of intrastrand and interstrand crosslinks on the melting temperature, $T_\mathrm{m}$. $T_\mathrm{m}$ is the temperature at which half of DNA duplexes dissociate into single-stranded DNA.

Dicycloplatin, a third-generation platinum-based anticancer drug, was developed to reduce the dose-limiting toxicities that restrict the clinical use of cisplatin. Dicycloplatin crystals precipitate from a saturated aqueous solution containing $\mathbf{Pt\text{-}4}$ and 1,1-cyclobutanedicarboxylic acid ($\mathrm{H_2CBDCA}$) in a 1:1 molar ratio. Dicycloplatin was found to have four hydrogen bonds in one structural unit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-24-fig3.png

3. Draw the structural formulae of particles $\mathbf{Pt\text{-}1}$, $\mathbf{Pt\text{-}2}$, $\mathbf{Pt\text{-}3}$ and $\mathbf{Pt\text{-}4}$. The mass percentage of platinum in $\ce{PtCl4^{2-}}$ to $\mathbf{Pt\text{-}4}$ changes as 57.9% → 27.7% → 40.4% → 73.6% → 52.6%, respectively.

4. Draw the structural formula of dicycloplatin showing the hydrogen bonds.

$\mathbf{Pt\text{-}4}$ (carboplatin) was introduced into clinical use in the late 1980s and has been widely used in cancer treatment. One practical challenge with platinum-based drugs is that, in aqueous solution, they can undergo hydrolysis, which may affect their stability and reactivity.

5. Explain which drug, $\mathbf{Pt\text{-}4}$ or dicycloplatin, is more resistant to hydrolysis in aqueous solution.

Part 2. Camptothecin and its derivatives

Alkaloid camptothecin and its derivatives form another group of drugs that show antitumor activity by inhibiting topoisomerase I, the enzyme that 'untangles' the DNA helix. Total synthesis of camptothecin derivative, $\mathbf{SN\text{-}38}$, was carried out by coupling two building blocks $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{N}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-24-fig4.png

6. Draw the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{G}$ showing stereochemistry, if the step from $\mathbf{B}$ to $\mathbf{C}$ requires an excess of benzyl bromide.

The second part of the synthesis is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-24-fig5.png

7. Draw the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{J}$–$\mathbf{O}$ and $\mathbf{SN\text{-}38}$ showing stereochemistry where applicable.

problems.title: The equilibria in DNA
problems.problem:
Problem 25. The equilibria in DNA

A single-stranded DNA (ss-DNA) molecule can dimerise into a double-stranded one (ds-DNA) in the case that the ss-DNA is complementary to itself. Complementarity arises due to the ability of nitrogenous bases to form hydrogen bonds with each other. As shown below, guanine (G) forms three hydrogen bonds with cytosine (C), whereas adenine (A) forms two hydrogen bonds with thymine (T):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-25-fig1.png

Tetranucleotide 5'-CCGG-3' can dimerise as follows:

$$\begin{array}{c} \text{5'-CCGG-3'} \\ + \\ \text{3'-GGCC-5'} \end{array} \;\rightleftharpoons\; \begin{array}{c} \text{5'-CCGG-3'} \\ \vert\,\vert\,\vert\,\vert \\ \text{3'-GGCC-5'} \end{array}$$

1. Deduce how many tetranucleotides exist that are capable of dimerisation with pairing of all 4 nucleotides in the strands.

Dimerisation of tetranucleotide 5'-CCGG-3' was studied at different temperatures by measuring the absorbance, $A$, of solutions at 280 nm, with total initial concentration of single strands $[\text{ss-DNA}]_0 = 10\,\mathrm{\mu M}$. The results of the experiments were as follows: $A = 0.89$ at $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $A = 1.17$ at $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

2. Calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ and $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^\circ$ values for the dimerisation reaction of tetranucleotide 5'-CCGG-3', if they are independent of temperature and $\varepsilon_\text{ss-DNA} = 2.44\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}\,M^{-1}}$, $\varepsilon_\text{ds-DNA} = 2.93\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}\,M^{-1}}$ at 280 nm for tetranucleotide 5'-CCGG-3', $l = 5\,\mathrm{cm}$.

The melting temperature of ds-DNA, $T_\mathrm{m}$, is the temperature at which half of ds-DNA dissociates into ss-DNA.

3. Calculate $T_\mathrm{m}$ for the double strand of tetranucleotide 5'-CCGG-3' when the total concentration of single strands, $[\text{ss-DNA}]_0 = 10\,\mathrm{\mu M}$.

Another driving force for ds-DNA formation is the $\pi$-$\pi$-stacking between the nitrogenous bases in addition to hydrogen bonds. To estimate the contribution of the $\pi$-$\pi$-stacking to the stabilisation energy of ds-DNA, the dimerisation of oligonucleotides 5'-ACCGG-3', 5'-CCGGT-3', and 5'-ACCGGT-3' was investigated.

4. Deduce what dimers do oligonucleotides 5'-ACCGG-3', 5'-CCGGT-3', 5'-ACCGGT-3' form. Draw them schematically.

The $T_\mathrm{m}$ of these oligonucleotides has the following dependence on the total concentration of single strands:

$$\frac{1}{T_\mathrm{m}} = k\times\ln[ss-\mathrm{DNA}]_0 + b$$

The following table shows $k$ and $b$ parameters for some oligonucleotides:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{Oligonucleotide} & \boldsymbol{k}\ \mathbf{/\ K^{-1}} & \boldsymbol{b}\ \mathbf{/\ K^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{5'-ACCGG-3'} & -5.15\times10^{-5} & 2.76\times10^{-3} \\ \text{5'-CCGGT-3'} & -4.80\times10^{-5} & 2.78\times10^{-3} \end{array}$$

5. Calculate the $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ values for the dimerisation reactions of oligonucleotides 5'-ACCGG-3' and 5'-CCGGT-3', assuming they are independent of temperature.

6. Determine the $\pi$-$\pi$-stacking energies for A-CG and T-GC stackings (see figure below). Assume that there is no $\pi$-$\pi$ stacking in ss-DNA.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-25-fig2.png

A-CG $\pi$-$\pi$ stacking (left); T-GC $\pi$-$\pi$ stacking (right)

7. Predict the $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ value for the dimerisation reaction of oligonucleotide 5'-ACCGGT-3', if the total hydrogen bond energy in an A=T pair is $28842.0\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$.

problems.title: Sensing of acetaldehyde
problems.problem:
Problem 26. Sensing of acetaldehyde

Acetaldehyde ($\mathbf{AA}$) is a reactive aldehyde primarily produced in cells as a metabolic intermediate during ethanol oxidation:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-26-fig1.png

ADH – alcohol dehydrogenase, ALDH – aldehyde dehydrogenase.

Excess $\mathbf{AA}$, often resulting from impaired $\mathbf{AA}$ detoxification, leads to aberrant DNA, protein, and/or lipid damage, and increases risk of diseases such as cancer, hepatitis, and cirrhosis. Recently, G. Li, C. Chang et al. reported the development of a highly selective method for the detection of $\mathbf{AA}$ in living cells. In this system, $\mathbf{AAP\text{-}1}$ reacts with $\mathbf{AA}$ to form a fluorescent product $\mathbf{P}$ by the following mechanism:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-26-fig2.png

$\mathbf{A}$ is an enamine, $\mathbf{C}$ is an inorganic byproduct, and $\mathbf{P}$ contains the same number of rings as $\mathbf{AAP\text{-}1}$. The above mechanism includes [4+2] and retro [4+2] cycloaddition reactions:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-26-fig3.png

1. Draw the structures of intermediates $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{B}$, product $\mathbf{P}$, and determine the inorganic byproduct $\mathbf{C}$. Note: Molecular ions of $\mathbf{AAP\text{-}1}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ in mass spectra have peaks with masses of 494 and 492, respectively.

Although biological fluids contain different types of aldehydes and ketones, $\mathbf{AAP\text{-}1}$ reacts only with $\mathbf{AA}$.

2. Give the reason why formaldehyde (methanal) and methylglyoxal (2-oxopropanal) do not react with $\mathbf{AAP\text{-}1}$.

Aldehydes and ketones on relatively large molecules also do not react with $\mathbf{APP\text{-}1}$ due to the steric effects during transformation of enamine $\mathbf{A}$ to [4+2] cycloaddition product $\mathbf{B}$. The following table shows the [4+2] cycloaddition reaction participants' Gibbs energies relative to reagents for $\mathbf{AA}$ ($\mathbf{A}$, transition state #1 and $\mathbf{B}$) and hexanal ($\mathbf{A'}$, transition state #2 and $\mathbf{B'}$):

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \textbf{Species} & \Delta\boldsymbol{G}\ /\ \mathbf{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & \textbf{Species} & \Delta\boldsymbol{G}\ /\ \mathbf{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \text{enamine } \mathbf{A} & -8.36 & \text{enamine } \mathbf{A'} & -12.96 \\ \text{transition state \#1} & 63.95 & \text{transition state \#2} & 68.13 \\ \text{cycloaddition product } \mathbf{B} & -21.74 & \text{cycloaddition product } \mathbf{B'} & -19.23 \end{array}$$

3. Calculate the Gibbs energy changes ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) for processes $\mathbf{A}\rightarrow\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{A'}\rightarrow\mathbf{B'}$. Conclude whether these reactions are spontaneous.

4. Calculate the ratio of the rate constants corresponding to the $\mathbf{A}\rightarrow\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{A'}\rightarrow\mathbf{B'}$ transformations at 310 K. Assume that in both reactions pre-exponential constant is the same, and that activation energy is equal to activation Gibbs energy.

The excitation and emission spectra of product $\mathbf{P}$ are shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-26-fig4.png

5. Match the spectral lines $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ with excitation and emission processes.

The fluorescence intensity, $F$, of $\mathbf{P}$ depends linearly on its concentration: $F = F_0 + k[\mathbf{P}]$. The following table shows the fluorescence intensities (in arbitrary units) of solutions with different concentrations of $\mathbf{P}$:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} F\ /\ \text{arb.u.} & 92.50 & 97.50 & 102.50 & 107.50 \\ \hline [\mathbf{P}]\ /\ \mathrm{\mu M} & 10 & 20 & 30 & 40 \end{array}$$

6. Calculate the values of $F_0$ and $k$.

The lower detection limit of the fluorescence intensity of $\mathbf{P}$ is 90.65 arb.u. In the absence of ethanol, the concentration of $\mathbf{AA}$ can very quickly decrease due to enzyme ALDH ($r_\mathrm{max} = 4.1\,\mathrm{mM\,min^{-1}}$, $K_\mathrm{M} = 0.2\,\mathrm{\mu M}$).

7. Calculate the time needed (in seconds) for the fluorescence intensity of the product of $\mathbf{AA}$ with $\mathbf{AAP\text{-}1}$ to decrease from 137.50 arb.u. to 90.65 arb.u. in the absence of ethanol. Note: ALDH obeys Michaelis–Menten kinetics.

Adding inhibitors to cell cultures where the concentration of $\mathbf{AA}$ is determined using $\mathbf{AAP\text{-}1}$ affects the intensity of fluorescence:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \begin{array}{c}\text{Control}\\ \text{(no inhibitor, no EtOH)}\end{array} & \text{EtOH} & \begin{array}{c}\text{EtOH + Fomepizole}\\ \text{(ADH inhibitor)}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{EtOH + CVT-10216}\\ \text{(ALDH inhibitor)}\end{array} \\ \hline F_1 & F_2 & F_3 & F_4 \end{array}$$

8. Arrange $F_1$–$F_4$ in order of increasing fluorescence intensity.

problems.title: Archaeal metabolism
problems.problem:
Problem 27. Archaeal metabolism

Archaea, along with bacteria and eukaryotes, constitute a distinct domain of living organisms. Archaea were previously grouped with bacteria, but this classification is now considered obsolete, as it has been established that archaea have their own independent evolutionary history and are characterised by many biochemical features that distinguish them from other life forms. Archaea appeared on Earth 3.5–4 billion years ago during the Archean Eon and have evolved continuously since then.

1. Select from the options provided a measurable, planetary-scale quantitative parameter that has not changed within reasonable accuracy throughout the entire evolution of archaea and to changes to which they can quickly adapt:

a) Chemical parameters: the concentration of a gaseous substance in the atmosphere (oxygen, nitrogen or carbon dioxide), the composition of the environment (reservoirs) as the ratio of various compounds (salinity, pH, buffer capacity), etc.

b) Physical parameters: temperature, atmospheric pressure, radioactivity, gravitational force, total luminosity of the Sun.

To demonstrate the differences between the three main domains of living organisms, one can cite as an example the quinone derivatives that play a role in oxidation-reduction processes in archaea (menaquinone MK-7), bacteria (menaquinone MK-10), and eukaryotes (ubiquinone, presented in the form of coenzyme $\mathrm{Q_{10}}$, $\mathrm{CoQ_{10}}$):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-27-fig1.png

2. Draw the structure of the two-electron reduction product of MK-7.

The standard biochemical redox potentials, $E^{\circ\prime}$, of some redox pairs are given in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{Redox pair} & \boldsymbol{E}^{\circ\prime}\ \mathbf{/\ V} \\ \hline 0.5\,\ce{O2}/\ce{H2O} & 0.82 \\ \text{cytochrome } c\ (+3)/\ \text{cytochrome } c\ (+2) & 0.22 \\ \mathrm{CoQ_{10}}/\mathrm{CoQ_{10}H_2} & 0.10 \\ \text{fumarate/succinate} & 0.03 \\ \text{MK-10}/\mathrm{MKH_2}\text{-10} & -0.07 \\ \text{acetaldehyde/ethanol} & -0.20 \end{array}$$

3. Based on the information provided, qualitatively explain why menaquinone was displaced by ubiquinone in the ancestors of modern eukaryotes and is currently not found in eukaryotes, with a few exceptions.

Natural ubiquinol (reduced form of ubiquinone), obtained from eukaryotic cell culture, is a hydrophobic unsaturated compound that can be incorporated into the standard method for determining bromine value (strictly in the dark!).

4. Suggest at least two chemical structural features of natural samples of ubiquinol that distinguish it from, for example, the triacylglycerol of linoleic acid, often called linolein, and that should be considered when analysing the obtained results of interaction with molecular bromine.

The unique habitat of archaea, from their very inception, has led some species to possess an enzyme involved in the metabolism of extremely intriguing substrates – substances $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$, which exhibit similar chemical properties. Thus, structural isomers $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ react in vitro with menaquinol ($\mathrm{MKH_2}$-7), catalysed by an enzyme commonly referred to as $\mathbf{Z}$-reductase, according to the following reaction equations:

$$\mathbf{X} + \mathrm{MKH_2} \rightarrow \mathbf{X1} + \mathbf{X2} + \mathrm{MK} \qquad (1)$$

$$\mathbf{Y} + \mathrm{MKH_2} \rightarrow \mathbf{Y1} + \mathbf{Y2} + \mathrm{MK} \qquad (2)$$

For the molar masses of unknown substances rounded to the nearest integer, three strict inequalities hold: $M(\mathbf{X}) < 250\,\mathrm{g/mol}$; $M(\mathbf{X1}) > M(\mathbf{X2})$; $M(\mathbf{Y1}) > M(\mathbf{Y2})$.

5. Using only the information above, find the upper limit of the range of possible integer molar masses of $\mathbf{X2}$.

$\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X2}$ each contain 22% of element $\mathbf{E1}$ and 1.0% of element $\mathbf{E2}$ by mass, while $\mathbf{X}$ contains 23.4% oxygen by mass.

6. Calculate the percentage by mass of $\mathbf{E2}$ in $\mathbf{X}$ to the nearest whole number.

7. Without disclosing any elements other than $\mathbf{E2}$, narrow the range of possible whole-number molecular masses of $\mathbf{X2}$ as much as possible, taking into account the mass fractions given above.

8. Suggest two potential explanations for the apparent logical inconsistency between the equal mass fractions of elements in two compounds despite different whole-number molecular masses; discriminate against one of them for the purposes of the problem.

Despite the lack of any direct information, the problem statement provides sufficient information to unambiguously determine the structures of $\mathbf{Y1}$ and $\mathbf{Y2}$.

9. Draw the molecular formulae of $\mathbf{Y1}$ and $\mathbf{Y2}$, and propose the structural formulae of substrates $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$.

Compounds $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, unlike compound $\mathbf{Z}$, are not found in nature.

10. Based on the principles of enzymatic catalysis, propose the molecular formula of $\mathbf{Z}$.

Surprisingly, there is a substrate $\mathbf{W}$ that, when catalysed by the enzyme $\mathbf{Z}$-reductase, yields two products with identical molecular masses when rounded to the nearest whole number.

11. Suggest two variants of the molecular formula of $\mathbf{W}$, both containing $\mathbf{E1}$.

12. Describe the metabolic characteristics and habitat of the archaea species whose metabolic fragment was discussed above.

Most of the IChO 2026 problem authors are recent medalists of the International Chemistry Olympiads. Try testing your skills by creating an Olympiad problem based on the composition you've just solved. Your goal is to simplify this problem somewhat, guiding the participants' thinking toward the correct answers.

13. Analyse the reaction equations (1) and (2) and, based on the interesting coincidences/patterns you've identified, offer two hints to make the problem easier for the solvers without oversimplifying it.

problems.title: Non-archea-typal form of life
problems.problem:
Problem 28. Non-archea-typal form of life

Molecule $\mathbf{A}$, with the formula $\mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_y\mathrm{O}_z$, where $x, y, z \in \mathbb{N}$, is found in some fossil deposits (such as oil), and serves as a biomarker for the presence of archaea in a particular region of the planet in the past.

Molecule $\mathbf{A}$ can be represented using a simplified version of knot notation: each covalent bond, regardless of the type of atoms forming it, is represented by a strand, with the atoms themselves being the knots at the ends of one or more strands. The ethane molecule, written in this notation, looks like this:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-28-fig1.png

Using scissors, it takes 123 cuts to completely separate molecule $\mathbf{A}$ into individual nodes along the strands (the same operation with ethane requires 7 cuts). Note that two nodes are separated by the number of cuts equal to the number of strands between them (for example, a double bond requires two cuts). It is known that there is a single cut that bisects the molecule $\mathbf{A}$ into two identical fragments (similarly to ethane, as shown by the dashed line in the figure above).

1. Based on the data presented above, decide whether the indices $x$, $y$, and $z$ are even or odd numbers or can be either of these. Is it possible to decide wither $x \le 60$ or not? For $x = 60$, suggest two fundamentally different theoretically possible structures that meet the conditions (ignore the reality of their existence; this is just a theoretical concept).

Hint: Using the method of incomplete mathematical induction, try to consider the dependence of the number of bonds on the molecular formula for the first members of the homologous series of alkanes or saturated alcohols, as well as the acetylene-ethylene-ethane series.

2. Deduce whether there exists a theoretical acyclic form of $\mathbf{A}$ that can be divided into two identical fragments: a) by two cuts; b) by three cuts. If you answered yes, propose a molecular formula supporting your choice.

It is known that $\mathbf{A}$ has a molecular mass, rounded to the nearest whole number, of 595 g/mol.

3. Without guessing, uniquely find the molecular formula of $\mathbf{A}$.

Molecule $\mathbf{A}$, containing 8 stereocentres, can be cut along the strands into two types of fragments (fragments of the same type are defined as those that can be superimposed). Note that the cuts are made at equal distances from each other (the shortest number of strands between them, excluding branches), and one of the cuts coincides in location with the one that bisects $\mathbf{A}$ into two identical fragments as described above. Based on the experiment, $\mathbf{A}$ can be represented as a sequence of two fragments, $c$ and $d$, as $dccccccccd$.

4. State whether the hydroxy groups in $\mathbf{A}$ can be: a) secondary; b) tertiary? If so, draw the corresponding structural formula(e) representing the cuts by dashed lines. Showing stereochemistry is not required.

5. Draw all possible structural formulae of $\mathbf{A}$ that form the $dccccccccd$ pattern with cuts spaced apart by at least three intact strands.

6. Knowing the prevalence of certain structural biochemical motifs, choose the variant(s) of $\mathbf{A}$ (from those found in question 5) that best fit(s) to the metabolites of living things.

$\mathbf{A}$ is formed by the hydrolysis of compound $\mathbf{B}$ ($\mathrm{C}_k\mathrm{H}_l\mathrm{O}_m$), which is involved in the formation of membranes in most archaeal species. The number of covalent bonds ($n$) in $\mathbf{B}$ is in the range $261 \le n \le 265$. The hydrolysis process is abiotic in nature and is a classic example of diagenesis (the long-term decomposition of organic material in geological deposits). The reaction equation for the decomposition of $\mathbf{B}$ can be written as follows:

$$\mathbf{B} + 4\,\ce{H2O} \rightarrow 2\mathbf{A} + 2\mathbf{C}$$

Note:

• Optically inactive $\mathbf{C}$ has a symmetry axis passing through one of the carbon atoms;
• The molecular formula of both $\mathbf{C}$ residues in $\mathbf{B}$ is the same.

7. Prove, without determining the formulae, that $l \le 2k$.

8. Find all structural formulae of $\mathbf{C}$ that satisfy the above condition.

By combining pairwise the structures of $\mathbf{A}$ obtained in question 6 with the structures of $\mathbf{C}$ from question 8, we can see that one variant of $\mathbf{C}$ yields more structural isomers of $\mathbf{B}$ than all the other variants of $\mathbf{C}$ combined. This variant of $\mathbf{C}$ is found in archaeal lipids.

9. Find the final structure of $\mathbf{C}$ and determine the number of structural isomers of $\mathbf{B}$. Draw the structural formulae of any two isomers of $\mathbf{B}$.

10. Explain why the hydrolysis of $\mathbf{B}$ takes long and is not catalysed by enzymes of other microorganisms.

It is known that esterified derivatives of $\mathbf{B}$ are located in the membranes of some species of archaea in two fundamentally different ways ($O$- and $U$-conformations), shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-28-fig2.png

11. Of the $\mathbf{B}$ isomers proposed earlier, select those that can form similar membrane types. Give the advantage that such membranes have over those formed by bacterial and eukaryotic cells.

12. Suggest two explanations why the evolution chose $\mathbf{C}$ for the synthesis of $\mathbf{B}$, rather than compounds from the same group with lower molecular weights.

13. Based on the information obtained in questions 11 and 12, narrow down as much as possible the range of isomers of $\mathbf{B}$ that meet the biological requirements of archaea.

Archaea of the phylum Thaumarchaeota adapt to rising environmental temperatures through a process virtually unique to them. It is known as homeoviscous adaptation, which involves modifying the structure of $\mathbf{B}$ by forming saturated cycles of either only five or only six carbon atoms (but not spirocycles) and, as a consequence, the biosynthesis of a separate family of lipids ($\mathbf{D}$).

It is known that this modification of the structure of $\mathbf{B}$ is catalysed by two enzymes that are extremely similar in function and structure and exhibit strict positional specificity. Theoretically, based on the number of suitable loci, there could be up to four such enzymes, which would lead to an expansion of the $\mathbf{D}$ family (however, the third and fourth enzymes are not present in nature).

14. Determine the molecular formula of lipid $\mathbf{D1}$, found in archaea, which withstands extreme temperature conditions better than other members of the family.

It is known that symmetrical molecule $\mathbf{D1}$ contains 26 stereocentres.

15. How many structural isomers that meet the condition can be proposed for $\mathbf{D1}$? Draw any one of them. In this case, keep in mind that it is necessary to carefully analyse which carbon atoms can participate in the closure of the hydrocarbon ring, whether this option leads to an increase in the number of chiral centres and, if so, by what value.

problems.title: Archaea-ology
problems.problem:
Problem 29. Archaea-ology

Structural differences between biopolymers form one of fundamental criteria by which life forms are classified into separate domains. Biopolymers $\mathbf{A}$ (found in some archaea) and $\mathbf{B}$ (found in bacteria) have molecular weights over 100 kDa. The biopolymer fragments important for formation of spatial structures are shown below as I-shaped sequences of monomers ($\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$) linked by covalent bonds.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-29-fig1.png

Each of the above fragments can be separated from the respective polymers ($\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{B}$) by cleaving four bonds.

1. The molecular masses of all $\mathbf{X}_i$ were rounded to the nearest integer. Determine whether the difference between the molecular masses of the fragment from $\mathbf{A}$ and the fragment from $\mathbf{B}$ is an even or odd number or can be any of these.

The ratio of all monomers forming the biopolymer $\mathbf{B}$ is close to equimolar.

2. Propose the regular two-dimensional structures of biopolymers $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. Note that $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ contain no monomers other than those shown in the figure.

Hint: It may be useful to redraw the I-shaped fragments with $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$ depicted as dots of different colours.

A set of 6 molecular formulae is needed to be able to describe any $\mathbf{X}_i$ of $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$. Note: the $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$ monomers might be both D- and L-compounds.

3. Based only on the information given above, choose the theoretically correct statements from the given hereunder:

a) $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$ can belong to different classes of biomolecules;
b) Some of $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$ are isomers;
c) Some of $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$ contain phosphorus;
d) Some of $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$ are interclass isomers;
e) 50% of $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$ are homologs.

In fact, only the first two statements are correct for $\mathbf{X_1}$–$\mathbf{X_8}$.

4. State whether it is now possible to determine unambiguously the nature of biopolymers $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

Any of the fragments (from $\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{B}$) can be divided into three pairs of smaller fragments containing at least two monomers linked together. The molecular mass of any of these resulting fragments (after rounding) belongs to the set: 217, 218, 275, 642 and 700. In $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, monomers with identical molecular masses do not form covalent bonds with each other, and $M(\mathbf{X_6}) > M(\mathbf{X_2})$.

5. Determine unambiguously the molecular formulae of as many monomers as possible. If you fail doing so, determine the molecular masses of the monomers without assigning them to specific $\mathbf{X}_i$.

The sums of the molecular masses of all fragments formed from $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, rounded to the nearest integer, are the same, 2270 g/mol.

6. Explain why these sums are equal. Choose the correct statement(s):

a) occasionally;
b) because the fragments from $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are isomers;
c) due to evolution reasons (only polymers with such molecular masses are functional).

7. Determine the molecular formulae of the yet unknown monomers.

Monomer $\mathbf{X_1}$ is synthesised from the product of photosynthesis, substance $\mathbf{D}$, via the following biochemical pathway:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-29-fig2.png

where CoA is coenzyme A, UDP is uridine diphosphate, UTP is uridine triphosphate, and PPi is pyrophosphate.

It is known that:

• $\mathbf{F}$ reacts with the Tollens reagent;
• $\mathbf{X_1}$ molecule is formed by atoms of four elements (C, H, N, and O);
• $\mathbf{X_1}$ contains 8 carbon atoms;
• Only two carbon atoms are involved in transformations;
• Three pairs can be arranged from compounds $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{X_7}$, and $\mathbf{X_7'}$. The molecular masses of these pairs differ by 1.

8. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{D}$–$\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{X_1}$. Explain how you decided which isomer is encoded by $\mathbf{D}$ and which by $\mathbf{E}$.

To finally identify the structures of polymers $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, previously unidentified fragments $\mathbf{A\text{-}1}$ and $\mathbf{B\text{-}1}$ were isolated. They were methylated on alcoholic hydroxy groups, followed by exhaustive hydrolysis. In the case of $\mathbf{B}$, this resulted in the formation of the 3,4,6-tri-O-methyl derivative of $\mathbf{X_1}$, the 1,4,6-tri-O-methyl derivative of $\mathbf{X_1}$, and the 6-mono-O-methyl derivative of $\mathbf{X_6}$. For $\mathbf{A}$, this resulted in the formation of the 1,4,6-tri-O-methyl derivative of $\mathbf{X_1}$, the 3,4,6-tri-O-methyl derivative of $\mathbf{X_1}$, and the 4-mono-O-methyl derivative of $\mathbf{X_2}$.

9. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A\text{-}1}$ and $\mathbf{B\text{-}1}$, designating the unknown substituents as $\mathrm{R}_i$.

Complete acidic hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A\text{-}1}$ and $\mathbf{B\text{-}1}$, followed by oxidation with $\ce{HIO4}$, leads to the formation of acetaldehyde in the amount equimolar to that of the starting fragment for only one of $\mathbf{A\text{-}1}$ and $\mathbf{B\text{-}1}$.

10. Propose the complete structural formulae of $\mathbf{A\text{-}1}$ and $\mathbf{B\text{-}1}$.

problems.title: Pilaf ingredients
problems.problem:
Problem 30. Pilaf ingredients

Pilaf is one of the most delicious, traditional meals in Uzbekistan. We asked a chef who works in Besh Qozon, a famous restaurant, how they make pilaf so delicious. The chef described the procedure as follows:

"Oil is first heated in a kazan. Chopped onions are fried until they reach a uniform golden-brown color. Pieces of meat are then added and cooked until they develop a caramelised surface. Afterwards, sliced carrots are introduced, and the mixture is seasoned with black pepper and cumin. Water is added, whole garlic bulbs are placed on top, and the mixture is simmered until the meat becomes tender. Subsequently, pre-washed rice is added in a separate upper layer without stirring. Additional water is poured carefully to cover the rice. The mixture is cooked until all the water is absorbed. Finally, the kazan is covered, and the pilaf is allowed to steam for approximately 30 minutes. After gentle mixing, the pilaf is ready to be served".

One of the key aromatic components of pilaf is cumin. Its characteristic flavour is largely due to the presence of the compound cuminaldehyde. This aldehyde can be obtained synthetically starting from benzene, isopropyl chloride, dimethylformamide, and appropriate inorganic reagents.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-30-fig1.png

1. Suggest the synthesis scheme for cuminaldehyde using the reagents mentioned above.

The monomer $\mathbf{X}$ of the major polymeric compound present in rice undergoes several transformations during cooking. These reactions lead to the formation of volatile and non-volatile products that contribute to the characteristic aroma and flavour of the dish. The synthesis of one of these products is shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-30-fig2.png

Hints:

• Among $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{D}$ only compound $\mathbf{D}$ contains a ring.
• $\mathbf{D}$ does not have any acyclic tautomers.
• $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are tautomers.

2. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ without stereochemistry details.

The hydrolysis of the amide bond in the main component $\mathbf{Z}$ of black pepper produces compounds $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$. Upon oxidative ozonolysis, acyclic compound $\mathbf{F}$, having one oxygen-containing group, yields an equimolar mixture of $\mathrm{C}_\alpha\mathrm{H}_\beta\mathrm{O}_\gamma$ ($\mathbf{F_1}$) and $\mathrm{C}_\delta\mathrm{H}_\varepsilon\mathrm{O}_\alpha$ ($\mathbf{F_2}$), where $\alpha \ne \beta \ne \gamma \ne \delta \ne \varepsilon$.

It is also known that:

• The indexes $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are members of a geometric progression (not exactly in this order) and $\delta + \alpha = \varepsilon$;
• The total number ($N$) of all atoms in molecules $\mathbf{F_1}$ and $\mathbf{F_2}$ is an even number less than 45.

3. a) Using mathematical logic and chemical considerations, rigorously prove that the coefficients in compounds $\mathbf{F_1}$ and $\mathbf{F_2}$ ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$) are even numbers.

b) Find the molecular formulae of $\mathbf{F_1}$ and $\mathbf{F_2}$.

The $\mathbf{F_1}$ and $\mathbf{F_2}$ structures contain three types of hydrogen atoms and at least one plane of symmetry, while these compounds lack stereocentres and alcohol groups.

4. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{F_1}$, $\mathbf{F_2}$, and $\mathbf{F}$.

Combustion of 1.000 g of $\mathbf{E}$ at high temperature gives 3.0385 g of a gaseous mixture. Passing this mixture through solid sodium hydroxide increases the mass of the solid by 2.9470 g. $\mathbf{E}$ ($w(\mathrm{O}) = 20.92\%$) has a trisubstituted aromatic ring.

5. Determine the empirical formula of $\mathbf{E}$.

The biosynthesis of $\mathbf{E}$ from L-tyrosine is shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-30-fig3.png

Hints:

• $\mathbf{G}$ contains an aldehyde group.
• The initial hydroxy group in L-tyrosine is unchanged during the biosynthesis of $\mathbf{E}$.
• $\mathbf{I}$ is an ortho-quinone derivative.

6. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{E}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$.

Numerous peptides and amino acids are contained in meat. A non-canonical $\alpha$-amino acid $\mathbf{W}$ is one of these. The reaction of $\mathbf{W}$ with $\ce{NaIO4}$ yields a mixture of formaldehyde ($\ce{CH2O}$) and $\mathbf{K}$. The oxidation of $\mathbf{K}$ with Fehling's reagent, gives the anion of acid $\mathbf{L}$. Acid $\mathbf{L}$ is achiral and has three different hydrogen atom environments.

7. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{J}$, $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{L}$, and $\mathbf{W}$.

Another notable non-canonical amino acid is alliin, $\mathbf{M}$, found in garlic, which serves as the precursor of the compounds responsible for its characteristic odour. Alliin, which contains a stereogenic sulfur atom, can be synthesised from cysteine in two steps. Firstly, cysteine reacts with allyl bromide under mildly basic conditions. The resulting intermediate, $\mathbf{N}$, is then subjected to oxidation of the sulfur atom with $\ce{H2O2}$, yielding $\mathbf{M}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-30-fig4.png

8. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{N}$.

Garlic also contains several other interesting molecules, e.g. four compounds $\mathbf{P_1}$–$\mathbf{P_4}$, which exhibit structural similarity. Their molar masses are members of an arithmetic progression, in which the first member is $\mathbf{P_1}$. Molar masses of the second and third molecules are $146\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ and $178\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ respectively. Each of them contains at least one terminal C=C bond and possesses two planes of symmetry.

9. Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{P_1}$–$\mathbf{P_4}$, if it is known that $\mathbf{P_1}$ is biosynthesised from alliin.

There are a lot of dishes in the world using the combination of meat, rice, and carrots. However, Pilaf is the only one which utilises yellow carrot. The reason behind the different colour of these carrots is the presence of two pigments – $\beta$-carotene and lutein. In plants, they are synthesised from the tetraterpene, lycopene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2026-30-fig5.png

10. Draw the structures of $\alpha$-, $\gamma$-, $\delta$-, $\varepsilon$-carotenes and zeaxanthin.

11. Determine whether zeaxanthin is optically active or not, justify your answer.

12. Classify Enzymes 1–4 according to the main enzyme classes below:

• Oxidoreductases – Oxidation/reduction reactions.
• Transferases – Transfer of a methyl-, acyl-, amino-, or phosphate group from one substance to another; kinases forming a subclass catalyse the transfer of phosphate group(s) from high-energy phosphorylated species to accepting substrate(s).
• Hydrolases – Hydrolytic formation of two products from a substrate.
• Lyases – Non-hydrolytic addition or removal of groups from substrates, with C–C, C–N, C–O, or C–S bonds cleavage in the latter case.
• Isomerases – Intramolecular rearrangement.
• Ligases – Joining together two molecules by formation of new C–O, C–S, C–N, or C–C bonds with simultaneous breakdown of ATP.

The chef in Besh Qozon did not mention the most important spice used in the preparation of pilaf.

13. Identify this unmentioned spice in Tashkent's pilaf.
